chunks.heading: The question
chunks.title: Chapter 1, The Econometric Question — 1.0 The question
chunks.body:
The Question
Does additional schooling cause higher earnings, or do individuals who obtain more schooling earn more for reasons that schooling did not produce?

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.title: Chapter 1, The Econometric Question — 1.0 Overview
chunks.body: Econometrics is the use of data to answer quantitative questions about the economic world. This chapter introduces no estimation formulae. Its purpose is to establish a single principle on which the remainder of the book depends: data can establish that two variables are associated, but cannot, without further assumptions, establish that one causes the other. The chapter defines the basic objects of the subject — variables, the distinction between a population and a sample, association, and the causal comparison — and introduces the data-handling tools in Python on which later computation rests.

chunks.heading: Data, variables, and averages
chunks.title: Chapter 1, The Econometric Question — 1.1 Data, variables, and averages
chunks.body:
Economic data are typically organized as a table in which each row records one unit of observation — an individual, a firm, a country — and each column records one variable, a measured characteristic that takes different values across units. The following table records two variables, years of schooling and hourly earnings, for five individuals.
individual | years of schooling | hourly earnings ($) |
A | 10 | 14 |
B | 12 | 15 |
C | 12 | 18 |
D | 16 | 24 |
E | 16 | 30 |
The most elementary summary of a variable is its average, or mean: the sum of its values divided by their number. The mean of hourly earnings is
\[ \bar y \;=\; \frac{14+15+18+24+30}{5} \;=\; 20.2 \text{ dollars per hour.} \]
The mean is the foundation of the subject; the estimators developed in later chapters are, in a precise sense, conditional means computed under various assumptions.

chunks.heading: Association
chunks.title: Chapter 1, The Econometric Question — 1.2 Association
chunks.body: To describe the relationship between two variables, compute the mean of one within groups defined by the other. Among the two individuals with twelve years of schooling, mean earnings are \((15+18)/2 = 16.5\); among the two with sixteen years, \((24+30)/2 = 27.0\). Mean earnings rise with schooling. In a representative sample of the labour force this pattern is among the most robust empirical regularities in economics: a positive association between schooling and earnings.

chunks.heading: Definition (Association)
chunks.title: Chapter 1, The Econometric Question — 1.2 Definition (Association)
chunks.body:
Definition 1.1 — Association
Two variables are positively associated if larger values of one tend to occur with larger values of the other, and negatively associated if larger values of one tend to occur with smaller values of the other. Association is a descriptive property of the joint distribution of the variables; it carries no implication about cause.

chunks.heading: The distinction between association and causation
chunks.title: Chapter 1, The Econometric Question — 1.3 The distinction between association and causation
chunks.body:
The observed association admits two fundamentally different explanations, and the data cannot discriminate between them.
Explanation A (a causal effect of schooling). Schooling raises productivity, and higher productivity commands higher earnings. Under this explanation, increasing an individual's schooling would raise that individual's earnings.
Explanation B (selection). Individuals who acquire more schooling differ systematically in other respects — ability, family resources, preferences — that independently raise earnings. Under this explanation, the more-schooled would have earned more regardless of their schooling, and schooling itself need have no effect.
Both explanations imply the same observed table. No quantity computed from these data, and no increase in sample size, distinguishes them. This is the central difficulty of the discipline.

chunks.heading: Key idea (The distinction between association and causation)
chunks.title: Chapter 1, The Econometric Question — 1.3 Key idea (The distinction between association and causation)
chunks.body:
Key Idea
Data identify association. A causal conclusion requires, in addition to the data, an assumption about the process that generated them — specifically, an assumption about how the units being compared differ in their unobserved determinants of the outcome. The credibility of a causal conclusion is the credibility of that assumption.

chunks.heading: The causal comparison and its missing half
chunks.title: Chapter 1, The Econometric Question — 1.4 The causal comparison and its missing half
chunks.body: Define the causal effect of schooling for a single individual as the difference between the earnings that individual would receive with additional schooling and the earnings the same individual would receive without it. These two quantities are the individual's potential outcomes. The difficulty is that, for any individual, only one potential outcome is realized — the one corresponding to the schooling actually obtained — while the other is never observed. The causal effect for an individual is therefore not directly measurable, because one of its two components is missing for every unit.

chunks.heading: Definition (The causal comparison and its missing half)
chunks.title: Chapter 1, The Econometric Question — 1.4 Definition (The causal comparison and its missing half)
chunks.body:
Definition 1.2 — Ceteris paribus effect
The ceteris paribus (other things equal) effect of a variable on an outcome is the change in the outcome produced by a change in that variable while all other determinants of the outcome are held fixed. Estimating such an effect from observational data requires approximating the unobserved potential outcome of each treated unit using the observed outcomes of comparable untreated units.

chunks.heading: The causal comparison and its missing half
chunks.title: Chapter 1, The Econometric Question — 1.4 The causal comparison and its missing half
chunks.body: Every method in this book is a strategy for constructing such comparisons. Their validity rests on the comparability of the treated and untreated units in all respects other than the treatment — a requirement that the subsequent chapters make precise and, by various devices, attempt to satisfy.

chunks.heading: A first map of the strategies
chunks.title: Chapter 1, The Econometric Question — 1.5 A first map of the strategies
chunks.body: It is worth seeing the whole map before studying any single route. The skill the rest of the book builds — and the one the Causal Courtroom arena asks you to practise — is recognising which strategy a given question calls for. You are not yet expected to estimate any of them; you only need to know, in plain terms, what each one does and the situation it fits. Five recur throughout.

chunks.heading: Assumptions (A first map of the strategies)
chunks.title: Chapter 1, The Econometric Question — 1.5 Assumptions (A first map of the strategies)
chunks.body:
The five comparison strategies
Randomized controlled trial (RCT). Decide who is treated by something like a coin flip. Randomization makes the treated and untreated groups comparable in every respect, observed and unobserved, so a plain difference in their average outcomes is already the causal effect. When a real experiment is possible it is the benchmark; the remaining four are devices for imitating it when randomization is not possible.
Controlling for confounders. When the two groups differ in measured characteristics, compare only units that share those characteristics — equivalently, put the characteristics into a regression as control variables. This removes the part of the gap explained by the controls, but is only as credible as the claim that the important confounders are observed. (Chapters 2–6.)
Instrumental variables (IV). When a key confounder is unobserved, find a third variable — an instrument — that nudges the treatment but touches the outcome only through the treatment. The part of the treatment driven by that nudge is as good as random, and reveals the effect. (Chapter 9.)

chunks.heading: Assumptions (A first map of the strategies)
chunks.title: Chapter 1, The Econometric Question — 1.5 Assumptions (A first map of the strategies)
chunks.body:
Difference-in-differences (DiD). When a treatment switches on for one group at a known date, compare the before-to-after change in that group with the change over the same window in a group that was never treated. Subtracting the untreated group's change nets out whatever was trending anyway. (Chapter 12.)
Regression discontinuity (RD). When treatment is assigned by a sharp cutoff in some running variable — a scholarship granted just above a test-score threshold — compare units just above the cutoff with those just below. Being a hair apart on the score, they are otherwise nearly identical, so the jump in outcomes at the cutoff is the effect. (Chapter 13.)

chunks.heading: A first map of the strategies
chunks.title: Chapter 1, The Econometric Question — 1.5 A first map of the strategies
chunks.body: These are not interchangeable. Each buys its credibility with a different assumption, and each suits some questions and not others. The Courtroom puts a causal claim on trial and asks you to call the strategy whose assumption is defensible for that claim — the judgement this entire book is about. You will return to each strategy in depth in its own chapter; for now, the goal is simply to tell them apart.

chunks.heading: Structures of economic data
chunks.title: Chapter 1, The Econometric Question — 1.6 Structures of economic data
chunks.body: The applicable methods depend on the structure of the data, of which four recur throughout the book.

chunks.heading: Assumptions (Structures of economic data)
chunks.title: Chapter 1, The Econometric Question — 1.6 Assumptions (Structures of economic data)
chunks.body:
Data structures
Cross-sectional data: many units observed at a single point in time. The setting of Chapters 2–9 and 14.
Time-series data: a single unit observed at many points in time, in which the ordering of observations is informative. The setting of Chapters 15–16.
Panel (longitudinal) data: many units each observed at several points in time, permitting each unit to be compared with itself across time. The setting of Chapters 10–12.
Pooled cross-sections: independent cross-sectional samples drawn at different times, not following the same units. Employed in Chapter 12.

chunks.heading: Handling data in Python
chunks.title: Chapter 1, The Econometric Question — 1.7 Handling data in Python
chunks.body:
The computations in this book use the pandas library for data manipulation and, in later chapters, statsmodels and scikit-learn for estimation. A dataset is loaded into a DataFrame, the central tabular object, from which rows, columns, and summaries are obtained.
import pandas as pd
# a dataset is a table; each row is one unit of observation, each column a variable
# real datasets load from a file with pd.read_csv("path.csv"); here we build the
# small table from Section 1.1 directly, so the example runs on its own
df = pd.DataFrame({
"schooling": [10, 12, 12, 16, 16],
"earnings": [14, 15, 18, 24, 30],
})
print(df.shape) # (number of rows, number of columns)
print(df.head()) # the first five rows
print(df.describe()) # count, mean, standard deviation, min, max per column
Means, group means, and the correlation between variables — the quantities of Sections 1.1 and 1.2 — are computed directly.
# the average (mean) of a column
print(df["wage"].mean())
# the average of one variable within groups defined by another
print(df.groupby("educ")["wage"].mean())
# a numerical summary of how two variables move together
print(df[["educ", "wage"]].corr())

chunks.title: Chapter 1, The Econometric Question — 1.7 Handling data in Python
chunks.body: The method groupby("educ")["wage"].mean() implements exactly the within-group averaging used above to describe the schooling–earnings association. The demonstration below constructs an illustrative dataset in which the data-generating process is known, so that the association and its components can be examined directly.

chunks.heading: Reading the output (1.6.1 Demonstration)
chunks.title: Chapter 1, The Econometric Question — 1.7 Reading the output (1.6.1 Demonstration)
chunks.body: Reading the output. The constructed data exhibit a clear positive association between schooling and earnings, reproduced both in the group means and in the correlation. Because the data-generating process includes an unobserved determinant of earnings that is itself related to schooling, the association overstates the causal effect — the quantitative analysis of this distortion is the subject of Chapter 3.

chunks.heading: Instructor's take (1.6.1 Demonstration)
chunks.title: Chapter 1, The Econometric Question — 1.7 Instructor's take (1.6.1 Demonstration)
chunks.body:
★ Sharma's Take
A discipline that repays adoption from the outset is to state, before any data are examined, the experiment one would conduct if experimentation were possible. For the schooling question, the experiment is the random assignment of additional schooling to otherwise identical individuals, followed by comparison of their earnings. This hypothetical experiment serves as a standard against which every observational method is to be judged: each technique in this book is an attempt to approximate it when assignment is not under the analyst's control. The formulation also functions as a diagnostic. If the experiment cannot be stated precisely, the causal question itself has not been posed precisely, and no estimation procedure can supply the missing clarity.

chunks.heading: Chapter summary (Using your own data)
chunks.title: Chapter 1, The Econometric Question — 1.8 Chapter summary (Using your own data)
chunks.body:
Chapter Summary
Economic data are organized as units (rows) by variables (columns); the mean is the elementary summary of a variable, and within-group means describe association (Sections 1.1–1.2).
Association is a descriptive property and does not imply causation; an observed association is consistent with both a causal effect and selection (Section 1.3).
The causal effect for a unit is defined by its two potential outcomes, only one of which is ever observed; estimation proceeds by approximating the unobserved outcome with comparable units (Section 1.4).
Four data structures — cross-section, time series, panel, and pooled cross-sections — determine which methods apply (Section 1.5).
The pandas library provides the tools for loading data and computing means, group means, and correlations (Section 1.6).

chunks.heading: The question
chunks.title: Chapter 2, Simple Linear Regression — 2.0 The question
chunks.body:
The Question
By how much does hourly earnings change, on average, with one additional year of schooling?

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.title: Chapter 2, Simple Linear Regression — 2.0 Overview
chunks.body: This chapter builds the one tool the rest of the book extends: the simple linear regression. Everything here serves a single, very practical task — drawing the "best" straight line through a cloud of points, then saying clearly what its slope means, how much to trust it, and when it may mislead. The plain-English account comes first; each derivation is tucked into a collapsible box for readers who want the formal version.

chunks.heading: Key idea
chunks.title: Chapter 2, Simple Linear Regression — 2.0 Key idea
chunks.body:
A motivating question
Suppose you are pricing houses. For hundreds of recent sales you know each home's size in square feet and its sale price. Bigger homes clearly sell for more — but by how much? Is it $100 a square foot, or $200? And how confident can you be in that number, given just this sample? "How much does one more unit of \(x\) move \(y\), and how sure are we?" is precisely what simple regression answers. We develop the method on this housing question, then turn the very same machinery on the book's running question — the earnings return to a year of schooling.

chunks.heading: Definition (The model and its assumptions)
chunks.title: Chapter 2, Simple Linear Regression — 2.1 Definition (The model and its assumptions)
chunks.body:
Definition 2.1 — Simple linear regression model
The model is \( y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + u \), where \(y\) is the outcome, \(x\) the explanatory variable, \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) unknown population parameters (the intercept and slope), and \(u\) the disturbance, comprising all unobserved determinants of \(y\) other than \(x\). The slope \(\beta_1\) is the change in \(y\) associated with a one-unit change in \(x\); it is the ceteris paribus effect of \(x\) on \(y\) only under Assumption SLR.4 below. The disturbance \(u\) is worth pausing on: it is everything else that moves the outcome and that we have not put in the model — location, age, and condition for a house; ability and family background for a worker. We never observe \(u\), and the entire question of whether a slope is causal comes down to how \(u\) relates to \(x\).

chunks.heading: The model and its assumptions
chunks.title: Chapter 2, Simple Linear Regression — 2.1 The model and its assumptions
chunks.body: The model rests on five assumptions, and they reward being understood one at a time — much of the book is the story of what happens when each one fails and how to cope (non-constant variance in Chapter 7, mismeasured regressors in Chapter 8, unobserved confounders in Chapter 9, and so on). Stated plainly once, the later chapters become variations on a theme.

chunks.heading: Assumptions (The model and its assumptions)
chunks.title: Chapter 2, Simple Linear Regression — 2.1 Assumptions (The model and its assumptions)
chunks.body:
Assumptions SLR.1–SLR.5
SLR.1 (linearity in parameters): \(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + u\). Why we assume it: it fixes the shape we are fitting — a line in the parameters — so that a single number \(\beta_1\) can summarise the effect. The restriction is only on how \(\beta_0,\beta_1\) enter; \(x\) may itself be a \(\log\) or a square, so genuinely curved relationships remain within reach (Chapter 5).
SLR.2 (random sampling): the \(n\) observations are drawn independently from the population. Why: it lets the sample stand in fairly for the population, so that what we learn generalises. It fails for clustered or time-dependent data, handled later (Chapters 10–12, 15).
SLR.3 (variation in \(x\)): \(\sum_i (x_i-\bar x)^2 > 0\); \(x\) is not constant. Why: a slope measures how \(y\) changes as \(x\) changes — if \(x\) never varies there is nothing to measure, and the more \(x\) varies the sharper the estimate (Section 2.3).

chunks.heading: Assumptions (The model and its assumptions)
chunks.title: Chapter 2, Simple Linear Regression — 2.1 Assumptions (The model and its assumptions)
chunks.body:
SLR.4 (zero conditional mean): \(\mathrm{E}[u\mid x]=0\); equivalently, \(x\) is uncorrelated with the unobserved determinants of \(y\) collected in \(u\). Why it is the crucial one: this is what turns a slope into a cause. It says the units we compare at different \(x\) do not also differ systematically in what we left out. It is the most often violated and the hardest to defend — bigger houses sit in nicer neighbourhoods, more-schooled workers tend to have higher ability — and nearly every method after this chapter exists to rescue it.
SLR.5 (homoskedasticity): \(\mathrm{Var}(u\mid x)=\sigma^2\), constant across \(x\). Why: it is not needed to get the slope right — only for the textbook standard-error formula to be valid. When it fails (Chapter 7) the estimate stays unbiased but our stated precision is wrong, so we switch to robust standard errors.

chunks.heading: The model and its assumptions
chunks.title: Chapter 2, Simple Linear Regression — 2.1 The model and its assumptions
chunks.body: Note the division of labour: SLR.1–SLR.4 make the estimate trustworthy (right on average), while SLR.5 affects only how we gauge its precision. That split is why some violations bias the answer itself and others merely distort the error bars.

chunks.heading: How OLS chooses the line
chunks.title: Chapter 2, Simple Linear Regression — 2.2 How OLS chooses the line
chunks.body:
Through any cloud of points one could draw countless straight lines; we need a rule that picks one. The rule is this: for each candidate line, measure how far it misses every point vertically — those misses are the residuals \(\hat u_i = y_i - \hat y_i\), where \(\hat y_i=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1 x_i\) is the line's prediction — and choose the line that makes the misses collectively smallest. "Smallest" is made precise by squaring each miss and adding them up: ordinary least squares (OLS) chooses \(\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1\) to minimise the sum of squared residuals,
\[ \mathrm{SSR}(\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1) = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\big(y_i - \hat\beta_0 - \hat\beta_1 x_i\big)^2. \]
Why squared, rather than the plain or absolute miss? Three practical reasons. Squaring makes every miss count as positive, so over- and under-predictions cannot cancel; it penalises a few large misses far more than many tiny ones, so the line refuses to badly fit any point it could fit; and — decisively — it yields a clean calculus solution, a single closed-form formula rather than an iterative search. That last property is why this rule, among all sensible ones, became the workhorse.

chunks.heading: How OLS chooses the line
chunks.title: Chapter 2, Simple Linear Regression — 2.2 How OLS chooses the line
chunks.body:
Carrying out the minimisation gives the two estimates we use throughout:
\[ \hat\beta_1 = \frac{\sum_i (x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)}{\sum_i (x_i-\bar x)^2}, \qquad \hat\beta_0 = \bar y - \hat\beta_1\bar x. \]
Read them in words. The slope \(\hat\beta_1\) is how \(x\) and \(y\) move together, divided by how much \(x\) moves on its own — co-movement scaled by \(x\)'s own spread. The intercept then shifts the line so it passes through the average point \((\bar x,\bar y)\). For the housing data, \(\hat\beta_1\) is simply the dollars of price that come, on average, with each extra square foot.

chunks.heading: Derivation (How OLS chooses the line)
chunks.title: Chapter 2, Simple Linear Regression — 2.2 Derivation (How OLS chooses the line)
chunks.body:
For the mathematically curious: deriving the estimates
Setting the partial derivatives of \(\mathrm{SSR}\) to zero gives the normal equations
\[ \sum_i \hat u_i = 0, \qquad \sum_i x_i \hat u_i = 0, \]
which say the residuals average to zero and are uncorrelated with the regressor — the two facts OLS uses up. The first gives \(\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x\); substituting into the second and solving for \(\hat\beta_1\) yields the slope formula above. These two conditions, not any distributional assumption, are the entire content of "least squares."

chunks.heading: Why we can trust the estimate
chunks.title: Chapter 2, Simple Linear Regression — 2.3 Why we can trust the estimate
chunks.body:
OLS hands us a number, \(\hat\beta_1\). A different random sample of houses would hand us a slightly different one. So the honest question is not "is \(\hat\beta_1\) correct?" — it never is, exactly — but "does our recipe for producing it have good properties across the samples we might have drawn?" Four properties matter, and each answers a worry a sceptic would raise.
Is it right on average? (Unbiasedness.) A sceptic might fear the method systematically overstates or understates the effect. Unbiasedness answers that worry: averaged over all the samples we might have drawn, the estimate lands on the truth. It promises nothing about any single estimate — only that the procedure is not tilted.

chunks.heading: Proposition (Why we can trust the estimate)
chunks.title: Chapter 2, Simple Linear Regression — 2.3 Proposition (Why we can trust the estimate)
chunks.body:
Proposition 2.1 — Unbiasedness
Under SLR.1–SLR.4, \(\mathrm{E}[\hat\beta_1]=\beta_1\): on average across samples, OLS recovers the true slope. The load-bearing assumption is SLR.4; if \(x\) is correlated with what we left out, this breaks and the estimate is biased — the subject of Chapter 3.
For the mathematically curious: the proof
Substituting \(y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+u_i\) into the slope formula gives \(\hat\beta_1 = \beta_1 + \sum_i w_i u_i\), where \(w_i = (x_i-\bar x)/\sum_j (x_j-\bar x)^2\) depends only on the regressor. Conditioning on the \(x_i\) and applying SLR.4, \(\mathrm{E}[\sum_i w_i u_i \mid x]=\sum_i w_i\,\mathrm{E}[u_i\mid x]=0\). Hence \(\mathrm{E}[\hat\beta_1\mid x]=\beta_1\), and unconditionally \(\mathrm{E}[\hat\beta_1]=\beta_1\). The estimate is the truth plus a weighted average of the disturbances; SLR.4 makes that second piece vanish on average.

chunks.heading: Why we can trust the estimate
chunks.title: Chapter 2, Simple Linear Regression — 2.3 Why we can trust the estimate
chunks.body: How sharp is it? (Sampling variance.) Unbiased is not enough — an estimate that is right on average but swings wildly from sample to sample is still useless in the one sample we hold. The variance measures that swing.

chunks.heading: Proposition (Why we can trust the estimate)
chunks.title: Chapter 2, Simple Linear Regression — 2.3 Proposition (Why we can trust the estimate)
chunks.body:
Proposition 2.2 — Sampling variance
Under SLR.1–SLR.5, \( \mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta_1\mid x) = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{\sum_i (x_i-\bar x)^2}. \) In words: precision improves when the noise \(\sigma^2\) is small and when \(x\) varies widely. This is why observing very different house sizes buys more precision than collecting many similar houses — with real consequences for how one gathers data (see Sharma's Take). The noise is estimated by \(\hat\sigma^2=\mathrm{SSR}/(n-2)\), the divisor \(n-2\) reflecting the two parameters already used.
For the mathematically curious: where the formula comes from
From \(\hat\beta_1-\beta_1=\sum_i w_i u_i\) with non-random weights \(w_i\), independence (SLR.2) gives \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta_1\mid x)=\sum_i w_i^2\,\mathrm{Var}(u_i\mid x)\). Under homoskedasticity (SLR.5) each \(\mathrm{Var}(u_i\mid x)=\sigma^2\), so the variance is \(\sigma^2\sum_i w_i^2 = \sigma^2/\sum_i (x_i-\bar x)^2\), using \(\sum_i w_i^2 = 1/\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2\). When SLR.5 fails, \(\sigma^2\) cannot be pulled out and this formula is wrong — the motivation for robust standard errors in Chapter 7.

chunks.heading: Why we can trust the estimate
chunks.title: Chapter 2, Simple Linear Regression — 2.3 Why we can trust the estimate
chunks.body:
Is it the best such estimate? (Efficiency.) Among all estimators that are both linear in \(y\) and unbiased, OLS has the smallest variance — it wastes no information. This is the Gauss–Markov theorem, and it is why OLS, rather than some other unbiased rule, is the default: under SLR.1–SLR.5 you cannot do better without giving something up.
Does more data help? (Consistency.) As the sample grows, \(\hat\beta_1\) converges to the true \(\beta_1\): the denominator \(\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2\) grows, the variance shrinks toward zero, and with enough data the estimate is almost surely close to the truth — provided SLR.4 holds. Consistency is the large-sample counterpart of unbiasedness, and it is the property we lean on when exact unbiasedness is out of reach in later chapters.

chunks.heading: Key idea (Why we can trust the estimate)
chunks.title: Chapter 2, Simple Linear Regression — 2.3 Key idea (Why we can trust the estimate)
chunks.body:
The four properties, in one breath
Unbiased = right on average; small variance = sharp in your one sample; efficient = the sharpest among fair (linear, unbiased) rules; consistent = converges to the truth with enough data. The first three rest on SLR.1–SLR.4 for "right" and add SLR.5 for honest error bars. Lose SLR.4 and "right on average" is the first casualty — which is why the entire second half of the book is devoted to defending it.

chunks.heading: Goodness of fit
chunks.title: Chapter 2, Simple Linear Regression — 2.4 Goodness of fit
chunks.body:
Decompose the total variation in \(y\) into explained and residual components. With \(\mathrm{SST}=\sum_i (y_i-\bar y)^2\), \(\mathrm{SSE}=\sum_i (\hat y_i-\bar y)^2\), and \(\mathrm{SSR}=\sum_i \hat u_i^2\), the normal equations imply \(\mathrm{SST}=\mathrm{SSE}+\mathrm{SSR}\). The coefficient of determination is
\[ R^2 = \frac{\mathrm{SSE}}{\mathrm{SST}} = 1 - \frac{\mathrm{SSR}}{\mathrm{SST}} \in [0,1], \]
the proportion of the variation in \(y\) accounted for by the regression. \(R^2\) measures fit, not the validity of a causal interpretation; a high \(R^2\) is neither necessary nor sufficient for an unbiased estimate of \(\beta_1\).
Worked Example 2.1

chunks.heading: Goodness of fit
chunks.title: Chapter 2, Simple Linear Regression — 2.4 Goodness of fit
chunks.body: For the five individuals of Chapter 1 (\(x=(10,12,12,16,16)\), \(y=(14,15,18,24,30)\)), the means are \(\bar x = 13.2\) and \(\bar y = 20.2\). The required sums are \(\sum (x-\bar x)(y-\bar y)=66.8\) and \(\sum (x-\bar x)^2 = 28.8\), giving \(\hat\beta_1 = 66.8/28.8 = 2.32\) and \(\hat\beta_0 = 20.2 - 2.32(13.2) = -10.4\). The fitted line is \(\widehat{\text{wage}} = -10.4 + 2.32\,\text{educ}\), with \(R^2 = 0.86\). The intercept lies far outside the range of the data and is not interpretable as the earnings of an individual with no schooling.

chunks.heading: Estimating a regression in Python
chunks.title: Chapter 2, Simple Linear Regression — 2.5 Estimating a regression in Python
chunks.body:
A regression is estimated with statsmodels using a formula of the form "y ~ x", in which an intercept is included by default. The fitted object exposes the coefficients, their standard errors, and the goodness-of-fit statistics.
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
# the formula "y ~ x" specifies a regression of y on x with an intercept
result = smf.ols("wage ~ educ", data=df).fit()
print(result.summary()) # full output: coefficients, standard errors, R-squared
b0 = result.params["Intercept"] # estimated intercept
b1 = result.params["educ"] # estimated slope
print(b1)
The estimates may be reproduced from the formulae of Section 2.2 directly in numpy, which confirms that the regression coefficient is the covariation of \(x\) and \(y\) divided by the variation of \(x\).
import numpy as np
x = df["educ"].values
y = df["wage"].values
xbar, ybar = x.mean(), y.mean()
# slope = covariation of x and y, divided by variation of x
b1 = np.sum((x - xbar) * (y - ybar)) / np.sum((x - xbar)**2)
b0 = ybar - b1 * xbar
print(b0, b1) # identical to the statsmodels estimates

chunks.heading: Reading the output (2.5.1 The motivating example: house price on size)
chunks.title: Chapter 2, Simple Linear Regression — 2.5 Reading the output (2.5.1 The motivating example: house price on size)
chunks.body:
Reading the output, line by line.
The coef column holds two numbers. The one on size — about 0.15 — is the slope: because price is measured in thousands of dollars, it says each additional square foot adds roughly $150 to the predicted price, so a home 200 sq ft larger is predicted to cost about $30,000 more. The Intercept, near 30, is the predicted price of a zero-square-foot house — a meaningless extrapolation far outside the data, and a reminder that an intercept is often just the number that makes the line pass through the average point, not a quantity to interpret.
Beside the slope, std err says how much that 0.15 would wobble from sample to sample; the t statistic is the slope divided by its standard error; and P>|t| — here essentially 0 — is the probability of a slope this large if size truly had no effect, so a tiny value means the relationship is far too strong to be chance. The [0.025 0.975] columns give the 95% confidence interval — the range of slopes the data are consistent with.

chunks.heading: Reading the output (2.5.1 The motivating example: house price on size)
chunks.title: Chapter 2, Simple Linear Regression — 2.5 Reading the output (2.5.1 The motivating example: house price on size)
chunks.body: R-squared is the share of the variation in price that size alone explains; the remainder lives in \(u\) — location, age, condition, lot size. That is exactly the force behind SLR.4: if larger homes also sit in pricier neighbourhoods, size is correlated with that omitted quality, and our $150 is part size and part neighbourhood. Chapter 3 adds such controls. Here, with simulated data in which size is the only true driver, the estimate is clean and recovers the built-in $150.

chunks.heading: Instructor's take (2.5.2 The book's question: wage on schooling)
chunks.title: Chapter 2, Simple Linear Regression — 2.5 Instructor's take (2.5.2 The book's question: wage on schooling)
chunks.body:
★ Sharma's Take
The sampling variance of the slope, \(\sigma^2/\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2\), shows that precision is determined not only by sample size but by the dispersion of the explanatory variable: the estimate is sharp when \(x\) varies widely and imprecise when \(x\) is concentrated, irrespective of \(n\). This has a consequence for the design of data collection that is frequently overlooked. Where the analyst can influence which observations are gathered, precision is increased by deliberately securing variation in the explanatory variable of interest, rather than by accumulating observations that are similar in that variable. A moderate sample with wide variation in \(x\) yields a more precise slope than a large sample in which \(x\) is nearly constant. Precision is a property to be designed into the data, not merely estimated from them.

chunks.heading: Chapter summary (2.5.2 The book's question: wage on schooling)
chunks.title: Chapter 2, Simple Linear Regression — 2.5 Chapter summary (2.5.2 The book's question: wage on schooling)
chunks.body:
Chapter Summary
The simple linear regression model is \(y=\beta_0+\beta_1 x+u\); the slope is a causal effect only under the zero-conditional-mean assumption SLR.4 (Section 2.1).
OLS minimizes the sum of squared residuals; the normal equations yield \(\hat\beta_1 = \sum(x-\bar x)(y-\bar y)/\sum(x-\bar x)^2\) and \(\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x\) (Section 2.2).
Under SLR.1–SLR.4 the estimator is unbiased; under SLR.1–SLR.5 its variance is \(\sigma^2/\sum(x-\bar x)^2\) and it is the minimum-variance linear unbiased estimator (Section 2.3).
The coefficient of determination \(R^2\) measures fit, not causal validity (Section 2.4).
In Python, smf.ols("y ~ x", data=df).fit() estimates the model and reports the full output (Section 2.5).

chunks.body: Chapter 3 · Controlling for Confounders

chunks.heading: The question
chunks.title: Chapter 3, Multiple Regression and Omitted-Variable Bias — 3.0 The question
chunks.body:
The Question
Is the estimated return to schooling a genuine effect of schooling, or does it reflect ability, which is correlated with both schooling and earnings?

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.title: Chapter 3, Multiple Regression and Omitted-Variable Bias — 3.0 Overview
chunks.body: Chapter 2's single slope can be read as a causal effect only if the one regressor is unrelated to everything else that moves the outcome — a demanding requirement that rarely holds. Multiple regression is the workhorse remedy: by adding the confounders we can observe as extra regressors, it compares units that are alike in those variables and differ only in the one we care about. This chapter explains, in plain language first, what “controlling for” a variable actually does, why leaving a confounder out biases the estimate in a direction we can usually predict in advance, and what collinearity does and does not do. The formal statements sit in collapsible boxes for those who want them.

chunks.heading: Key idea
chunks.title: Chapter 3, Multiple Regression and Omitted-Variable Bias — 3.0 Key idea
chunks.body:
A motivating example
Does an extra year of schooling really raise earnings — or do people who get more schooling also tend to have more of something else (ability, drive, family resources) that would have raised their earnings anyway? If that something is left out of the regression, the schooling coefficient quietly absorbs it and overstates the true return. Multiple regression lets us hold observable pieces of that confounding (experience, a test-score proxy for ability) fixed and watch the schooling coefficient move as we do. The direction it moves is itself a clue about the confounding. We estimate exactly this in Python below.

chunks.heading: Definition (The model)
chunks.title: Chapter 3, Multiple Regression and Omitted-Variable Bias — 3.1 Definition (The model)
chunks.body:
Definition 3.1 — Multiple regression model
The model is \( y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \cdots + \beta_k x_k + u \). The coefficient \(\beta_j\) is the change in \(y\) associated with a one-unit change in \(x_j\) holding the other regressors fixed — the partial effect of \(x_j\).

chunks.heading: Assumptions (The model)
chunks.title: Chapter 3, Multiple Regression and Omitted-Variable Bias — 3.1 Assumptions (The model)
chunks.body:
Assumptions MLR.1–MLR.5
MLR.1 (linear in parameters): \(y=\beta_0+\sum_{j}\beta_j x_j+u\). Linear in the coefficients (the \(x\)'s may be logs, squares, or interactions). Why: it is what lets us read each \(\beta_j\) as a constant partial effect.
MLR.2 (random sampling). Why: so sample relationships estimate population ones. Breaks under selection or clustered/dependent data.
MLR.3 (no perfect collinearity): no regressor is an exact linear combination of the others. Why: if two regressors move in lockstep, no data can separate their effects, so the partial effects are not even defined. High-but-imperfect correlation is allowed — see §3.4.
MLR.4 (zero conditional mean): \(\mathrm{E}[u\mid x_1,\dots,x_k]=0\) — the unobserved factors are, on average, unrelated to every included regressor. Why: this is the identifying assumption, the one that makes each \(\hat\beta_j\) unbiased. Breaks when a confounder is omitted or a regressor is mismeasured. It now requires only that \(u\) be unrelated to the included regressors — which is exactly why adding good controls helps.

chunks.heading: Assumptions (The model)
chunks.title: Chapter 3, Multiple Regression and Omitted-Variable Bias — 3.1 Assumptions (The model)
chunks.body: MLR.5 (homoskedasticity): \(\mathrm{Var}(u\mid x_1,\dots,x_k)=\sigma^2\), the same for all regressor values. Why: not needed for unbiasedness, but needed for the textbook variance formulas and for OLS to be efficient. Breaks when the spread of \(u\) widens with an \(x\) (Chapter 7).

chunks.heading: The model
chunks.title: Chapter 3, Multiple Regression and Omitted-Variable Bias — 3.1 The model
chunks.body: OLS estimates \(\hat\beta_0,\dots,\hat\beta_k\) by minimizing the sum of squared residuals, exactly as in Chapter 2. Under MLR.1–MLR.4 each \(\hat\beta_j\) is unbiased for \(\beta_j\); adding MLR.5, OLS is BLUE — the minimum-variance linear unbiased estimator, the Gauss–Markov theorem for multiple regression — and the usual standard errors are valid. As the sample grows the estimators are also consistent, converging to the true coefficients.

chunks.heading: What “controlling for” really means
chunks.title: Chapter 3, Multiple Regression and Omitted-Variable Bias — 3.2 What “controlling for” really means
chunks.body: When we add experience and ability to a wage regression and report the schooling coefficient as “controlling for experience and ability,” here is what the math is doing. It strips out of schooling the part that can be predicted from experience and ability, leaving only the schooling variation that has nothing to do with them — and relates wages to that. In effect it compares people with the same experience and ability who happen to differ in schooling. That is exactly the ceteris paribus comparison of Chapter 1, reconstructed from observational data. It also explains why a coefficient changes when you add a control: it is now computed from a different, leftover slice of the regressor, so it answers a slightly different question.

chunks.heading: Derivation (What “controlling for” really means)
chunks.title: Chapter 3, Multiple Regression and Omitted-Variable Bias — 3.2 Derivation (What “controlling for” really means)
chunks.body:
For the mathematically curious: the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem
The multiple-regression coefficient \(\hat\beta_1\) equals the slope from the simple regression of \(y\) on \(\tilde x_1\), where \(\tilde x_1\) is the residual from regressing \(x_1\) on all the other regressors. Equivalently, \(\hat\beta_1\) is obtained by (i) removing from \(x_1\) the part explained by the other regressors, and (ii) relating \(y\) to the remaining variation in \(x_1\). The demonstration below verifies this numerically: residualize both wage and schooling against the controls, regress one residual on the other, and recover the multiple-regression coefficient exactly.

chunks.heading: Key idea (What “controlling for” really means)
chunks.title: Chapter 3, Multiple Regression and Omitted-Variable Bias — 3.2 Key idea (What “controlling for” really means)
chunks.body:
Key Idea
A regression coefficient changes when a control is added because it is then computed from a different, residualized regressor — it answers a different question. Neither the controlled nor the uncontrolled estimate is automatically correct; the appropriate set of controls is the set under which MLR.4 holds.

chunks.heading: Omitting a confounder: a bias you can sign in advance
chunks.title: Chapter 3, Multiple Regression and Omitted-Variable Bias — 3.3 Omitting a confounder: a bias you can sign in advance
chunks.body:
Leave out a variable that (a) belongs in the model and (b) is correlated with a regressor you kept, and that regressor's coefficient gets contaminated. It picks up not only its own effect but a slice of the missing variable's effect, smuggled in through their correlation. The useful part is that you can usually predict the direction of the damage before running anything, from two judgments: does the omitted variable raise or lower the outcome, and is it positively or negatively related to the included regressor? Same-sign answers push the coefficient up; opposite-sign answers push it down.
For schooling and ability: ability raises earnings (positive) and ability rises with schooling (positive), so the two positives multiply to an upward bias — the uncontrolled schooling coefficient overstates the true return. That is exactly why, in the demonstration, the coefficient falls as the ability proxy enters: we are stripping out an upward bias.

chunks.heading: Derivation (Omitting a confounder: a bias you can sign in advance)
chunks.title: Chapter 3, Multiple Regression and Omitted-Variable Bias — 3.3 Derivation (Omitting a confounder: a bias you can sign in advance)
chunks.body:
For the mathematically curious: the omitted-variable bias formula
Let the population model be \(y=\beta_0+\beta_1 x_1+\beta_2 x_2+u\), but suppose \(x_2\) is omitted and we regress \(y\) on \(x_1\) alone. Let \(\delta_1\) be the slope from regressing the omitted \(x_2\) on the included \(x_1\). Then
\[ \mathrm{E}[\tilde\beta_1] = \beta_1 + \underbrace{\beta_2\,\delta_1}_{\text{bias}}. \]
The bias is the product of the omitted variable's effect on the outcome (\(\beta_2\)) and its association with the included regressor (\(\delta_1\)); its sign is the product of their signs — exactly the two-judgment rule above. It vanishes if the omitted variable either does not affect \(y\) (\(\beta_2=0\)) or is uncorrelated with \(x_1\) (\(\delta_1=0\)).

chunks.heading: Collinearity: imprecision, not bias
chunks.title: Chapter 3, Multiple Regression and Omitted-Variable Bias — 3.4 Collinearity: imprecision, not bias
chunks.body: When two regressors are highly (but not perfectly) correlated, multiple regression still identifies their separate effects — it just struggles to pin them down precisely. The intuition follows from §3.2: to estimate the partial effect of \(x_j\), OLS uses only the part of \(x_j\) not explained by the other regressors. If most of \(x_j\) is explained by the others, little independent variation is left, and a coefficient estimated from little variation is noisy. So collinearity inflates standard errors but introduces no bias — the estimates stay centered on the truth, just wobbly. The tempting fix of dropping one collinear regressor usually reintroduces omitted-variable bias, trading a precision problem for a bias problem; the honest response is more, or more variable, data.

chunks.heading: Derivation (Collinearity: imprecision, not bias)
chunks.title: Chapter 3, Multiple Regression and Omitted-Variable Bias — 3.4 Derivation (Collinearity: imprecision, not bias)
chunks.body:
For the mathematically curious: the variance of a coefficient and the VIF
\[ \mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta_j) = \frac{\sigma^2}{\mathrm{SST}_j\,(1-R_j^2)}, \]
where \(R_j^2\) is the \(R^2\) from regressing \(x_j\) on all the other regressors. The factor \(1/(1-R_j^2)\) is the variance inflation factor (VIF): it equals 1 when \(R_j^2=0\) (no inflation) and diverges as \(R_j^2\to 1\). A noisier outcome (larger \(\sigma^2\)) and less spread in \(x_j\) (smaller \(\mathrm{SST}_j\)) also enlarge the variance — the same precision levers as simple regression, now with collinearity added.

chunks.heading: Estimating multiple regression in Python
chunks.title: Chapter 3, Multiple Regression and Omitted-Variable Bias — 3.5 Estimating multiple regression in Python
chunks.body:
Additional regressors are included by extending the formula with +. Comparing the coefficient on the variable of interest across specifications reveals the influence of the added controls.
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
# additional regressors are added with "+"
short = smf.ols("wage ~ educ", data=df).fit()
long = smf.ols("wage ~ educ + exper + IQ", data=df).fit()
print(short.params["educ"]) # schooling coefficient, no controls
print(long.params["educ"]) # schooling coefficient, controlling for exper and IQ
The Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem can be verified directly: residualize both the outcome and the regressor of interest against the remaining controls, then regress one residual on the other.
# Frisch-Waugh-Lovell: the multiple-regression coefficient on educ equals the
# slope from regressing residualized wage on residualized educ
e_y = smf.ols("wage ~ exper + IQ", data=df).fit().resid # wage with controls removed
e_x = smf.ols("educ ~ exper + IQ", data=df).fit().resid # educ with controls removed
import numpy as np
b_fwl = np.sum(e_x * e_y) / np.sum(e_x**2)
print(b_fwl) # equals long.params["educ"]

chunks.title: Chapter 3, Multiple Regression and Omitted-Variable Bias — 3.5 Estimating multiple regression in Python
chunks.body: The demonstration below estimates the schooling coefficient with no controls, with experience added, and with a measure of ability added, exhibiting the reduction in omitted-variable bias as the confounders are included.

chunks.heading: Reading the output (3.5.1 Demonstration)
chunks.title: Chapter 3, Multiple Regression and Omitted-Variable Bias — 3.5 Reading the output (3.5.1 Demonstration)
chunks.body:
Reading the output.
Read the three numbers as one story about bias, not three unrelated estimates. The short coefficient on educ is the largest because it carries the full upward bias from ability; adding exper nudges it, and adding the ability proxy iq pulls it down toward the built-in truth of 0.060. A coefficient that falls as a control enters is the signature of positive omitted-variable bias — exactly what the sign rule predicted. In the full summary() table, read each coefficient as a partial effect (holding the others fixed), check the standard errors and \(t\)-statistics for precision, and note that \(R^2\) rises as regressors are added but says nothing about whether the schooling coefficient is now unbiased. One caution: iq is only a proxy for ability, so it removes part — not all — of the bias; the leftover gap is the measurement-error problem of Chapter 8.

chunks.heading: 3.5.2 Another example: job training and motivation
chunks.title: Chapter 3, Multiple Regression and Omitted-Variable Bias — 3.5 3.5.2 Another example: job training and motivation
chunks.body: The same machinery works far from schooling. Suppose we evaluate whether a voluntary job-training program raises earnings. People who sign up tend to be more motivated, and motivation raises earnings on its own. Motivation is the omitted variable: it lifts earnings (positive) and is positively associated with enrolling (motivated people enroll more), so two positives multiply to an upward bias — the program looks more effective than it truly is. Holding an observable proxy for motivation fixed (a worker's prior earnings trajectory, say) shrinks the estimate toward the truth, just as the ability proxy did for schooling. The lesson generalizes: whenever a treatment is voluntary and self-selected, expect this upward bias and ask what variable would absorb it.

chunks.heading: Instructor's take (3.5.2 Another example: job training and motivation)
chunks.title: Chapter 3, Multiple Regression and Omitted-Variable Bias — 3.5 Instructor's take (3.5.2 Another example: job training and motivation)
chunks.body:
★ Sharma's Take
The direction in which a coefficient moves as a control is added is itself informative about the sign of the confounding, and this information is frequently left unused. The omitted-variable bias formula states that the movement equals minus the bias removed; thus a coefficient that falls when a control enters indicates that the omitted control was biasing it upward, while a coefficient that rises indicates downward bias. Reporting that an estimate is “robust to controls” discards this content. The disciplined practice is to record the direction of each control's effect on the coefficient of interest and to compare it with the sign predicted by \(\beta_2\delta_1\); agreement corroborates the analyst's understanding of the confounding structure, and disagreement signals a determinant that has not been correctly conceived.

chunks.heading: Chapter summary (3.5.2 Another example: job training and motivation)
chunks.title: Chapter 3, Multiple Regression and Omitted-Variable Bias — 3.5 Chapter summary (3.5.2 Another example: job training and motivation)
chunks.body:
Chapter Summary
The multiple-regression coefficient \(\beta_j\) is the partial effect of \(x_j\) holding the other regressors fixed (Section 3.1).
By the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem, \(\hat\beta_j\) is the slope relating the outcome to the part of \(x_j\) orthogonal to the other regressors; this defines “controlling for” precisely (Section 3.2).
Omitting a relevant variable biases the included coefficient by \(\beta_2\delta_1\), whose sign is predictable from subject-matter knowledge (Section 3.3).
Collinearity inflates the variance of the estimates but does not bias them; the remedy is more data, not deletion of regressors (Section 3.4).
In Python, controls are added with + in the formula; FWL may be verified by residualization (Section 3.5).

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.title: Chapter 4,  — 4.0 Overview
chunks.body: Chapter 4 · Statistical Inference

chunks.heading: The question
chunks.title: Chapter 4, Sampling Uncertainty, Confidence Intervals, and Tests — 4.0 The question
chunks.body:
The Question
An estimate is computed from one sample. How is its uncertainty quantified, and how is the hypothesis that an effect is zero to be assessed?

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.title: Chapter 4, Sampling Uncertainty, Confidence Intervals, and Tests — 4.0 Overview
chunks.body: An estimate with no measure of its uncertainty is uninterpretable: you cannot tell a real signal from a lucky draw. This chapter builds the machinery that attaches uncertainty to a regression coefficient — where sampling uncertainty comes from, the standard error that measures it, the confidence interval that reports a range of plausible values, and the t- and F-tests that ask whether an effect, or a group of effects, could plausibly be zero.

chunks.heading: Key idea
chunks.title: Chapter 4, Sampling Uncertainty, Confidence Intervals, and Tests — 4.0 Key idea
chunks.body:
A motivating example
A school district pilots a new online tutoring tool for a semester and estimates a positive effect on test scores. Two different questions follow, and inference answers only the first. Could the estimate be noise? — a single sample can show a positive effect even when the true effect is zero, so we need the standard error, a confidence interval, and a t-test to judge whether zero is still plausible. Is the effect big enough to matter? — that is a question of economic, not statistical, significance, and no p-value answers it. Keeping these two questions apart is the central discipline of this chapter.

chunks.heading: The sampling distribution
chunks.title: Chapter 4, Sampling Uncertainty, Confidence Intervals, and Tests — 4.1 The sampling distribution
chunks.body: Distinguish the population, the entirety of units of interest, from the sample, the subset observed. The parameter \(\beta_1\) is a fixed feature of the population; the estimator \(\hat\beta_1\) is computed from the sample and varies across samples. A different sample, drawn from the same population, would yield a different value of \(\hat\beta_1\).

chunks.heading: Definition (The sampling distribution)
chunks.title: Chapter 4, Sampling Uncertainty, Confidence Intervals, and Tests — 4.1 Definition (The sampling distribution)
chunks.body:
Definition 4.1 — Sampling distribution
The sampling distribution of an estimator is the distribution of its values across the repeated samples that might be drawn from the population. Inference concerns two features of this distribution: its centre, which determines bias, and its dispersion, which determines precision.

chunks.heading: The sampling distribution
chunks.title: Chapter 4, Sampling Uncertainty, Confidence Intervals, and Tests — 4.1 The sampling distribution
chunks.body: Under MLR.1–MLR.4 the estimator is unbiased: the sampling distribution is centred on \(\beta_1\) (Chapter 2). The remaining task is to characterize its dispersion and shape.

chunks.heading: Why the estimator is bell-shaped
chunks.title: Chapter 4, Sampling Uncertainty, Confidence Intervals, and Tests — 4.2 Why the estimator is bell-shaped
chunks.body: The estimate is built by adding up the random noise across all the observations. When you add up many small independent random pieces, the total comes out bell-shaped almost no matter what the individual pieces look like — this is the central limit theorem, and it is why the sampling distribution of a regression coefficient is approximately normal in reasonable samples. The practical upshot: estimates near the truth are common, estimates far from it are rare, and how fast “far” becomes rare is set by the standard error.

chunks.heading: Derivation (Why the estimator is bell-shaped)
chunks.title: Chapter 4, Sampling Uncertainty, Confidence Intervals, and Tests — 4.2 Derivation (Why the estimator is bell-shaped)
chunks.body:
For the mathematically curious: normality, MLR.6, and the t distribution
The estimator is a linear function of the disturbances, \(\hat\beta_1 = \beta_1 + \sum_i w_i u_i\). Under MLR.1–MLR.4 with random sampling, for large \(n\) the standardized estimator \((\hat\beta_1-\beta_1)/\mathrm{se}(\hat\beta_1)\) is approximately standard normal. If the disturbances are exactly normal (the optional assumption MLR.6), the result holds exactly in finite samples, with the standard normal replaced by Student's \(t\) distribution with \(n-k-1\) degrees of freedom. In large samples the \(t\) and the normal are practically identical, which is why the “approximately 2” critical value works.

chunks.heading: Definition (The standard error)
chunks.title: Chapter 4, Sampling Uncertainty, Confidence Intervals, and Tests — 4.3 Definition (The standard error)
chunks.body:
Definition 4.2 — Standard error
The standard error of \(\hat\beta_1\), denoted \(\mathrm{se}(\hat\beta_1)\), is the estimated standard deviation of its sampling distribution — the typical magnitude of the deviation of the estimate from \(\beta_1\). For the simple-regression slope, \(\mathrm{se}(\hat\beta_1)=\hat\sigma/\sqrt{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2}\), where \(\hat\sigma^2=\mathrm{SSR}/(n-k-1)\).

chunks.heading: The standard error
chunks.title: Chapter 4, Sampling Uncertainty, Confidence Intervals, and Tests — 4.3 The standard error
chunks.body: The standard error is computed from a single sample; it estimates the dispersion that would be observed across repeated samples without requiring them. It decreases with the residual dispersion \(\hat\sigma\) and increases as the variation in the regressor falls, reproducing the variance formula of Chapter 2.

chunks.heading: Key idea (The standard error)
chunks.title: Chapter 4, Sampling Uncertainty, Confidence Intervals, and Tests — 4.3 Key idea (The standard error)
chunks.body:
The two-standard-error rule
For a bell-shaped sampling distribution, approximately 95% of estimates lie within two standard errors of the centre (more precisely, 1.96). This fact underlies both confidence intervals and tests.

chunks.heading: Definition (Confidence intervals)
chunks.title: Chapter 4, Sampling Uncertainty, Confidence Intervals, and Tests — 4.4 Definition (Confidence intervals)
chunks.body:
Definition 4.3 — Confidence interval
The 95% confidence interval for \(\beta_1\) is \(\hat\beta_1 \pm c\cdot\mathrm{se}(\hat\beta_1)\), where \(c\approx 1.96\) for large samples. The interval is constructed by a procedure that, across repeated samples, contains the true \(\beta_1\) in 95% of instances.

chunks.heading: Confidence intervals
chunks.title: Chapter 4, Sampling Uncertainty, Confidence Intervals, and Tests — 4.4 Confidence intervals
chunks.body: The confidence interval reports magnitude and precision jointly: a narrow interval distant from zero and a wide interval containing zero may share the same point estimate yet convey different conclusions. It is generally more informative than a test outcome alone.

chunks.heading: Hypothesis tests
chunks.title: Chapter 4, Sampling Uncertainty, Confidence Intervals, and Tests — 4.5 Hypothesis tests
chunks.body: This is the book's first hypothesis test, so here is the whole idea in plain terms before any formulas. A hypothesis test is a disciplined way to ask whether the data are compatible with a specific claim about the population. We begin from a null hypothesis — a sceptical default we are willing to believe until the data argue otherwise, almost always “the effect is zero” (\(H_0:\beta_1=0\)). Against it stands the alternative we suspect (\(H_1:\beta_1\ne 0\), some non-zero effect). The reasoning is proof-by-contradiction softened for a noisy world: assume the null is true, then ask how surprising our actual estimate would be under that assumption. If an estimate this far from zero would almost never arise by chance when the true effect really is zero, we treat the null as implausible and reject it; if such an estimate is unremarkable, we fail to reject.

chunks.heading: Hypothesis tests
chunks.title: Chapter 4, Sampling Uncertainty, Confidence Intervals, and Tests — 4.5 Hypothesis tests
chunks.body:
Two cautions are built into the language. First, we never “accept” or “prove” the null — failing to reject zero means only that the data do not rule it out, not that the effect is truly zero (a wide confidence interval can be consistent with both zero and a large effect). Second, a test can err two ways: it can reject a null that is actually true (a false positive, or Type I error, whose rate we fix in advance as the significance level \(\alpha\), usually 5%), or it can fail to reject a null that is actually false (a false negative, or Type II error, more likely in small samples). Choosing \(\alpha=0.05\) says we accept a 5% false-alarm rate in exchange for the power to detect real effects.
With that framework in place, the test of \(H_0:\beta_1=0\) is mechanical. Form the \(t\)-statistic \(t=\hat\beta_1/\mathrm{se}(\hat\beta_1)\), the number of standard errors separating the estimate from zero. Under \(H_0\), \(t\) follows the \(t_{n-k-1}\) distribution, so we know which values are surprising. The hypothesis is rejected at the 5% level when \(|t|\) exceeds the critical value (approximately 2 for large samples) — equivalently, whenever the 95% confidence interval excludes zero.

chunks.heading: Definition (Hypothesis tests)
chunks.title: Chapter 4, Sampling Uncertainty, Confidence Intervals, and Tests — 4.5 Definition (Hypothesis tests)
chunks.body:
Definition 4.4 — p-value
The p-value is the probability, computed under the null hypothesis, of obtaining a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, nor the probability that the result is due to chance; it is a measure, computed under the assumption that the null holds, of the discrepancy between the data and that assumption.

chunks.heading: Hypothesis tests
chunks.title: Chapter 4, Sampling Uncertainty, Confidence Intervals, and Tests — 4.5 Hypothesis tests
chunks.body: Testing several coefficients at once. Sometimes the question is not “does this one variable matter?” but “do these variables, as a group, matter?” — for example, whether a set of neighborhood dummies jointly belongs in a price regression. The F-test answers this by asking how much worse the model fits when the whole group is forced to zero: a big jump in unexplained variation means the group matters. A large F (small p) rejects the joint null that all of them are zero. The F-test is especially valuable under collinearity, where two variables can each look individually insignificant yet be jointly significant — their shared variation keeps either from standing out alone, but together they clearly belong.

chunks.heading: Derivation (Hypothesis tests)
chunks.title: Chapter 4, Sampling Uncertainty, Confidence Intervals, and Tests — 4.5 Derivation (Hypothesis tests)
chunks.body:
For the mathematically curious: the F statistic
To test that \(q\) coefficients are jointly zero, compare the residual sum of squares of the unrestricted and restricted (group-dropped) models:
\[ F = \frac{(\mathrm{SSR}_r - \mathrm{SSR}_{ur})/q}{\mathrm{SSR}_{ur}/(n-k-1)} \sim F_{q,\,n-k-1}. \]
The numerator is the per-restriction rise in unexplained variation when the group is dropped; the denominator is the leftover variance. A large ratio means the restrictions hurt the fit a lot relative to noise, so the joint null is rejected.

chunks.heading: Key idea (Hypothesis tests)
chunks.title: Chapter 4, Sampling Uncertainty, Confidence Intervals, and Tests — 4.5 Key idea (Hypothesis tests)
chunks.body:
One test vs. many: the multiple-testing trap
A 5% test wrongly rejects a true null about 5% of the time. Run one test and that is a calculated risk; run twenty and you should expect roughly one “significant” result even if nothing is going on. Searching across many regressions, subsamples, or specifications and reporting only the significant one — p-hacking — turns a 5% error rate into a near-certainty of a false positive. The honest defenses are deciding the test in advance, reporting every test you ran, and tightening thresholds when you test many hypotheses. You will feel this directly in The p-Hacking Casino.

chunks.heading: Inference in Python
chunks.title: Chapter 4, Sampling Uncertainty, Confidence Intervals, and Tests — 4.6 Inference in Python
chunks.body:
The fitted statsmodels object exposes the standard errors, \(t\)-statistics, p-values, and confidence intervals for all coefficients.
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
result = smf.ols("wage ~ educ + exper", data=df).fit()
print(result.bse["educ"]) # standard error of the schooling coefficient
print(result.tvalues["educ"]) # t-statistic for H0: coefficient = 0
print(result.pvalues["educ"]) # corresponding p-value
print(result.conf_int().loc["educ"]) # 95% confidence interval
Joint hypotheses are tested with the f_test method, which accepts a string specifying the restrictions.
# joint test that experience and its square contribute nothing: H0 both coefficients = 0
result = smf.ols("wage ~ educ + exper + I(exper**2)", data=df).fit()
ftest = result.f_test("exper = 0, I(exper ** 2) = 0")
print(ftest) # F-statistic and its p-value
The demonstration below fits a wage regression and reports the full inferential output, including a confidence interval and a joint test.

chunks.heading: Reading the output (4.6.1 Demonstration)
chunks.title: Chapter 4, Sampling Uncertainty, Confidence Intervals, and Tests — 4.6 Reading the output (4.6.1 Demonstration)
chunks.body: Reading the output. Walk the educ row across: the coefficient is the estimated effect, the standard error is its typical sampling wobble, the \(t\) is coefficient-over-se (how many standard errors from zero), and the p-value is how surprising that \(t\) would be if the true effect were zero. The 95% CI is roughly coefficient \(\pm\,2\,\mathrm{se}\); because it excludes zero, schooling is significant at 5%. Read the printed CI for educ as the range of returns the data find plausible — more informative than the bare verdict “significant.” The joint F-test on exper and tenure asks whether experience and tenure together belong; its small p-value says yes, even where an individual t might waver. The \(F\)-statistic at the head of summary() tests whether all the regressors are jointly zero. Remember: a small p-value flags a detectable effect, not necessarily an important one — always check the magnitude against what would matter in practice.

chunks.heading: 4.6.2 Another example: bedrooms and location in a price regression
chunks.title: Chapter 4, Sampling Uncertainty, Confidence Intervals, and Tests — 4.6 4.6.2 Another example: bedrooms and location in a price regression
chunks.body: Suppose you regress house price on size, number of bedrooms, and a set of neighborhood dummies. The t-test on bedrooms is a single-coefficient question: holding size fixed, is an extra bedroom associated with a detectable price difference? (Often the answer is “barely,” or even negative, once size is controlled — bedrooms mostly proxy for size.) The joint F-test on the neighborhood dummies is a group question: do location effects, taken together, belong in the model? This is where the F-test earns its keep: any single neighborhood dummy may be individually insignificant, yet the set is overwhelmingly jointly significant, because location clearly matters even when no one neighborhood stands out alone. Reporting the CI on bedrooms alongside the joint F on location conveys far more than a row of significance stars.

chunks.heading: Instructor's take (4.6.2 Another example: bedrooms and location in a price regression)
chunks.title: Chapter 4, Sampling Uncertainty, Confidence Intervals, and Tests — 4.6 Instructor's take (4.6.2 Another example: bedrooms and location in a price regression)
chunks.body:
★ Sharma's Take
A failure to reject the null hypothesis is frequently reported as evidence of no effect, which it is not. The confidence interval distinguishes two cases that the verdict “not significant” conflates. An interval extending from a small negative value to a substantial positive value indicates that the data are uninformative: a large effect remains consistent with the evidence. An interval tightly bracketing zero indicates that a large effect has genuinely been excluded. The two situations have opposite substantive implications despite identical significance verdicts. The disciplined practice, on failing to reject, is to report the range of effects the data exclude rather than merely the failure to detect one; the confidence interval, not the p-value, carries this information.

chunks.heading: Chapter summary (4.6.2 Another example: bedrooms and location in a price regression)
chunks.title: Chapter 4, Sampling Uncertainty, Confidence Intervals, and Tests — 4.6 Chapter summary (4.6.2 Another example: bedrooms and location in a price regression)
chunks.body:
Chapter Summary
Sampling uncertainty arises because the estimator varies across the samples that might be drawn; its distribution is the sampling distribution (Section 4.1).
By the central limit theorem the estimator is approximately normal in large samples; with normal disturbances the \(t\) distribution applies exactly (Section 4.2).
The standard error estimates the dispersion of the sampling distribution from a single sample (Section 4.3).
The 95% confidence interval \(\hat\beta_1\pm 1.96\,\mathrm{se}\) reports magnitude and precision jointly (Section 4.4).
The \(t\)-statistic tests a single coefficient; the p-value is the probability of a statistic at least as extreme under the null; the \(F\)-statistic tests joint restrictions (Section 4.5).
In Python, bse, tvalues, pvalues, conf_int(), and f_test provide the inferential quantities (Section 4.6).

chunks.title: Chapter 5,  — 5.0 Overview
chunks.body: Chapter 5 · Functional Form

chunks.heading: The question
chunks.title: Chapter 5, Logarithms, Polynomials, and Interactions — 5.0 The question
chunks.body:
The Question
How are relationships that are proportional, curved, or dependent on a second variable represented within a model that remains linear in its parameters?

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.title: Chapter 5, Logarithms, Polynomials, and Interactions — 5.0 Overview
chunks.body: “Linear” regression is more flexible than it sounds: the linearity it requires is in the parameters, not the variables. So we can capture relationships that are proportional, curved, or dependent on a second variable simply by transforming the inputs — taking logs, adding squared terms, or multiplying two regressors — and OLS runs exactly as before. The work, and the interest, is almost entirely in interpretation: each transformation changes what a coefficient means.

chunks.heading: Key idea
chunks.title: Chapter 5, Logarithms, Polynomials, and Interactions — 5.0 Key idea
chunks.body:
A motivating example
Two everyday claims about wages need shapes a straight line cannot draw. First, “each extra year of experience helps, but less and less” — earnings rise with experience, then flatten and eventually peak. A straight line forces a constant effect; a quadratic lets the slope shrink and turn over. Second, “an extra year of schooling raises wages by about the same percentage for everyone” — not the same number of dollars (a level effect), but the same proportional bump. A log outcome expresses exactly that. This chapter gives you the small toolkit — logs, polynomials, interactions — for saying such things precisely, and estimates the experience profile below.

chunks.heading: The logarithmic transformation
chunks.title: Chapter 5, Logarithms, Polynomials, and Interactions — 5.1 The logarithmic transformation
chunks.body: Economists reach for the natural log constantly, for one reason: differences in \(\ln(y)\) are proportional (percentage) changes in \(y\). Take logs of wages and a coefficient stops meaning “dollars per unit” and starts meaning “percent per unit” — usually the more natural economic statement, and one that also tames skewed, all-positive variables like wages, prices, and firm size. The four combinations of logging the outcome, the regressor, both, or neither give four interpretations worth committing to memory.

chunks.heading: Derivation (The logarithmic transformation)
chunks.title: Chapter 5, Logarithms, Polynomials, and Interactions — 5.1 Derivation (The logarithmic transformation)
chunks.body:
For the mathematically curious: why \(\Delta\ln y\) is a proportional change
For small changes, \(\Delta\ln(y) \approx \dfrac{\Delta y}{y}\), the proportional change in \(y\); multiplying by 100 gives the percentage change. The approximation is excellent for changes under about 10% and drifts for larger ones (see the exact formula below). This is why a coefficient in a regression of \(\ln y\) reads as a proportional, or percentage, effect.

chunks.heading: Definition (The logarithmic transformation)
chunks.title: Chapter 5, Logarithms, Polynomials, and Interactions — 5.1 Definition (The logarithmic transformation)
chunks.body:
Definition 5.1 — Interpretation of logarithmic specifications
Level–level (\(y\) on \(x\)): a one-unit increase in \(x\) changes \(y\) by \(\beta_1\) units.
Log–level (\(\ln y\) on \(x\)): a one-unit increase in \(x\) changes \(y\) by approximately \(100\beta_1\) percent.
Level–log (\(y\) on \(\ln x\)): a one-percent increase in \(x\) changes \(y\) by approximately \(\beta_1/100\) units.
Log–log (\(\ln y\) on \(\ln x\)): a one-percent increase in \(x\) changes \(y\) by approximately \(\beta_1\) percent. Here \(\beta_1\) is the elasticity of \(y\) with respect to \(x\).

chunks.heading: Derivation (The logarithmic transformation)
chunks.title: Chapter 5, Logarithms, Polynomials, and Interactions — 5.1 Derivation (The logarithmic transformation)
chunks.body:
For the mathematically curious: the exact percentage effect
In a log–level model the “\(100\beta\) percent” rule is a small-change approximation. The exact percentage effect of a one-unit rise in \(x\) is \(100\,(e^{\beta}-1)\). For \(\beta=0.05\) this is 5.13% (about 5%); for \(\beta=0.30\) it is 35.0%, not 30% — so prefer the exact form when a coefficient is large or the regressor is a 0/1 dummy.

chunks.heading: Polynomial terms
chunks.title: Chapter 5, Logarithms, Polynomials, and Interactions — 5.2 Polynomial terms
chunks.body: Adding a squared term lets the line bend. In \( y=\beta_0+\beta_1 x+\beta_2 x^2+u \), the effect of \(x\) is no longer a single number — it grows or shrinks as \(x\) itself grows. With \(\beta_2<0\) the curve rises then falls, peaking at a turning point; the experience–earnings profile (up fast early, flattening, eventually declining) is the textbook case.

chunks.heading: Derivation (Polynomial terms)
chunks.title: Chapter 5, Logarithms, Polynomials, and Interactions — 5.2 Derivation (Polynomial terms)
chunks.body:
For the mathematically curious: marginal effect and turning point
Differentiating, the marginal effect is \(\partial y/\partial x = \beta_1+2\beta_2 x\), which varies with \(x\). Setting it to zero gives the turning point \(x^\ast=-\beta_1/(2\beta_2)\) — a maximum when \(\beta_2<0\), a minimum when \(\beta_2>0\).

chunks.heading: Key idea (Polynomial terms)
chunks.title: Chapter 5, Logarithms, Polynomials, and Interactions — 5.2 Key idea (Polynomial terms)
chunks.body:
Key Idea
In any specification containing a power of a regressor, the effect of that regressor is not a single coefficient but a function of its level, \(\beta_1+2\beta_2 x\). It must be reported at specified values — typically the mean or several points across the range — rather than as one number.

chunks.heading: Interactions
chunks.title: Chapter 5, Logarithms, Polynomials, and Interactions — 5.3 Interactions
chunks.body: An interaction term represents an effect that depends on a second variable. In \( y=\beta_0+\beta_1 x_1+\beta_2 x_2+\beta_3 x_1 x_2+u \), the effect of \(x_1\) is \(\partial y/\partial x_1 = \beta_1+\beta_3 x_2\), a function of \(x_2\). A nonzero \(\beta_3\) indicates that the two variables modify each other's effects; the sign of \(\beta_3\) determines whether they are complementary or substitutive. A positive \(\beta_3\) means each variable raises the other's marginal effect: the two are complements — for example, if the wage return to a year of schooling is larger for workers who also have more experience. A negative \(\beta_3\) means each variable lowers the other's marginal effect: the two are substitutes — the return to schooling is smaller for the more experienced, as though experience and schooling were alternative routes to the same earning power. A useful check: read \(\partial y/\partial x_1=\beta_1+\beta_3 x_2\) and ask whether a larger \(x_2\) makes the effect of \(x_1\) bigger (complements) or smaller (substitutes).

chunks.heading: Influential observations
chunks.title: Chapter 5, Logarithms, Polynomials, and Interactions — 5.4 Influential observations
chunks.body: Because the OLS criterion weights observations by their distance from the mean of the regressor (Chapter 2), a small number of extreme observations can determine the estimated form. A nonlinear specification supported only by a few outlying points is not robust. Two safeguards are standard: inspection of a scatter plot before adopting a functional form, and re-estimation with the extreme observations excluded to confirm that the conclusion does not depend on them.

chunks.heading: Functional forms in Python
chunks.title: Chapter 5, Logarithms, Polynomials, and Interactions — 5.5 Functional forms in Python
chunks.body:
Transformations are written directly into the formula. The function np.log applies the logarithm; the wrapper I(...) protects an arithmetic expression such as a square; the colon : forms an interaction.
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
# log outcome: coefficient is approximately a proportional (percentage) effect
m_log = smf.ols("np.log(wage) ~ educ", data=df).fit()
# quadratic: I(...) protects an arithmetic expression inside a formula
m_quad = smf.ols("wage ~ exper + I(exper**2)", data=df).fit()
# interaction: the colon forms the product term
m_int = smf.ols("wage ~ educ + exper + educ:exper", data=df).fit()
In a polynomial specification the marginal effect and the turning point are computed from the coefficients.
# in the quadratic model the marginal effect of experience depends on its level
b1 = m_quad.params["exper"]
b2 = m_quad.params["I(exper ** 2)"]
exper0 = 10
marginal_effect = b1 + 2*b2*exper0 # derivative of the fitted curve at exper = 10
turning_point = -b1 / (2*b2) # experience level at which the curve peaks
print(marginal_effect, turning_point)
