chunks.heading: Reading the output (5.5.1 Demonstration)
chunks.title: Chapter 5, Logarithms, Polynomials, and Interactions — 5.5 Reading the output (5.5.1 Demonstration)
chunks.body: Reading the output. Start with educ in the log-wage model: its coefficient is a proportional return — multiply by 100 to read it as a percent per year of schooling (or use \(100(e^\beta-1)\) for the exact figure). The two experience terms must be read together, never separately: the linear coefficient is positive and the squared coefficient is negative, so the marginal effect \(\beta_{\text{exper}}+2\beta_{\text{exper}^2}\cdot\text{exper}\) starts large and shrinks, hitting zero at the printed peak (here around the mid-20s of years), after which more experience is associated with lower wages. The plotted profile is exactly this marginal-effect story accumulated into a curve. The lesson generalizes: in any polynomial you cannot read the first coefficient alone as “the effect” — the effect is a function of the level.

chunks.heading: Instructor's take (5.5.1 Demonstration)
chunks.title: Chapter 5, Logarithms, Polynomials, and Interactions — 5.5 Instructor's take (5.5.1 Demonstration)
chunks.body:
★ Sharma's Take
The selection of a functional form is commonly treated as a technical convenience, but it constitutes a substantive hypothesis about the phenomenon under study, and should be made deliberately. A logarithmic outcome asserts that the effect of a regressor is proportional — of equal percentage magnitude for low and high values of the outcome — whereas a level outcome asserts a constant absolute effect. These are distinct economic claims, and the data themselves bear on their plausibility. The form should be chosen to express the hypothesis the analyst intends to test, rather than adopted by default; it is a component of the model's economic content, not a presentational detail.

chunks.heading: Chapter summary (5.5.1 Demonstration)
chunks.title: Chapter 5, Logarithms, Polynomials, and Interactions — 5.5 Chapter summary (5.5.1 Demonstration)
chunks.body:
Chapter Summary
Linearity in parameters permits nonlinear relationships in the variables through transformation; estimation remains OLS (Section 5.1).
A coefficient on a logged outcome is a proportional effect; a log–log coefficient is an elasticity (Definition 5.1).
In a polynomial specification the marginal effect depends on the level of the regressor, \(\beta_1+2\beta_2 x\), with turning point \(-\beta_1/(2\beta_2)\) (Section 5.2).
An interaction term makes the effect of one variable depend on another, \(\beta_1+\beta_3 x_2\) (Section 5.3).
In Python, transformations are written into the formula using np.log, I(...), and : (Section 5.5).

chunks.title: Chapter 6,  — 6.0 Overview
chunks.body: Chapter 6 · Categorical Regressors

chunks.heading: The question
chunks.title: Chapter 6, Dummy Variables — 6.0 The question
chunks.body:
The Question
How are qualitative characteristics — union membership, region, sex — incorporated into a regression, and how are the resulting coefficients interpreted?

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.title: Chapter 6, Dummy Variables — 6.0 Overview
chunks.body: Many of the things that move economic outcomes are not numbers but categories — union member or not, which region, which industry, male or female. A dummy variable turns a category into a 0/1 switch the regression can use, and the payoff is that its coefficient has a clean meaning: a difference in average outcome between groups. This chapter covers that interpretation, how to handle a category with many levels (and the trap that catches the unwary), and how to let a dummy change not just the intercept but the slope.

chunks.heading: Key idea
chunks.title: Chapter 6, Dummy Variables — 6.0 Key idea
chunks.body:
A motivating example
Suppose women in a sample earn less than men on average. Three questions follow, and dummy variables answer all three. How big is the raw gap? — a regression of log-wage on a single female dummy reads the percentage gap straight off. Does the gap survive controls? — add schooling and experience and the female coefficient becomes the gap between otherwise-similar workers. Does schooling pay off differently for women? — interact the female dummy with schooling and the slope itself is allowed to differ. We estimate all three below.

chunks.heading: The binary regressor
chunks.title: Chapter 6, Dummy Variables — 6.1 The binary regressor
chunks.body: Code a category as 1 for “yes” and 0 for “no,” drop it into the regression, and its coefficient is simply the average outcome gap between the yes-group and the no-group. With a log outcome that gap is a percentage difference — use the exact \(100(e^\beta-1)\) from Chapter 5, since dummy coefficients are often large enough that the approximation drifts. Nothing about OLS changes; only the reading does.

chunks.heading: Definition (The binary regressor)
chunks.title: Chapter 6, Dummy Variables — 6.1 Definition (The binary regressor)
chunks.body:
Definition 6.1 — Dummy variable
A dummy (or indicator) variable takes the value 1 when a condition holds and 0 otherwise. In the regression \( y=\beta_0+\beta_1 d+u \) with \(d\) a dummy, the conditional mean of \(y\) is \(\beta_0\) for the group with \(d=0\) and \(\beta_0+\beta_1\) for the group with \(d=1\). The coefficient \(\beta_1\) is the difference in mean outcome between the two groups.

chunks.heading: The binary regressor
chunks.title: Chapter 6, Dummy Variables — 6.1 The binary regressor
chunks.body: The group coded zero is the base (or reference) group, against which the dummy coefficient is measured. When the dummy is included alongside other regressors, its coefficient becomes the between-group difference holding those regressors fixed — a conditional, rather than unconditional, mean difference.

chunks.heading: Multi-category variables and the dummy-variable trap
chunks.title: Chapter 6, Dummy Variables — 6.2 Multi-category variables and the dummy-variable trap
chunks.body: For a category with \(m\) levels (say four regions), you create \(m-1\) dummies and leave one out as the base. Each coefficient then reads as that level's average gap from the base. You must omit one: include all \(m\) dummies and an intercept and the model breaks — the dummy-variable trap.

chunks.heading: Derivation (Multi-category variables and the dummy-variable trap)
chunks.title: Chapter 6, Dummy Variables — 6.2 Derivation (Multi-category variables and the dummy-variable trap)
chunks.body:
For the mathematically curious: why the trap is exact collinearity
The \(m\) dummies sum to exactly 1 for every observation (each unit is in exactly one category), which reproduces the intercept's column of 1s. That is an exact linear dependence among the regressors — a violation of MLR.3 — so the coefficients are not identified, and software either silently drops a column or returns an error. Omitting one category restores identification.

chunks.heading: Key idea (Multi-category variables and the dummy-variable trap)
chunks.title: Chapter 6, Dummy Variables — 6.2 Key idea (Multi-category variables and the dummy-variable trap)
chunks.body:
Key Idea
One category must be omitted to serve as the base. All coefficients are then interpreted relative to that base; the choice of base does not affect the fitted values but determines which comparisons the coefficients express, and should be made for interpretability.

chunks.heading: Letting the slope differ: dummy interactions
chunks.title: Chapter 6, Dummy Variables — 6.3 Letting the slope differ: dummy interactions
chunks.body: A dummy on its own shifts the whole line up or down — a different intercept for each group. Interact the dummy with a continuous regressor and you let the slope differ too: the return to schooling, say, can be steeper for one group than another. So a plain dummy answers “different starting level?” and a dummy interaction answers “different payoff per unit?” Use both and each group gets its own line entirely.

chunks.heading: Derivation (Letting the slope differ: dummy interactions)
chunks.title: Chapter 6, Dummy Variables — 6.3 Derivation (Letting the slope differ: dummy interactions)
chunks.body:
For the mathematically curious: two lines from one regression, and the Chow test
In \( y=\beta_0+\beta_1 x+\beta_2 d+\beta_3 (d\cdot x)+u \), the base group (\(d=0\)) follows \(\beta_0+\beta_1 x\) and the other group (\(d=1\)) follows \((\beta_0+\beta_2)+(\beta_1+\beta_3)x\). So \(\beta_2\) shifts the intercept and \(\beta_3\) shifts the slope. The two groups share one identical line exactly when \(\beta_2=\beta_3=0\); testing that joint hypothesis with an \(F\)-test is the Chow test.

chunks.heading: Dummy variables in Python
chunks.title: Chapter 6, Dummy Variables — 6.4 Dummy variables in Python
chunks.body:
A binary variable coded 0/1 enters the formula directly. A categorical variable is wrapped in C(...), which constructs the required dummies and omits a base level automatically; the base may be specified with Treatment.
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
# a binary regressor enters directly; its coefficient is the gap between the two groups
m1 = smf.ols("wage ~ educ + union", data=df).fit()
# a categorical variable: C(...) creates one dummy per category, omitting a base level
m2 = smf.ols("wage ~ educ + C(region)", data=df).fit()
# choose the base level explicitly with Treatment
m3 = smf.ols("wage ~ educ + C(region, Treatment(reference='North'))", data=df).fit()
An interaction between a category and a continuous regressor yields group-specific slopes, and the equality of the group regressions is tested jointly.
# interaction of a category with a continuous regressor: group-specific slopes
m4 = smf.ols("wage ~ educ + female + educ:female", data=df).fit()
# return to schooling for men is the educ coefficient; for women, educ + educ:female
# test whether the two groups share the same line (intercept and slope)
print(m4.f_test("female = 0, educ:female = 0"))

chunks.heading: Reading the output (6.4.1 Demonstration)
chunks.title: Chapter 6, Dummy Variables — 6.4 Reading the output (6.4.1 Demonstration)
chunks.body: Reading the output. First compare the raw and conditional female coefficients: the raw gap is the overall percentage difference in wages, while the conditional gap (after adding schooling and experience) is the difference between otherwise-similar men and women — usually smaller, because part of the raw gap reflects differences in experience rather than sex itself. Both are printed as exact percentage gaps via \(100(e^\beta-1)\), the right move for a log outcome with a sizeable dummy coefficient. In the interaction model, the educ coefficient is the return to schooling for the base group (men) and educ + female:educ is the return for women; the sign of female:educ says whose schooling pays off more steeply. A joint \(F\)-test that female and female:educ are both zero is the Chow test for whether men and women share a single wage line.

chunks.heading: Instructor's take (6.4.1 Demonstration)
chunks.title: Chapter 6, Dummy Variables — 6.4 Instructor's take (6.4.1 Demonstration)
chunks.body:
★ Sharma's Take
The choice of base category, although immaterial to the fitted model, governs the interpretability of the entire table, since every coefficient is expressed relative to it. A base chosen without consideration yields coefficients that answer questions of no interest; a base equal to the largest or most natural reference category yields coefficients that correspond to substantively meaningful comparisons. Furthermore, when two estimated tables are compared, a coefficient that differs between them may do so solely because the base category differs, not because any underlying quantity has changed. The base should therefore be selected deliberately and held constant across compared specifications.

chunks.heading: Chapter summary (6.4.1 Demonstration)
chunks.title: Chapter 6, Dummy Variables — 6.4 Chapter summary (6.4.1 Demonstration)
chunks.body:
Chapter Summary
A dummy variable encodes category membership; its coefficient is a difference in conditional means relative to the base group (Section 6.1).
A variable with \(m\) categories requires \(m-1\) dummies; including all \(m\) with an intercept causes exact collinearity (the dummy-variable trap) (Section 6.2).
A dummy interacted with a continuous regressor permits group-specific slopes; equality of group regressions is tested jointly (Section 6.3).
In Python, C(category) constructs the dummies and omits a base, selectable with Treatment (Section 6.4).

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.title: Chapter 7,  — 7.0 Overview
chunks.body: Chapter 7 · Non-Constant Variance

chunks.heading: The question
chunks.title: Chapter 7, Heteroskedasticity — 7.0 The question
chunks.body:
The Question
When the dispersion of the disturbance varies with the regressors, are the coefficient estimates and their standard errors still valid?

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.title: Chapter 7, Heteroskedasticity — 7.0 Overview
chunks.body: The homoskedasticity assumption MLR.5 — that the error has the same variance for every observation — is one of the first to fail in real economic data. The good news is that the failure is mild: it leaves the OLS coefficients unbiased and touches only the standard errors. The bad news is that the conventional standard errors then become wrong, so every t-test, F-test, confidence interval, and p-value built on them is unreliable. This chapter pins down exactly what breaks, and shows that a one-line fix — robust standard errors — restores valid inference and should be your default.

chunks.heading: Key idea
chunks.title: Chapter 7, Heteroskedasticity — 7.0 Key idea
chunks.body:
A motivating example
Regress household savings on income. Low-income households have little room to maneuver, so their savings cluster tightly around the line; high-income households can save heavily or splurge, so their savings scatter widely. Plot the residuals against income and they fan out — small on the left, large on the right. The line through the middle is still in the right place (the coefficient is fine), but the usual standard-error formula, which assumes uniform scatter, mismeasures how precisely that line is pinned down. We reproduce this fan below and fix the inference.

chunks.heading: Definition and consequences
chunks.title: Chapter 7, Heteroskedasticity — 7.1 Definition and consequences
chunks.body: Heteroskedasticity is a long word for a simple picture: the spread of the errors changes across the data instead of staying constant. It is the normal state of cross-sectional data — bigger units usually vary more — so it is worth knowing precisely what it does, and does not, ruin.

chunks.heading: Definition (Definition and consequences)
chunks.title: Chapter 7, Heteroskedasticity — 7.1 Definition (Definition and consequences)
chunks.body:
Definition 7.1 — Homoskedasticity and heteroskedasticity
The disturbance is homoskedastic if \(\mathrm{Var}(u\mid x)=\sigma^2\), constant across the regressors, and heteroskedastic if \(\mathrm{Var}(u\mid x)\) varies with them.

chunks.heading: Definition and consequences
chunks.title: Chapter 7, Heteroskedasticity — 7.1 Definition and consequences
chunks.body: Heteroskedasticity is the typical condition of cross-sectional economic data: units with larger values of a regressor frequently exhibit greater dispersion in the outcome. Its consequences are precisely delimited.

chunks.heading: Proposition (Definition and consequences)
chunks.title: Chapter 7, Heteroskedasticity — 7.1 Proposition (Definition and consequences)
chunks.body:
Proposition 7.1
Under MLR.1–MLR.4, the OLS estimator is unbiased irrespective of the form of \(\mathrm{Var}(u\mid x)\). Heteroskedasticity does not bias the coefficients. However, the conventional variance formula of Chapter 4, which assumes homoskedasticity, is no longer valid; the conventional standard errors are therefore incorrect, and the associated \(t\)- and \(F\)-statistics, confidence intervals, and p-values are invalid.

chunks.heading: Definition and consequences
chunks.title: Chapter 7, Heteroskedasticity — 7.1 Definition and consequences
chunks.body: Unbiasedness follows because it depends only on MLR.4, the conditional mean of the disturbance, not on its variance. The conventional standard errors are typically too small under heteroskedasticity, overstating precision and significance.

chunks.heading: Key idea (Definition and consequences)
chunks.title: Chapter 7, Heteroskedasticity — 7.1 Key idea (Definition and consequences)
chunks.body:
Key Idea
Heteroskedasticity affects the standard errors, not the coefficients. The remedy is therefore not to alter the estimator but to compute its standard errors by a method valid under non-constant variance.

chunks.heading: Robust standard errors
chunks.title: Chapter 7, Heteroskedasticity — 7.2 Robust standard errors
chunks.body: The heteroskedasticity-robust (or heteroskedasticity-consistent) standard errors, due to White, estimate the variance of the OLS estimator without assuming constant error variance, allowing each observation its own variance. They are valid whether or not heteroskedasticity is present: under homoskedasticity they coincide asymptotically with the conventional standard errors, and under heteroskedasticity they remain valid where the conventional standard errors fail. As they impose no cost when homoskedasticity holds and restore validity when it does not, they are the appropriate default for cross-sectional regression.

chunks.heading: Derivation (Robust standard errors)
chunks.title: Chapter 7, Heteroskedasticity — 7.2 Derivation (Robust standard errors)
chunks.body:
For the mathematically curious: what robust standard errors actually compute
The classical variance of \(\hat\beta\) is \(\sigma^2 (X'X)^{-1}\), which bakes in a single \(\sigma^2\). White's estimator replaces the middle with each observation's own squared residual, \((X'X)^{-1}\big(\sum_i \hat u_i^2\, x_i x_i'\big)(X'X)^{-1}\) — the “sandwich” form. It lets every observation carry its own variance, so no constant-variance assumption is needed. Variants HC1–HC3 add small-sample corrections; HC1 is the common default.

chunks.heading: Testing for heteroskedasticity
chunks.title: Chapter 7, Heteroskedasticity — 7.3 Testing for heteroskedasticity
chunks.body: The Breusch–Pagan test assesses whether the squared residuals are systematically related to the regressors. Its null hypothesis is homoskedasticity; rejection indicates non-constant variance. The related White test admits more general forms by including squares and cross-products of the regressors. In practice, because robust standard errors are valid regardless of the test's outcome, the tests are diagnostic rather than decisive; applied work generally proceeds directly to robust standard errors.

chunks.heading: Robust inference in Python
chunks.title: Chapter 7, Heteroskedasticity — 7.4 Robust inference in Python
chunks.body:
Robust standard errors are obtained by passing cov_type="HC1" to the fit method. The coefficients are unchanged; only the standard errors, and the statistics derived from them, differ.
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
ols = smf.ols("wage ~ educ + exper", data=df).fit() # classical SE
robust = smf.ols("wage ~ educ + exper", data=df).fit(cov_type="HC1") # robust SE
print(ols.bse["educ"]) # standard error assuming constant error variance
print(robust.bse["educ"]) # standard error valid under heteroskedasticity
# the coefficient is identical; only the standard error changes
The Breusch–Pagan test is available in statsmodels.stats.
import statsmodels.stats.api as sms
# Breusch-Pagan test: H0 is constant error variance (homoskedasticity)
bp = sms.het_breuschpagan(ols.resid, ols.model.exog)
print("LM statistic:", bp[0], " p-value:", bp[1])
The demonstration below reports the classical and robust standard errors side by side, exhibiting the unchanged coefficient and the altered standard error.

chunks.heading: Reading the output (7.4.1 Demonstration)
chunks.title: Chapter 7, Heteroskedasticity — 7.4 Reading the output (7.4.1 Demonstration)
chunks.body: Reading the output. The two rows show an identical inc coefficient and different standard errors — the whole point: heteroskedasticity moves the SE, not the estimate. Here the robust SE is larger than the classical one, so the classical t-statistic overstated how precisely savings track income; a result that looked comfortably significant under classical SEs is held to a stricter standard once the fan is accounted for. The Breusch–Pagan p-value (tiny here) formally rejects constant variance, and the residual plot shows why — the cloud widens with income. In practice you would jump straight to the robust row regardless of the test, since robust SEs are valid either way.

chunks.heading: Instructor's take (7.4.1 Demonstration)
chunks.title: Chapter 7, Heteroskedasticity — 7.4 Instructor's take (7.4.1 Demonstration)
chunks.body:
★ Sharma's Take
A residual plot that widens systematically with a regressor is conventionally read as evidence of heteroskedasticity, but the same pattern is produced by an incorrect functional form. If the true relationship is curved and a linear specification is fitted, the residuals fan out exactly as under heteroskedasticity; robust standard errors then correct the inference while leaving the misspecification of the conditional mean uncorrected. The systematic widening of residuals should therefore prompt, first, an examination of functional form — the introduction of a logarithm or a polynomial term — and only thereafter the application of robust standard errors. The diagnostic for non-constant variance and the diagnostic for incorrect form coincide in appearance, and the form should be addressed before the variance.

chunks.heading: Chapter summary (7.4.1 Demonstration)
chunks.title: Chapter 7, Heteroskedasticity — 7.4 Chapter summary (7.4.1 Demonstration)
chunks.body:
Chapter Summary
Heteroskedasticity is non-constant conditional variance of the disturbance; it is typical of cross-sectional data (Section 7.1).
It leaves the OLS coefficients unbiased but invalidates the conventional standard errors and all inference based on them (Proposition 7.1).
Heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors are valid with or without heteroskedasticity and are the appropriate default (Section 7.2).
The Breusch–Pagan and White tests assess non-constant variance but are diagnostic, since robust standard errors are valid regardless (Section 7.3).
In Python, fit(cov_type="HC1") produces robust standard errors (Section 7.4).

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.title: Chapter 8,  — 8.0 Overview
chunks.body: Chapter 8 · Measurement and Specification

chunks.heading: The question
chunks.title: Chapter 8, Measurement Error and Proxy Variables — 8.0 The question
chunks.body:
The Question
When a regressor is observed with error — reported rather than true income, a test score rather than ability — what is the consequence for the estimated coefficient?

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.title: Chapter 8, Measurement Error and Proxy Variables — 8.0 Overview
chunks.body: Economic variables are measured imperfectly — income is self-reported, ability is glimpsed through a test score, output is estimated. Where that noise lands matters enormously. Noise in the outcome is harmless to the coefficients (it merely costs precision); noise in a regressor is corrosive, dragging its coefficient toward zero in a predictable way called attenuation. This chapter draws that sharp line, connects attenuation to the proxy variables we lean on when something cannot be measured directly, and adds a test for the separate problem of a wrong functional form.

chunks.heading: Key idea
chunks.title: Chapter 8, Measurement Error and Proxy Variables — 8.0 Key idea
chunks.body:
A motivating example
Ask whether income affects health, using survey income — which people misremember, round, and shade. The true income is what matters, but you regress on a noisy version of it. Part of that noisy regressor is pure error, unrelated to health, and it dilutes the signal: the estimated income effect comes out smaller than the truth, never larger. The same logic explains why the test-score proxy for ability in Chapter 3 only partly cleaned up the schooling coefficient. We simulate this melting-toward-zero below.

chunks.heading: Measurement error in the outcome
chunks.title: Chapter 8, Measurement Error and Proxy Variables — 8.1 Measurement error in the outcome
chunks.body: Suppose the outcome is measured with error, the observed value being the true value plus a random term uncorrelated with the regressors. The measurement error is absorbed into the disturbance. Provided it satisfies MLR.4, the OLS estimator remains unbiased; the only consequence is a larger disturbance variance, hence larger standard errors. Measurement error in the outcome reduces precision but does not bias the coefficients.

chunks.heading: Measurement error in a regressor: attenuation
chunks.title: Chapter 8, Measurement Error and Proxy Variables — 8.2 Measurement error in a regressor: attenuation
chunks.body: Now put the noise in a regressor: you observe the true value plus an independent random error (the classical errors-in-variables setup). Part of what you feed the regression is junk — unrelated to the outcome — and OLS, unable to tell signal from junk, reports a coefficient pulled toward zero. The noisier the measurement, the more it shrinks. This is attenuation bias, and unlike most biases its direction is always known: toward zero.

chunks.heading: Derivation (Measurement error in a regressor: attenuation)
chunks.title: Chapter 8, Measurement Error and Proxy Variables — 8.2 Derivation (Measurement error in a regressor: attenuation)
chunks.body:
For the mathematically curious: the reliability ratio
Under classical errors-in-variables with a single regressor, \[ \operatorname{plim}\hat\beta_1 = \beta_1\cdot\frac{\sigma_{x^\ast}^2}{\sigma_{x^\ast}^2+\sigma_e^2}, \] where \(\sigma_{x^\ast}^2\) is the variance of the true regressor and \(\sigma_e^2\) the variance of the measurement error. The multiplier — the reliability ratio — lies strictly between 0 and 1, so the estimate is biased toward zero; it falls (more bias) as the noise variance \(\sigma_e^2\) grows. The demonstration below traces exactly this curve.

chunks.heading: Key idea (Measurement error in a regressor: attenuation)
chunks.title: Chapter 8, Measurement Error and Proxy Variables — 8.2 Key idea (Measurement error in a regressor: attenuation)
chunks.body:
Key Idea
Classical measurement error in the outcome reduces precision but preserves unbiasedness; classical measurement error in a regressor biases its coefficient toward zero. The distinction is essential: a noisy outcome warrants no special concern, whereas a noisy regressor warrants careful attention.

chunks.heading: Proxy variables
chunks.title: Chapter 8, Measurement Error and Proxy Variables — 8.3 Proxy variables
chunks.body: When a determinant of the outcome cannot be measured, an observable correlate — a proxy — may be substituted, as in the use of a test score for ability in Chapter 3. By Proposition 8.1, a proxy measured with error has an attenuated coefficient and therefore removes only part of the confounding it is intended to control. This accounts for the pattern observed in Chapter 3, in which the coefficient on the variable of interest continued to move as successively better proxies were introduced: each imperfect proxy performs only partial adjustment. A coefficient that has not stabilized across improving proxies should be regarded as incompletely corrected.

chunks.heading: Functional-form misspecification
chunks.title: Chapter 8, Measurement Error and Proxy Variables — 8.4 Functional-form misspecification
chunks.body: A distinct specification error is an incorrect functional form — the omission of a required nonlinear term (Chapter 5). The RESET test assesses this by adding powers of the fitted values to the regression and testing their joint significance; a significant result indicates that the conditional mean is misspecified. It serves as a general diagnostic for omitted nonlinearity.

chunks.heading: Measurement error and specification tests in Python
chunks.title: Chapter 8, Measurement Error and Proxy Variables — 8.5 Measurement error and specification tests in Python
chunks.body:
The attenuation result is demonstrated by adding noise of known variance to a correctly measured regressor and observing the resulting coefficient.
import numpy as np, statsmodels.formula.api as smf
# x_true is the correct regressor; we observe a noisy version x_obs = x_true + noise
df["x_obs"] = df["x_true"] + np.random.normal(0, sd_noise, len(df))
b_true = smf.ols("y ~ x_true", data=df).fit().params["x_true"] # if x measured perfectly
b_obs = smf.ols("y ~ x_obs", data=df).fit().params["x_obs"] # with measurement error
print(b_true, b_obs) # b_obs is attenuated toward zero
Functional-form misspecification is assessed with the RESET test.
import statsmodels.stats.api as sms
# RESET test: H0 is correct functional form; rejection suggests an omitted nonlinearity
result = smf.ols("wage ~ educ + exper", data=df).fit()
reset = sms.linear_reset(result, power=2, use_f=True)
print(reset)
The demonstration below adds measurement error of increasing magnitude to a regressor and reports the coefficient, which declines toward zero as predicted by Proposition 8.1.

chunks.heading: Reading the output (8.5.1 Demonstration)
chunks.title: Chapter 8, Measurement Error and Proxy Variables — 8.5 Reading the output (8.5.1 Demonstration)
chunks.body: Reading the output. Read down the Var(e) column: at zero measurement error the OLS slope sits at the true 0.50; as the noise variance climbs, the slope melts — tracking the theoretical \(\beta_1\times\lambda\) column almost exactly, where \(\lambda\) is the reliability ratio. The plot makes the two lines coincide. The lesson to carry away: a mismeasured regressor's coefficient is a lower bound in magnitude on the truth, so a noisy variable that still shows a clear effect is strong evidence the real effect is even larger — but a noisy variable that shows nothing may simply have been measured too poorly to detect.

chunks.heading: Instructor's take (8.5.1 Demonstration)
chunks.title: Chapter 8, Measurement Error and Proxy Variables — 8.5 Instructor's take (8.5.1 Demonstration)
chunks.body:
★ Sharma's Take
The known direction of attenuation may be turned to the analyst's advantage. Because classical measurement error in a regressor biases its coefficient toward zero, an estimate obtained from a noisily measured regressor is conservative: the true effect is at least as large in magnitude as the estimate. A regressor measured with error that nonetheless exhibits a substantial, clearly nonzero coefficient therefore licenses the stronger conclusion that the true effect is larger still. The corresponding caution applies to a null result: a regressor expected to matter but estimated as an imprecise zero may have been rendered so by measurement error alone, and its unimportance cannot be inferred without consideration of how well it was measured.

chunks.heading: Chapter summary (8.5.1 Demonstration)
chunks.title: Chapter 8, Measurement Error and Proxy Variables — 8.5 Chapter summary (8.5.1 Demonstration)
chunks.body:
Chapter Summary
Classical measurement error in the outcome reduces precision but preserves unbiasedness (Section 8.1).
Classical measurement error in a regressor biases its coefficient toward zero by the reliability ratio (Proposition 8.1).
A proxy measured with error removes only part of the confounding; a coefficient still moving as proxies improve is incompletely corrected (Section 8.3).
The RESET test detects functional-form misspecification by the significance of powers of the fitted values (Section 8.4).
In Python, attenuation is demonstrated by adding noise to a regressor, and the RESET test is provided by linear_reset (Section 8.5).

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.title: Chapter 9,  — 9.0 Overview
chunks.body: Chapter 9 · Endogeneity

chunks.heading: The question
chunks.title: Chapter 9, Instrumental Variables — 9.0 The question
chunks.body:
The Question
When a confounder cannot be measured, and no adequate proxy exists, can the causal effect of a regressor nonetheless be estimated?

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.title: Chapter 9, Instrumental Variables — 9.0 Overview
chunks.body: Sometimes the confounder you fear cannot be measured and no proxy will do — controls and robust standard errors are both powerless, because the regressor itself is tangled up with the error term. Instrumental variables is the escape hatch. The trick is to find a third variable that nudges the regressor for reasons that have nothing to do with the outcome, and to use only that clean, instrument-driven slice of variation. This chapter explains when a regressor is “endogenous,” what makes an instrument valid, how two-stage least squares puts it to work, and why a weak instrument can be worse than the disease.

chunks.heading: Key idea
chunks.title: Chapter 9, Instrumental Variables — 9.0 Key idea
chunks.body:
A motivating example
Return to the schooling puzzle: more-able people get more schooling and earn more for reasons unrelated to school, so OLS overstates the return — and we cannot observe ability to control for it. Now suppose that, decades ago, some students happened to grow up closer to a college — pure geography, unrelated to their ability. Proximity pushes them to get more schooling but has no direct line to their later wages. That is an instrument: it moves schooling for an “innocent” reason, and the wage difference it traces out estimates the causal return free of the ability bias. We build exactly this below.

chunks.heading: Endogeneity
chunks.title: Chapter 9, Instrumental Variables — 9.1 Endogeneity
chunks.body: “Endogenous” is the umbrella word for a regressor that is correlated with the error term — the very thing MLR.4 forbids. When it happens, OLS is not merely imprecise, it is inconsistent: more data will not save it. Three culprits produce it, and they recur throughout applied work: an omitted confounder, reverse causation (the outcome feeds back on the regressor), and measurement error in the regressor (Chapter 8).

chunks.heading: Definition (Endogeneity)
chunks.title: Chapter 9, Instrumental Variables — 9.1 Definition (Endogeneity)
chunks.body:
Definition 9.1 — Endogeneity
A regressor is endogenous if it is correlated with the disturbance, \(\mathrm{Cov}(x,u)\ne 0\), in violation of MLR.4. The OLS estimator is then biased and inconsistent. Three sources are standard: an omitted variable correlated with both the regressor and the outcome; simultaneity, in which the outcome also influences the regressor; and measurement error in the regressor (Chapter 8).

chunks.heading: The instrument
chunks.title: Chapter 9, Instrumental Variables — 9.2 The instrument
chunks.body: An instrument \(z\) is a variable that induces variation in the endogenous regressor that is unrelated to the disturbance. The endogenous regressor contains variation correlated with the disturbance (which biases OLS) and, through the instrument, variation that is not; the method uses only the latter. An instrument must therefore hold two jobs at once: it must genuinely move the regressor (relevance), and it must reach the outcome through no channel other than that regressor (exogeneity) — and only the first of these can be checked in the data.

chunks.heading: Definition (The instrument)
chunks.title: Chapter 9, Instrumental Variables — 9.2 Definition (The instrument)
chunks.body:
Definition 9.2 — Conditions for a valid instrument
Relevance: \(\mathrm{Cov}(z,x)\ne 0\); the instrument is correlated with the endogenous regressor. This condition is testable from the first-stage regression.
Exogeneity (the exclusion restriction): \(\mathrm{Cov}(z,u)=0\); the instrument is uncorrelated with the disturbance, affecting the outcome only through the regressor. This condition is not testable and must be justified by argument.

chunks.heading: Two-stage least squares
chunks.title: Chapter 9, Instrumental Variables — 9.3 Two-stage least squares
chunks.body: Two-stage least squares (2SLS) is the practical recipe. Stage one: regress the troublesome regressor on the instrument (and any controls) and keep the fitted values — this is the “clean” part of the regressor, the slice the instrument explains, scrubbed of its correlation with the error. Stage two: regress the outcome on that cleaned-up regressor. The resulting slope is the IV estimate. In a sentence: throw away the contaminated variation in the regressor and keep only the instrument-driven part.

chunks.heading: Derivation (Two-stage least squares)
chunks.title: Chapter 9, Instrumental Variables — 9.3 Derivation (Two-stage least squares)
chunks.body:
For the mathematically curious: the IV formula and why 2SLS is consistent
With a single instrument and no controls, the IV estimator has the closed form \[ \hat\beta_{IV} = \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(z,y)}{\operatorname{Cov}(z,x)}, \] the instrument's effect on the outcome divided by its effect on the regressor (a ratio of the reduced form to the first stage). The stage-one fitted values depend only on the instrument and the exogenous controls, so they are uncorrelated with the disturbance; regressing \(y\) on them therefore yields a consistent estimate under relevance and exogeneity (Definition 9.2). Note IV is consistent, not generally unbiased in finite samples.

chunks.heading: Two-stage least squares
chunks.title: Chapter 9, Instrumental Variables — 9.3 Two-stage least squares
chunks.body: Always estimate 2SLS with a dedicated routine rather than literally running the two regressions yourself: the hand-built second stage reports the wrong standard errors, because it ignores that the first-stage fitted values were themselves estimated. The coefficient comes out identical; the standard errors do not.

chunks.heading: Weak instruments
chunks.title: Chapter 9, Instrumental Variables — 9.4 Weak instruments
chunks.body: When the instrument is only weakly correlated with the endogenous regressor, the instrument-induced variation is small, and the 2SLS estimator is imprecise and may exhibit substantial bias — in extreme cases exceeding that of OLS. The strength of the instrument is assessed by the \(F\)-statistic on the excluded instrument in the first-stage regression; a common rule of thumb requires it to exceed ten.

chunks.heading: Key idea (Weak instruments)
chunks.title: Chapter 9, Instrumental Variables — 9.4 Key idea (Weak instruments)
chunks.body:
Key Idea
A valid instrument must satisfy both relevance and exogeneity. Relevance is verifiable from the first stage; exogeneity is not testable and rests on argument. A weak instrument (low relevance) yields imprecise and possibly biased estimates; a violation of exogeneity yields inconsistency that no diagnostic detects.

chunks.heading: Instrumental-variables estimation in Python
chunks.title: Chapter 9, Instrumental Variables — 9.5 Instrumental-variables estimation in Python
chunks.body:
Two-stage least squares is provided by the linearmodels library, whose formula syntax places the endogenous regressor and its instruments in square brackets. The routine computes correct standard errors.
from linearmodels.iv import IV2SLS
# syntax: dependent ~ exogenous + [endogenous ~ instruments]
# here educ is endogenous and z is the instrument; exper is an exogenous control
model = IV2SLS.from_formula("wage ~ 1 + exper + [educ ~ z]", data=df)
result = model.fit(cov_type="robust")
print(result.summary)
print(result.params["educ"]) # the 2SLS estimate of the schooling effect
The strength of the instrument is assessed by the first-stage \(F\)-statistic on the excluded instrument.
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
# first stage: regress the endogenous regressor on the instrument and controls
first = smf.ols("educ ~ z + exper", data=df).fit()
# strength of the instrument: F-statistic on the excluded instrument (rule of thumb > 10)
print(first.f_test("z = 0"))
The demonstration below constructs data in which the regressor is endogenous, exhibits the bias of OLS, and recovers the true effect by 2SLS using a valid instrument, reporting the first-stage strength.

chunks.heading: Reading the output (9.5.1 Demonstration)
chunks.title: Chapter 9, Instrumental Variables — 9.5 Reading the output (9.5.1 Demonstration)
chunks.body: Reading the output. Three numbers tell the story. The true return is 0.075; OLS comes out well above it, inflated by the ability bias baked into the data (able people get more schooling and earn more anyway). 2SLS lands back near 0.075 — it ignores the contaminated variation and uses only the schooling differences driven by the instrument, which are unrelated to ability. The first-stage F sits comfortably above 10, certifying the instrument is strong enough to trust. Notice the cost: the 2SLS standard error would exceed the OLS one — you buy consistency by discarding most of the variation in schooling and keeping only the instrument-driven slice. And the note in the cell is the practical lesson: the hand-built second stage gives the right coefficient but the wrong SE, so reach for a real IV routine.

chunks.heading: Instructor's take (9.5.1 Demonstration)
chunks.title: Chapter 9, Instrumental Variables — 9.5 Instructor's take (9.5.1 Demonstration)
chunks.body:
★ Sharma's Take
Because the exclusion restriction is not testable, the credibility of an instrumental-variables estimate rests entirely on a substantive argument, and that argument is best examined by attempting to refute it. The instrument should be stated as a complete proposition — that it influences the endogenous regressor and affects the outcome through no other channel — and the analyst should then enumerate alternative channels by which the instrument might affect the outcome directly. If any plausible such channel exists, the exclusion restriction is doubtful, and no statistical procedure will disclose the resulting inconsistency. The weakness of an instrument announces itself in the first-stage statistics; a violation of exogeneity does not, and it is therefore the point on which scrutiny should concentrate.

chunks.heading: Chapter summary (9.5.1 Demonstration)
chunks.title: Chapter 9, Instrumental Variables — 9.5 Chapter summary (9.5.1 Demonstration)
chunks.body:
Chapter Summary
A regressor is endogenous when correlated with the disturbance; OLS is then biased and inconsistent (Section 9.1).
A valid instrument satisfies relevance (correlated with the regressor) and exogeneity (uncorrelated with the disturbance); only the former is testable (Section 9.2).
Two-stage least squares replaces the endogenous regressor with the component explained by the instrument and yields a consistent estimate (Section 9.3).
Weak instruments produce imprecise and possibly biased estimates; first-stage strength is assessed by an \(F\)-statistic (Section 9.4).
In Python, linearmodels.IV2SLS estimates the model with correct standard errors (Section 9.5).

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.title: Chapter 10,  — 10.0 Overview
chunks.body: Chapter 10 · Panel Data

chunks.heading: The question
chunks.title: Chapter 10, Fixed Effects — 10.0 The question
chunks.body:
The Question
When the same units are observed over several periods, can the influence of their unobserved, time-invariant characteristics be eliminated?

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.title: Chapter 10, Fixed Effects — 10.0 Overview
chunks.body: When you observe the same units — people, firms, countries — in more than one period, a powerful move opens up: compare each unit only with itself over time. Any confounder that is a fixed trait of the unit (talent, location, culture, management quality) then cancels out, whether or not you can measure it. That is the appeal of fixed effects, and this chapter builds it from the within transformation, states precisely what it can and cannot do, and runs it in Python.

chunks.heading: Key idea
chunks.title: Chapter 10, Fixed Effects — 10.0 Key idea
chunks.body:
A motivating example
Imagine workers whose output quality you track over many weeks. Within each worker, the more hours worked, the lower the quality — fatigue. But skilled workers both work longer hours and produce higher quality, so when you pool everyone into one scatter, the cloud slopes the wrong way and longer hours look good. Skill is a fixed trait you never measured. Compare each worker only with himself across weeks and skill cancels — the true within-worker fatigue effect reappears. The demonstration below builds exactly this sign-flip and fixes it.

chunks.heading: Panel data and the fixed-effects model
chunks.title: Chapter 10, Fixed Effects — 10.1 Panel data and the fixed-effects model
chunks.body:
Panel data index each observation by unit \(i\) and time \(t\). The fixed-effects model assigns each unit its own intercept:
\[ y_{it} = \alpha_i + \beta_1 x_{it} + u_{it}, \]
where \(\alpha_i\), the fixed effect, captures all time-invariant characteristics of unit \(i\) — observed or unobserved. The parameter \(\beta_1\) is identified from variation within units over time.

chunks.heading: The within transformation
chunks.title: Chapter 10, Fixed Effects — 10.2 The within transformation
chunks.body: The mechanism is simple subtraction. For each unit, compute its own average over time, then express every variable as a deviation from that average. Because the fixed effect \(\alpha_i\) is the same in every period for unit \(i\), it equals its own time-average and the subtraction wipes it out — leaving a relationship estimated purely from how each unit deviates from its own norm over time.

chunks.heading: Derivation (The within transformation)
chunks.title: Chapter 10, Fixed Effects — 10.2 Derivation (The within transformation)
chunks.body:
For the mathematically curious: the demeaning algebra (and first differences)
Averaging the model over time for unit \(i\) gives \(\bar y_i = \alpha_i + \beta_1 \bar x_i + \bar u_i\). Subtracting this from the original equation eliminates the fixed effect: \[ (y_{it}-\bar y_i) = \beta_1 (x_{it}-\bar x_i) + (u_{it}-\bar u_i). \] OLS on these demeaned variables is the within (fixed-effects) estimator. First-differencing — subtracting the previous period, \(y_{it}-y_{i,t-1}\) — also removes \(\alpha_i\); it coincides with the within estimator when there are exactly two periods and is an alternative otherwise.

chunks.heading: Definition (The within transformation)
chunks.title: Chapter 10, Fixed Effects — 10.2 Definition (The within transformation)
chunks.body:
Definition 10.1 — Fixed-effects (within) estimator
The within transformation expresses each variable as a deviation from its unit-specific time mean. OLS applied to the transformed data yields the fixed-effects (or within) estimator. Because \(\alpha_i\) is eliminated, the estimator is consistent even when \(\alpha_i\) is correlated with the regressors — that is, in the presence of arbitrary time-invariant confounding.

chunks.heading: Properties and limitations
chunks.title: Chapter 10, Fixed Effects — 10.3 Properties and limitations
chunks.body:
The fixed-effects estimator controls for every time-invariant characteristic of the unit simultaneously, including unmeasured ones. This is its principal advantage. Two limitations follow from the same mechanism.
The effect of any regressor that is constant within a unit cannot be estimated, since the within transformation removes it. The effects of fixed attributes — an individual's sex, a firm's country of origin — are not identified.
The estimator addresses only time-invariant confounding. A confounder that varies over time in concert with the regressor remains, and biases the estimate.

chunks.heading: Key idea (Properties and limitations)
chunks.title: Chapter 10, Fixed Effects — 10.3 Key idea (Properties and limitations)
chunks.body:
Key Idea
Fixed effects eliminate confounding from time-invariant unit characteristics, observed or not, by comparing each unit with itself. They do not eliminate confounding from time-varying determinants, and they cannot identify the effects of characteristics that are constant within units.

chunks.heading: Fixed-effects estimation in Python
chunks.title: Chapter 10, Fixed Effects — 10.4 Fixed-effects estimation in Python
chunks.body:
The within transformation can be performed explicitly by subtracting unit means, computed with groupby(...).transform("mean"), and applying OLS to the demeaned variables.
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
# within transformation by hand: subtract each unit's own time-average from every variable
for col in ["y", "x"]:
df[col + "_dm"] = df[col] - df.groupby("firm")[col].transform("mean")
fe = smf.ols("y_dm ~ x_dm - 1", data=df).fit() # "-1": no intercept after demeaning
print(fe.params["x_dm"]) # the fixed-effects (within) estimate
In practice a dedicated panel routine is used. The linearmodels library provides PanelOLS, which performs the transformation, manages the degrees of freedom, and supports clustered standard errors (Chapter 11), once a unit–time index is set and EntityEffects is requested.
from linearmodels.panel import PanelOLS
# set a (unit, time) index, then request entity effects
panel = df.set_index(["firm", "year"])
fe = PanelOLS.from_formula("y ~ x + EntityEffects", data=panel).fit(
cov_type="clustered", cluster_entity=True) # cluster by unit (Chapter 11)
print(fe.params["x"])

chunks.heading: Reading the output (10.4.1 Demonstration)
chunks.title: Chapter 10, Fixed Effects — 10.4 Reading the output (10.4.1 Demonstration)
chunks.body: Reading the output. The true effect is negative (−0.40), yet pooled OLS reports a positive slope — a full sign reversal, because firms with large fixed effects have both higher x and higher y, and that between-firm pattern dominates the pooled cloud. Fixed effects (here implemented as firm dummies, identical to demeaning) discards the between-firm comparison and uses only each firm's movement around its own average, recovering the true −0.40. The plot is the whole lesson in one picture: every individual firm's line slopes down, while the dashed pooled line slopes up. This is Simpson's paradox in regression form — and exactly why one should ask, with Sharma, whether enough within-unit variation remains to trust the estimate once the between variation is thrown away.

chunks.heading: Instructor's take (10.4.1 Demonstration)
chunks.title: Chapter 10, Fixed Effects — 10.4 Instructor's take (10.4.1 Demonstration)
chunks.body:
★ Sharma's Take
The capacity of fixed effects to eliminate unobserved confounders invites uncritical application, but the transformation discards all between-unit variation and retains only within-unit variation, and the quantity of the latter should be examined before the estimate is trusted. If the regressor of interest changes little within units over the observation period — as is common for policies or characteristics that are stable for each unit — the within transformation leaves little variation from which to estimate the effect, and the resulting estimate rests on a small number of units that happen to change. An estimate may thus be simultaneously free of time-invariant confounding and founded on negligible identifying variation. The within-unit variation in the key regressor should therefore be assessed directly before the absence of confounding is taken to imply the reliability of the estimate.

chunks.heading: Chapter summary (10.4.1 Demonstration)
chunks.title: Chapter 10, Fixed Effects — 10.4 Chapter summary (10.4.1 Demonstration)
chunks.body:
Chapter Summary
The fixed-effects model assigns each unit its own intercept \(\alpha_i\), capturing all time-invariant characteristics (Section 10.1).
The within transformation subtracts unit-specific time means, eliminating \(\alpha_i\); OLS on the transformed data is the fixed-effects estimator, consistent under arbitrary time-invariant confounding (Section 10.2).
The estimator cannot identify effects of within-unit constant regressors, and does not address time-varying confounding (Section 10.3).
In Python, the transformation may be done by demeaning, or with linearmodels.PanelOLS and EntityEffects (Section 10.4).
