chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.title: Chapter 11,  — 11.0 Overview
chunks.body: Chapter 11 · Dependence and Panels

chunks.heading: The question
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Clustered Errors, Random Effects, and Dynamic Panels — 11.0 The question
chunks.body:
The Question
When observations within a group share unobserved influences, the assumption of independent observations fails. How is valid inference then obtained?

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Clustered Errors, Random Effects, and Dynamic Panels — 11.0 Overview
chunks.body: Every standard error in Chapter 4 assumed your observations were independent — each one a fresh, unrelated draw. In grouped and panel data that is simply false: students in one classroom, workers at one firm, people in one state all share unobserved influences, so their outcomes move together. When you ignore that and count each observation as independent, you credit yourself with more information than you actually have, and your standard errors come out too small — making noise look like signal. This chapter fixes the inference with clustered standard errors, and revisits the fixed-versus-random-effects choice for panels.

chunks.heading: Key idea
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Clustered Errors, Random Effects, and Dynamic Panels — 11.0 Key idea
chunks.body:
A motivating example
Suppose you test whether a teaching app raises scores, with 30 students in each of 50 classrooms. The 30 students in a room share a teacher, a room, a schedule — their scores are correlated, so they are not 30 independent facts; they are closer to a handful. Treat all 1,500 as independent and the formula will report a tiny standard error and a triumphant p-value — even when the app does nothing. Cluster the standard errors by classroom and the honest, much larger uncertainty reappears. The demonstration below builds exactly this trap, with a true effect of zero.

chunks.heading: Within-group dependence
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Clustered Errors, Random Effects, and Dynamic Panels — 11.1 Within-group dependence
chunks.body: Observations that share an environment — repeated observations on one unit, or distinct units within one cluster — have disturbances that are correlated, because they are influenced by common unobserved factors. The number of independent pieces of information is then smaller than the number of observations. The conventional standard-error formula, which counts each observation as independent, accordingly understates the sampling variability of the estimator.

chunks.heading: Definition (Clustered standard errors)
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Clustered Errors, Random Effects, and Dynamic Panels — 11.2 Definition (Clustered standard errors)
chunks.body:
Definition 11.1 — Clustered standard errors
Clustered standard errors estimate the variance of the OLS estimator allowing the disturbances to be arbitrarily correlated within each cluster, while treating distinct clusters as independent. The cluster is chosen to correspond to the level at which the disturbances are dependent — the unit, the industry, or the geographic area at which shocks are shared or treatment is assigned.

chunks.heading: Clustered standard errors
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Clustered Errors, Random Effects, and Dynamic Panels — 11.2 Clustered standard errors
chunks.body: The coefficients are unchanged; only the standard errors are recomputed. Clustering typically increases the standard errors, often substantially, by acknowledging the reduced quantity of independent information. The failure to cluster in grouped data is a common cause of spuriously significant findings.

chunks.heading: Derivation (Clustered standard errors)
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Clustered Errors, Random Effects, and Dynamic Panels — 11.2 Derivation (Clustered standard errors)
chunks.body:
For the mathematically curious: how badly are naive SEs wrong?
With clusters of equal size \(m\) and intra-cluster correlation \(\rho\) (the share of the disturbance variance that is common within a cluster), the conventional variance is too small by the design effect \[ 1 + (m-1)\rho. \] Naive standard errors are therefore too small by a factor of about \(\sqrt{1+(m-1)\rho}\). The damage grows with cluster size: even a mild \(\rho=0.1\) in clusters of 30 gives \(\sqrt{1+29(0.1)}\approx 2\), so the true standard error is understated about twofold. This is why ignoring clustering so reliably manufactures significance.

chunks.heading: Key idea (Clustered standard errors)
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Clustered Errors, Random Effects, and Dynamic Panels — 11.2 Key idea (Clustered standard errors)
chunks.body:
Key Idea
Standard errors should be clustered at the level at which the disturbances are correlated — generally the level at which treatment is assigned or shocks are shared. Clustering at too fine a level continues to overstate precision; the correct cluster is determined by the structure of the dependence, not by convenience.

chunks.heading: Random effects
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Clustered Errors, Random Effects, and Dynamic Panels — 11.3 Random effects
chunks.body: The fixed-effects estimator of Chapter 10 uses only within-unit variation, discarding between-unit variation and the effects of time-invariant regressors. The random-effects estimator instead retains both sources of variation, under the additional assumption that the unit effect is uncorrelated with the regressors.

chunks.heading: Definition (Random effects)
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Clustered Errors, Random Effects, and Dynamic Panels — 11.3 Definition (Random effects)
chunks.body:
Definition 11.2 — Random effects
The random-effects model treats the unit effect \(\alpha_i\) as a random component of the disturbance, assumed uncorrelated with the regressors. Under this assumption the estimator is more efficient than fixed effects and can identify the effects of time-invariant regressors. If the assumption fails — if \(\alpha_i\) is correlated with the regressors, the situation of unobserved confounding — the random-effects estimator is inconsistent, and fixed effects is required.

chunks.heading: Random effects
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Clustered Errors, Random Effects, and Dynamic Panels — 11.3 Random effects
chunks.body: The choice between the two is informed by comparing their estimates, and the Hausman test formalizes that comparison. Its null hypothesis is the random-effects assumption itself — that the unit effect is uncorrelated with the regressors. Under the null both estimators are consistent but random effects is efficient, so the two should sit close together; under the alternative only fixed effects is consistent, so they diverge. The test asks whether the gap between the two coefficient vectors is larger than sampling noise alone would produce.

chunks.heading: Derivation (Random effects)
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Clustered Errors, Random Effects, and Dynamic Panels — 11.3 Derivation (Random effects)
chunks.body:
For the mathematically curious: the Hausman statistic
The statistic weights the gap between the estimators by the variance the comparison itself carries: \[ H = (\hat\beta_{FE}-\hat\beta_{RE})'\,\big[\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_{FE})-\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_{RE})\big]^{-1}\,(\hat\beta_{FE}-\hat\beta_{RE}), \] distributed \(\chi^2\) with degrees of freedom equal to the number of compared coefficients under the null. The variance difference appears because, under the null, fixed effects is the less efficient of two consistent estimators, so \(\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_{FE})\ge\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_{RE})\) and the difference is itself a valid (positive) variance for the contrast.

chunks.heading: Random effects
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Clustered Errors, Random Effects, and Dynamic Panels — 11.3 Random effects
chunks.body: The reading is simple: reject the null and the unit effect is correlated with the regressors — the unobserved-confounding case — so fixed effects is required; fail to reject and random effects is admissible and, being more efficient, preferred. Two cautions: failing to reject is not proof the assumption holds (the test may simply lack power), and in finite samples the estimated variance difference can come out non-positive, leaving the statistic undefined — a signal to lean on the substantive argument rather than the number.

chunks.heading: Reading the output (11.3.1 Demonstration)
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Clustered Errors, Random Effects, and Dynamic Panels — 11.3 Reading the output (11.3.1 Demonstration)
chunks.body: Reading the output. Two panels, same true slope of 0.50, opposite verdicts. When \(x\) is correlated with the unit effect, fixed effects recovers 0.50 but random effects is badly biased (around 0.82, dragged up because it trusts the contaminated between-unit variation); the Hausman statistic is enormous and rejects, telling you to use fixed effects. When \(x\) is independent of the unit effect, fixed and random effects nearly coincide (both near 0.50), the Hausman statistic is tiny, and the test does not reject — here random effects is the right choice, since it is consistent and more efficient. The quasi-demeaning weight \(\theta\) also shifts between the cases: random effects is a weighted blend of within and between variation, and the test is really asking whether leaning on the between part can be trusted.

chunks.heading: Clustered and panel inference in Python
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Clustered Errors, Random Effects, and Dynamic Panels — 11.4 Clustered and panel inference in Python
chunks.body:
Clustered standard errors are requested through the cov_type and cov_kwds arguments of fit, with the cluster variable supplied as groups.
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
# cluster-robust standard errors: errors may be correlated within each firm
result = smf.ols("y ~ x", data=df).fit(
cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": df["firm"]})
print(result.bse["x"]) # clustered standard error (usually much larger)
The random-effects and fixed-effects estimators are provided by linearmodels; comparing their coefficients implements the Hausman comparison.
from linearmodels.panel import RandomEffects, PanelOLS
panel = df.set_index(["firm", "year"])
re_model = RandomEffects.from_formula("y ~ 1 + x", data=panel).fit()
fe_model = PanelOLS.from_formula("y ~ 1 + x + EntityEffects", data=panel).fit()
# compare: large divergence favours fixed effects (the Hausman comparison)
print(re_model.params["x"], fe_model.params["x"])
The demonstration below reports the standard error of a coefficient under the independence assumption and under clustering, exhibiting the increase that honest treatment of the dependence requires.

chunks.heading: Reading the output (11.4.1 Demonstration)
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Clustered Errors, Random Effects, and Dynamic Panels — 11.4 Reading the output (11.4.1 Demonstration)
chunks.body: Reading the output. Look at the two lines. The coefficient is identical in both — clustering never touches the point estimate, only its standard error. But the naive row shows a small SE and a significant-looking p-value, while the clustered row shows a much larger SE and a p-value that (correctly) finds nothing — the true effect is zero. The printed design effect explains the gap: with 20 per cluster and \(\rho=0.5\), the naive SE is too small by about \(\sqrt{1+19(0.5)}\approx 3.2\) times. Had you trusted the naive standard error, you would have published a confident finding about a coefficient that is genuinely nothing.

chunks.heading: Instructor's take (11.4.1 Demonstration)
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Clustered Errors, Random Effects, and Dynamic Panels — 11.4 Instructor's take (11.4.1 Demonstration)
chunks.body:
★ Sharma's Take
The principal difficulty in clustering is not computational but the selection of the cluster level, and the correct choice is frequently coarser than is comfortable. The cluster should correspond to the level at which the disturbances are dependent, which is typically the level at which treatment is assigned: when a policy applies to an entire jurisdiction, the independent units are the jurisdictions, not the individuals within them, however numerous. If this leaves few clusters, that paucity is an accurate reflection of the limited independent information in the data, not a deficiency to be circumvented by clustering more finely. The temptation to cluster at a fine level arises precisely because it yields smaller standard errors and more significant results; it should be resisted, and the cluster chosen to match the dependence structure of the data.

chunks.heading: Key idea (The dynamic panel problem)
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Clustered Errors, Random Effects, and Dynamic Panels — 11.5 Key idea (The dynamic panel problem)
chunks.body:
A motivating example
Many outcomes are persistent: a firm's productivity this year depends heavily on last year's; a country's growth, a person's earnings, a region's unemployment all carry forward. To capture that, we put the lagged outcome on the right-hand side — a dynamic panel, \(y_{it}=\rho\,y_{i,t-1}+\alpha_i+u_{it}\). The trouble: the lagged outcome is built from past shocks, and the unit effect \(\alpha_i\) sits inside every period's \(y\), so the lag is mechanically correlated with the error. Neither of our panel tools survives this.

chunks.heading: The dynamic panel problem
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Clustered Errors, Random Effects, and Dynamic Panels — 11.5 The dynamic panel problem
chunks.body: Pooled OLS is biased upward: the lagged outcome carries the unit effect \(\alpha_i\), which also sits in the current error, inflating the apparent persistence. Fixed effects is biased downward — the famous Nickell bias: demeaning the lag induces a mechanical negative correlation with the demeaned error, of order \(1/T\), so it bites hardest in the short panels that are common in practice. The two estimates therefore bracket the truth rather than pin it down.

chunks.heading: Derivation (The dynamic panel problem)
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Clustered Errors, Random Effects, and Dynamic Panels — 11.5 Derivation (The dynamic panel problem)
chunks.body:
For the mathematically curious: why fixed effects is biased here
The within transformation subtracts each unit's time-average. But the demeaned lag \(y_{i,t-1}-\bar y_i\) contains \(u_{i,t-1}\) (through \(y_{i,t-1}\)), and the demeaned error \(u_{it}-\bar u_i\) also contains \(u_{i,t-1}\) (through \(\bar u_i\)). They are negatively correlated by construction, so the within estimator is biased toward zero by an amount of order \(1/T\). As \(T\to\infty\) the bias vanishes; for the short panels typical in applied work it does not.

chunks.heading: Arellano–Bond and system GMM
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Clustered Errors, Random Effects, and Dynamic Panels — 11.6 Arellano–Bond and system GMM
chunks.body:
The escape is to instrument the troublesome lag with information already inside the panel. First-difference the equation to remove \(\alpha_i\): \(\Delta y_{it}=\rho\,\Delta y_{i,t-1}+\Delta u_{it}\). The differenced lag \(\Delta y_{i,t-1}\) is still endogenous (it shares \(u_{i,t-1}\) with \(\Delta u_{it}\)), but deeper lags of the level — \(y_{i,t-2},\,y_{i,t-3},\,\ldots\) — are uncorrelated with \(\Delta u_{it}\) yet correlated with \(\Delta y_{i,t-1}\). They are valid instruments.
The simplest version, using a single deep lag \(y_{i,t-2}\) as the instrument, is the Anderson–Hsiao estimator — ordinary 2SLS on the differenced equation, and the direct ancestor of what follows. Arellano–Bond (difference GMM) uses all available deeper lags at once, combining them efficiently by GMM. System GMM (Blundell–Bond) adds a second set of moment conditions — the levels equation instrumented by lagged differences — which is far more informative when the series is persistent (\(\rho\) near one), precisely the case where difference GMM alone grows weak.

chunks.heading: Key idea (Arellano–Bond and system GMM)
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Clustered Errors, Random Effects, and Dynamic Panels — 11.6 Key idea (Arellano–Bond and system GMM)
chunks.body:
Key Idea
In a dynamic panel, OLS is biased up and fixed effects biased down (Nickell bias). Arellano–Bond and system GMM difference away the unit effect and instrument the lagged outcome with its own deeper lags, recovering a consistent estimate of persistence.

chunks.heading: Arellano–Bond and system GMM
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Clustered Errors, Random Effects, and Dynamic Panels — 11.6 Arellano–Bond and system GMM
chunks.body: Two diagnostics are essential and should always be reported. The Hansen/Sargan test of overidentifying restrictions checks the joint validity of the instruments — a rejection signals invalid instruments. The Arellano–Bond AR(2) test checks for second-order serial correlation in the differenced residuals; its absence is what licenses using lag two and beyond as instruments. A standing danger is instrument proliferation: the count of GMM instruments grows with the square of \(T\), and too many instruments overfit the endogenous regressor, drag the estimate back toward the biased within value, and weaken the Hansen test — so the lag depth is usually capped or the instrument set “collapsed.”

chunks.heading: Reading the output (11.6.1 Demonstration)
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Clustered Errors, Random Effects, and Dynamic Panels — 11.6 Reading the output (11.6.1 Demonstration)
chunks.body: Reading the output. The block of estimates tells the whole story. Pooled OLS overshoots (around 0.92, inflated by the unit effect riding along in the lag) and fixed effects undershoots (around 0.34, the Nickell bias); the truth of 0.60 sits between them. Everything below is an attempt to land on it: Anderson–Hsiao (a single deep-lag instrument) and Arellano–Bond difference GMM (all deep lags, one- and two-step) recover roughly 0.53–0.56, and Blundell–Bond system GMM — adding the levels moments — comes closest at about 0.57, the expected ordering since difference GMM keeps a mild downward bias as persistence rises. Then the two gatekeeping diagnostics behave exactly as they should: the Hansen/Sargan tests do not reject (large p-values), so the instruments pass as a set; and the serial-correlation checks show the textbook signature — AR(1) is strongly significant (differencing mechanically creates first-order correlation) while AR(2) is not (no second-order correlation), which is precisely what licenses using lag two and deeper as instruments.

chunks.heading: Reading the output (11.6.1 Demonstration)
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Clustered Errors, Random Effects, and Dynamic Panels — 11.6 Reading the output (11.6.1 Demonstration)
chunks.body: A real study reports those four diagnostics alongside the coefficient; an AR(2) rejection or a borderline-perfect Hansen p-value near one would be the warning signs.

chunks.heading: Instructor's take (11.6.1 Demonstration)
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Clustered Errors, Random Effects, and Dynamic Panels — 11.6 Instructor's take (11.6.1 Demonstration)
chunks.body:
★ Sharma's Take
The seductive part of GMM is that the instruments come free, from inside the data; the dangerous part is that there are so many of them. When \(T\) is even moderate, difference GMM offers dozens or hundreds of moment conditions, and a specification with more instruments than units will quietly overfit, pull the estimate back toward the biased within value, and — worst of all — produce a Hansen test so weakened that it waves everything through with a suspiciously perfect p-value near one. The discipline is to keep the instrument count well below the number of units, to report that count, and to treat the AR(2) and Hansen statistics as gatekeepers rather than formalities. System GMM rescues the persistent case where differencing alone is weak, but it buys that power with an extra assumption about initial conditions; when that assumption is uncomfortable, a smaller, honest difference-GMM specification is the better citizen.

chunks.heading: Chapter summary (11.6.1 Demonstration)
chunks.title: Chapter 11, Clustered Errors, Random Effects, and Dynamic Panels — 11.6 Chapter summary (11.6.1 Demonstration)
chunks.body:
Chapter Summary
Observations within a group share unobserved influences, so their disturbances are correlated and the independence assumption fails (Section 11.1).
Dynamic panels (a lagged outcome on the right-hand side) break both OLS (biased up) and fixed effects (biased down — Nickell bias); the two bracket the truth (Section 11.5).
Arellano–Bond and system GMM difference away the unit effect and instrument the lagged outcome with its own deeper lags; the Hansen and AR(2) tests, and guarding against instrument proliferation, are essential (Section 11.6).
Clustered standard errors allow arbitrary within-cluster correlation; they leave the coefficients unchanged and typically increase the standard errors (Section 11.2).
Random effects retain within- and between-unit variation under the assumption that the unit effect is uncorrelated with the regressors; fixed effects is required when it is not (Section 11.3).
In Python, clustered standard errors are obtained with cov_type="cluster", and random effects with linearmodels.RandomEffects (Section 11.4).

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.title: Chapter 12,  — 12.0 Overview
chunks.body: Chapter 12 · Quasi-Experiments

chunks.heading: The question
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Difference-in-Differences — 12.0 The question
chunks.body:
The Question
A policy is introduced for one group and not another. How is its effect estimated, separating it from permanent differences between the groups and from trends common to both?

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Difference-in-Differences — 12.0 Overview
chunks.body: Difference-in-differences (DiD) is the predominant quasi-experimental design in applied microeconomics. It estimates the causal effect of an intervention administered to one group of units but not to another by contrasting the change in the treated group's outcome with the contemporaneous change in an untreated comparison group. The design removes two distinct sources of bias at once: time-invariant differences in levels between the groups, and time-varying shocks common to both. This chapter develops the estimand within the potential-outcomes framework, states the assumptions under which it is identified, derives the estimator and its regression representation, treats inference and the dynamic (event-study) specification, catalogues the principal threats to validity, and concludes with the failure of the conventional two-way fixed-effects estimator under staggered adoption and the heterogeneity-robust estimators that have superseded it.

chunks.heading: Key idea
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Difference-in-Differences — 12.0 Key idea
chunks.body:
Running example
Throughout, consider the evaluation of a state-level cigarette excise tax. In a given year a subset of states (“treated”) raise the tax while the remainder (“control”) do not. Per-capita cigarette consumption is declining secularly in all states, and the treated and control states differ in baseline consumption. A before-and-after comparison confined to the treated states would attribute the secular decline to the tax; a cross-sectional comparison of treated and control states in the post-period would attribute pre-existing level differences to the tax. Difference-in-differences is constructed precisely to remove both contaminations, and the design is estimated on this example in Section 12.6.

chunks.heading: Setup, estimand, and estimator
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Difference-in-Differences — 12.1 Setup, estimand, and estimator
chunks.body:
Consider two groups, indexed by treatment status \(D_i\in\{0,1\}\), each observed in two periods \(t\in\{0,1\}\), where \(t=0\) precedes and \(t=1\) follows the intervention. In the potential-outcomes notation, let \(Y_{it}(1)\) denote the outcome unit \(i\) would realize in period \(t\) under treatment and \(Y_{it}(0)\) the outcome it would realize absent treatment. Only one potential outcome is observed per unit-period; because treatment is active only for treated units in the post-period, the realized outcome is \(Y_{it}=Y_{it}(0)+D_i\,t\,[\,Y_{it}(1)-Y_{it}(0)\,]\).
The parameter of interest is the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) in the post-period,
\[ \tau_{ATT}=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,Y_{i1}(1)-Y_{i1}(0)\,\middle|\,D_i=1\,\right]. \]
The first term, \(\mathbb{E}[Y_{i1}(1)\mid D_i=1]\), is the observed post-period mean of the treated group. The counterfactual term \(\mathbb{E}[Y_{i1}(0)\mid D_i=1]\) — the outcome the treated group would have realized absent treatment — is never observed and must be supplied by the identifying assumption of Section 12.2.
Under that assumption the ATT is identified by the difference in differences of the four group-by-period means,

chunks.heading: Setup, estimand, and estimator
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Difference-in-Differences — 12.1 Setup, estimand, and estimator
chunks.body:
\[ \hat\tau=\big(\bar Y_{1,\text{post}}-\bar Y_{1,\text{pre}}\big)-\big(\bar Y_{0,\text{post}}-\bar Y_{0,\text{pre}}\big), \]
where the leading subscript denotes treatment status. The inner differences eliminate each group's time-invariant level; the outer difference eliminates the trend common to both groups, which under parallel trends coincides with the treated group's counterfactual trend. What remains is the treatment effect.

chunks.heading: Derivation (Setup, estimand, and estimator)
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Difference-in-Differences — 12.1 Derivation (Setup, estimand, and estimator)
chunks.body:
The regression and two-way fixed-effects representations
The double difference \(\hat\tau\) is algebraically the ordinary-least-squares coefficient on the interaction term in the saturated regression
\[ Y_{it}=\beta_0+\beta_1 D_i+\beta_2\,\text{Post}_t+\tau\,(D_i\times\text{Post}_t)+\varepsilon_{it}, \]
in which \(\beta_1\) absorbs the permanent level difference between the groups, \(\beta_2\) the common time effect, and \(\tau\) is the interaction coefficient, identical to the double difference (Exercise 1). With many units and periods the same logic is expressed through the two-way fixed-effects (TWFE) specification
\[ Y_{it}=\alpha_i+\lambda_t+\tau\,\text{Treat}_{it}+\varepsilon_{it}, \]
where \(\alpha_i\) and \(\lambda_t\) are unit and period effects and \(\text{Treat}_{it}\) indicates active treatment. With a single adoption date and two groups this reproduces \(\hat\tau\) exactly. The regression form is preferred because it admits covariates, generalizes to many periods, and supplies a standard-error apparatus; the qualifications it acquires under staggered adoption are the subject of Section 12.7.

chunks.heading: Definition (Identification: parallel trends and auxiliary assumptions)
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Difference-in-Differences — 12.2 Definition (Identification: parallel trends and auxiliary assumptions)
chunks.body:
Assumption 12.1 — Parallel (common) trends
In the absence of treatment, the expected change in the untreated potential outcome is identical across the two groups:
\[ \mathbb{E}\!\left[Y_{i1}(0)-Y_{i0}(0)\mid D_i=1\right]=\mathbb{E}\!\left[Y_{i1}(0)-Y_{i0}(0)\mid D_i=0\right]. \]

chunks.heading: Identification: parallel trends and auxiliary assumptions
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Difference-in-Differences — 12.2 Identification: parallel trends and auxiliary assumptions
chunks.body:
Assumption 12.1 licenses the control group's observed change as the counterfactual change for the treated group, and hence point-identifies the ATT. It concerns an unobservable counterfactual trend and so cannot be verified directly; its plausibility is assessed from pre-treatment data (Section 12.4). Two properties merit emphasis. First, the assumption restricts trends, not levels: the groups may differ arbitrarily at baseline, and the design is invariant to such differences. Second, parallel trends is not scale-invariant — trends that are parallel in levels need not remain parallel after a logarithmic or other nonlinear transformation — so the choice of functional form is itself a substantive identifying decision (Section 12.6).
Three auxiliary conditions are required for the standard interpretation.

chunks.heading: Derivation (Identification: parallel trends and auxiliary assumptions)
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Difference-in-Differences — 12.2 Derivation (Identification: parallel trends and auxiliary assumptions)
chunks.body:
The auxiliary identifying assumptions
No anticipation. Units do not alter behaviour in the pre-period in anticipation of treatment; formally \(Y_{i0}=Y_{i0}(0)\) for treated units, so the baseline outcome is untreated. Anticipatory responses contaminate the baseline and bias the estimate.
Stable unit treatment values (SUTVA / no interference). A unit's potential outcomes depend only on its own treatment status, not on the treatment of others. Spillovers from treated to control units violate this condition; when controls are partially affected in the same direction, the estimate is typically biased toward zero.
Stable composition. The groups consist of the same populations (or random samples thereof) in both periods. If treatment induces selective entry or exit, the observed change conflates the treatment effect with a change in composition.

chunks.heading: Derivation (Identification: parallel trends and auxiliary assumptions)
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Difference-in-Differences — 12.2 Derivation (Identification: parallel trends and auxiliary assumptions)
chunks.body: When parallel trends holds only after conditioning on covariates \(X\), the assumption becomes conditional parallel trends, and identification proceeds within covariate strata, by regression adjustment, by inverse-probability weighting on the propensity score, or by doubly-robust combinations of the two that remain consistent if either the outcome model or the propensity model is correctly specified.

chunks.heading: Inference
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Difference-in-Differences — 12.3 Inference
chunks.body: Observations on a given unit across periods are serially correlated, and units sharing a treatment assignment are subject to common shocks; treating unit-period observations as independent therefore understates the sampling variability, frequently to a severe degree. Standard errors should be clustered at the level at which treatment is assigned — typically the unit, such as the state. Bertrand, Duflo, and Mullainathan (2004) showed that neglect of within-unit serial correlation produces badly overstated significance in difference-in-differences applications, with conventional standard errors rejecting true null hypotheses far more often than their nominal size. When the number of clusters is small the asymptotic justification for the cluster-robust variance estimator is weak, and corrections are warranted: the wild cluster bootstrap, critical values from a \(t\)-distribution with degrees of freedom governed by the number of clusters rather than observations, or, with very few treated clusters, randomization (permutation) inference.

chunks.heading: Dynamic effects and the event study
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Difference-in-Differences — 12.4 Dynamic effects and the event study
chunks.body:
The two-period design compresses the entire post-treatment response into a single number. With multiple periods, the event-study (dynamic) specification estimates a separate treatment-group–period interaction for each period relative to a normalized base, conventionally the period immediately preceding treatment:
\[ Y_{it}=\alpha_i+\lambda_t+\sum_{k\neq-1}\delta_k\,\mathbf{1}\{t-t^*_i=k\}\,D_i+\varepsilon_{it}, \]
where \(t^*_i\) is the adoption date, \(k\) indexes event time (periods since treatment), and \(k=-1\) is omitted as the reference. The coefficients \(\delta_k\) for \(k\ge 0\) trace the trajectory of the treatment effect; the coefficients \(\delta_k\) for \(k<-1\) — the pre-treatment leads — should be statistically and economically indistinguishable from zero if the groups evolved in parallel before treatment.

chunks.heading: Dynamic effects and the event study
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Difference-in-Differences — 12.4 Dynamic effects and the event study
chunks.body: The event study discharges two functions. First, the pre-treatment leads constitute the central empirical evidence for Assumption 12.1: their flatness is the visible support for the design, and a systematic pre-trend signals a violation. Second, the post-treatment coefficients reveal whether the effect appears immediately or with delay and whether it persists, decays, or grows — information of independent substantive importance that the scalar ATT conceals. Two cautions attend the leads: a test of them has limited statistical power, so failure to reject zero pre-trends does not establish parallel trends; and conditioning the analysis on having passed a pre-trends test itself distorts subsequent inference, as analyzed by Roth (2022). Flat leads are corroborating evidence, not proof.

chunks.heading: Key idea (Dynamic effects and the event study)
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Difference-in-Differences — 12.4 Key idea (Dynamic effects and the event study)
chunks.body:
Key Idea
The credibility of a difference-in-differences estimate rests on the parallel-trends assumption, which cannot be proved but can be rendered plausible by demonstrating that the groups moved in parallel before treatment. The event study supplies that demonstration and, through its post-treatment coefficients, the time profile of the effect.

chunks.heading: Implementation
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Difference-in-Differences — 12.5 Implementation
chunks.body:
The headline estimate is the coefficient on the treatment–period interaction, with standard errors clustered at the assignment level (Section 12.3); the event study is obtained by interacting the treatment indicator with a full set of period indicators, omitting the base period.
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
# difference-in-differences: the interaction is the ATT; cluster by assignment unit
did = smf.ols("y ~ treated + post + treated:post", data=df).fit(
cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": df["state"]})
print(did.params["treated:post"])
# event study: interact treated with each period (base period omitted)
event = smf.ols("y ~ treated + C(year) + treated:C(year)", data=df).fit(
cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": df["state"]})
The demonstration below estimates the difference-in-differences coefficient and plots the event-study coefficients, which are approximately zero before treatment and depart from zero thereafter.

chunks.heading: Reading the output (12.5.1 Demonstration: the cigarette tax)
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Difference-in-Differences — 12.5 Reading the output (12.5.1 Demonstration: the cigarette tax)
chunks.body: Reading the output. The reported DiD estimate is the coefficient on the taxed:post interaction, which lies close to the data-generating value of −15: the tax reduced per-capita consumption by approximately fifteen packs relative to the counterfactual path implied by the control states' trend. The accompanying clustered se is computed with clustering by state, since the repeated annual observations within a state are serially dependent (Section 12.3); treating state-years as independent would understate the standard error. The event-study figure is the credibility check: each plotted coefficient is the estimated taxed–untaxed gap in a given year, normalized so that the final pre-treatment year is zero. The pre-2015 coefficients are approximately zero, evidencing parallel pre-trends, while the post-2015 coefficients fall and persist, tracing the magnitude and durability of the effect. A pre-treatment series that already exhibited a slope would indicate prior divergence and would invalidate the design.

chunks.heading: Threats to validity
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Difference-in-Differences — 12.6 Threats to validity
chunks.body:
Beyond the failure of parallel trends itself, several distinct mechanisms can invalidate a difference-in-differences estimate; each corresponds to the violation of an assumption in Section 12.2.
Anticipation. If units respond before the nominal treatment date — because the policy was announced in advance or otherwise expected — the pre-period outcome is no longer the untreated potential outcome and the baseline is contaminated. Anticipation manifests as nonzero leads immediately preceding adoption and can sometimes be accommodated by redefining the treatment date or excluding the anticipation window.
Ashenfelter's dip. A common form of pre-treatment divergence arises when selection into treatment is driven by a transitory shock — the classic instance being enrolment in a training programme after a temporary fall in earnings. The treated group's pre-period outcome is then atypically depressed; mechanical mean reversion inflates its subsequent change and the effect is overstated. The dip appears in the event study as a downward pre-trend that reverses at treatment.

chunks.heading: Threats to validity
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Difference-in-Differences — 12.6 Threats to validity
chunks.body:
Compositional change. When the membership of the groups changes between periods — through selective migration, attrition, or treatment-induced entry — the observed change confounds the treatment effect with a change in who is measured. Repeated cross-sections are especially vulnerable; panel data on fixed units mitigate but do not eliminate the problem where attrition is itself treatment-related.
Spillovers. If the treatment of one unit affects the outcomes of control units — through general-equilibrium effects, geographic proximity, or strategic responses — SUTVA fails and the control group ceases to measure the treated group's counterfactual. The bias is typically toward zero when controls are affected in the same direction as the treated. Buffer zones, exclusion of proximate controls, or explicit spatial models are used to address it.

chunks.heading: Threats to validity
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Difference-in-Differences — 12.6 Threats to validity
chunks.body: Functional form. Because parallel trends is not scale-invariant, the estimate depends on whether the outcome enters in levels, logarithms, or another transformation, and the assumption can hold in at most one of them. Where no single scale is defensible, the changes-in-changes estimator of Athey and Imbens (2006) identifies the entire counterfactual distribution under a weaker, scale-free monotonicity assumption and is the appropriate generalization.

chunks.heading: Staggered adoption and heterogeneity-robust estimators
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Difference-in-Differences — 12.7 Staggered adoption and heterogeneity-robust estimators
chunks.body: The preceding analysis assumes a single adoption date common to all treated units. Many policies instead diffuse over time, with units adopting in different periods — staggered adoption. The natural response is to estimate the two-way fixed-effects regression \(Y_{it}=\alpha_i+\lambda_t+\tau\,\text{Treat}_{it}+\varepsilon_{it}\) and report the single coefficient \(\tau\). Recent work has established that this practice is unreliable when treatment effects are heterogeneous across cohorts or dynamic over time.

chunks.heading: Staggered adoption and heterogeneity-robust estimators
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Difference-in-Differences — 12.7 Staggered adoption and heterogeneity-robust estimators
chunks.body: Goodman-Bacon (2021) demonstrates that the TWFE estimand is a weighted average of all two-group, two-period difference-in-differences comparisons embedded in the panel. These comprise not only the desired comparisons of treated cohorts against not-yet-treated units, but also forbidden comparisons in which a later-treated cohort serves as the control for an earlier-treated cohort. In such a comparison the “control” is itself already treated, so its outcome reflects the evolving treatment effect rather than the untreated counterfactual. When effects vary over time, these comparisons enter with negative weights, and a weighted average containing negative weights need not lie within the range of the underlying effects; the TWFE coefficient can therefore be attenuated, inflated, or even of the wrong sign while every unit's true effect is positive.

chunks.heading: Key idea (Staggered adoption and heterogeneity-robust estimators)
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Difference-in-Differences — 12.7 Key idea (Staggered adoption and heterogeneity-robust estimators)
chunks.body:
Key Idea
With a single adoption date and two groups, two-way fixed effects is valid. Under staggered adoption with heterogeneous or dynamic effects, the single TWFE coefficient is a contaminated weighted average and may be severely biased; a heterogeneity-robust estimator is required.

chunks.heading: Staggered adoption and heterogeneity-robust estimators
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Difference-in-Differences — 12.7 Staggered adoption and heterogeneity-robust estimators
chunks.body: The remedy is to restrict attention to clean comparisons — treated cohorts against not-yet-treated or never-treated units — to estimate a separate effect for each adoption cohort and event time, and to aggregate these with non-negative weights. The estimators of Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021), Sun and Abraham (2021), and de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfœuille (2020), together with the imputation approach of Borusyak, Jaravel, and Spiess (2024), implement this programme and have become standard for staggered designs; the Goodman-Bacon decomposition is the diagnostic that reveals how much of a given TWFE estimate derives from forbidden comparisons. The two-group, single-date design of this chapter is immune to the problem, which arises only once adoption dates differ.

chunks.heading: Instructor's take (Staggered adoption and heterogeneity-robust estimators)
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Difference-in-Differences — 12.7 Instructor's take (Staggered adoption and heterogeneity-robust estimators)
chunks.body:
★ Sharma's Take
The event-study figure is presented as a test of parallel trends, which it is, but the post-policy coefficients additionally convey the time profile of the effect, which is itself a principal finding. An effect that appears immediately and persists differs in its implications from one that emerges gradually or one that decays, although all three may share the same average. Before the estimate is reduced to a single number, the post-policy trajectory should be read as a result in its own right: whether the effect is immediate or delayed, and whether it is durable or transient, bears directly on the value of the policy and is frequently the information a decision-maker most requires. The average answers whether the policy had an effect; the trajectory answers how that effect evolved.

chunks.heading: Chapter summary (Staggered adoption and heterogeneity-robust estimators)
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Difference-in-Differences — 12.7 Chapter summary (Staggered adoption and heterogeneity-robust estimators)
chunks.body:
Chapter Summary
The estimand is the average treatment effect on the treated; difference-in-differences identifies it by subtracting the control group's change from the treated group's change, eliminating both permanent level differences and common time shocks (Section 12.1).
The estimator equals the coefficient on the treatment×period interaction in the saturated regression and generalizes to the two-way fixed-effects specification (Section 12.1).
Identification rests on parallel trends, supported by no-anticipation, SUTVA, and stable composition; parallel trends restricts trends rather than levels and is not scale-invariant (Section 12.2).
Inference requires clustering at the assignment level; neglect of within-unit serial correlation grossly overstates significance, and few-cluster corrections are needed when clusters are scarce (Section 12.3).
The event study estimates period-specific effects relative to a base period: flat pre-treatment leads corroborate parallel trends and the post-treatment path gives the effect's dynamics, though pre-trend tests have limited power (Section 12.4).

chunks.heading: Chapter summary (Staggered adoption and heterogeneity-robust estimators)
chunks.title: Chapter 12, Difference-in-Differences — 12.7 Chapter summary (Staggered adoption and heterogeneity-robust estimators)
chunks.body:
The principal threats are anticipation, Ashenfelter's dip, compositional change, spillovers, and functional-form dependence (Section 12.6).
Under staggered adoption with heterogeneous or dynamic effects, the single two-way fixed-effects coefficient is a negatively-weighted average of comparisons and can be badly biased; heterogeneity-robust estimators are required (Section 12.7).

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.title: Chapter 13,  — 13.0 Overview
chunks.body: Chapter 13 · Discontinuities

chunks.heading: The question
chunks.title: Chapter 13, Regression Discontinuity — 13.0 The question
chunks.body:
The Question
When a treatment is assigned by a strict threshold on a continuous variable, can the units just above and just below the threshold be used to identify its effect?

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.title: Chapter 13, Regression Discontinuity — 13.0 Overview
chunks.body: The regression-discontinuity (RD) design is among the most credible quasi-experimental designs in the empirical social sciences. It applies whenever treatment is assigned by whether a continuous running variable (equivalently, forcing or assignment variable) crosses a fixed cutoff. Under a continuity assumption, units arbitrarily close to the cutoff on opposite sides are comparable in all determinants of the outcome save treatment, so the discontinuity in the outcome at the cutoff identifies the treatment effect for units at the threshold. This chapter formalizes that identification in both the sharp and fuzzy designs, develops local polynomial estimation and the central role of the bandwidth, treats the falsification tests on which the design's credibility rests, and addresses the local character of the resulting estimand.

chunks.heading: Key idea
chunks.title: Chapter 13, Regression Discontinuity — 13.0 Key idea
chunks.body:
Running example
In the United States the legal right to purchase alcohol commences at age 21. Individuals just below and just above this threshold are, in expectation, indistinguishable in maturity, health, and circumstance, yet they differ in legal access to alcohol. A discontinuous increase in the mortality rate precisely at age 21, within an otherwise smooth age–mortality profile, is therefore attributable to the change in legal access rather than to age itself. Here the running variable is age, the cutoff is 21, and the running variable cannot be manipulated — no individual can alter the date of birth — which renders the design especially clean. The method is developed on this example and estimated in Section 13.5.

chunks.heading: The sharp design: setup and estimand
chunks.title: Chapter 13, Regression Discontinuity — 13.1 The sharp design: setup and estimand
chunks.body: Let \(X_i\) denote the running variable and \(c\) the cutoff. In the sharp design, treatment is a deterministic, discontinuous function of the running variable, \(D_i=\mathbf{1}\{X_i\ge c\}\), so every unit at or above the cutoff is treated and every unit below is untreated. In the potential-outcomes notation, unit \(i\) has outcomes \(Y_i(1)\) and \(Y_i(0)\) under treatment and control, with observed outcome \(Y_i=Y_i(0)+D_i[Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)]\).

chunks.heading: Definition (The sharp design: setup and estimand)
chunks.title: Chapter 13, Regression Discontinuity — 13.1 Definition (The sharp design: setup and estimand)
chunks.body:
Assumption 13.1 — Continuity
The conditional expectations of the potential outcomes are continuous in the running variable at the cutoff: the maps \(x\mapsto\mathbb{E}[Y_i(0)\mid X_i=x]\) and \(x\mapsto\mathbb{E}[Y_i(1)\mid X_i=x]\) are continuous at \(x=c\).

chunks.heading: The sharp design: setup and estimand
chunks.title: Chapter 13, Regression Discontinuity — 13.1 The sharp design: setup and estimand
chunks.body:
Continuity formalizes the comparability of units on either side of the cutoff: absent the discontinuous treatment rule, the outcome would evolve smoothly through \(c\), so any discontinuity in the observed outcome at \(c\) is attributable to treatment alone. Under Assumption 13.1 the treatment effect at the cutoff is identified as the difference of one-sided limits of the conditional mean of the observed outcome,
\[ \tau_{SRD}=\lim_{x\downarrow c}\mathbb{E}[Y_i\mid X_i=x]-\lim_{x\uparrow c}\mathbb{E}[Y_i\mid X_i=x]=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)\mid X_i=c\,\right]. \]
The estimand is thus the average treatment effect for units located at the cutoff — a local parameter whose interpretation and limits are taken up in Section 13.4 and the closing remark. Because no unit is observed both just above and just below the cutoff, identification rests on extrapolating each conditional mean to the boundary, which is why estimation reduces to careful local approximation (Section 13.3).

chunks.heading: The fuzzy design
chunks.title: Chapter 13, Regression Discontinuity — 13.2 The fuzzy design
chunks.body:
In many applications, crossing the cutoff does not determine treatment but only alters its probability: eligibility is conferred at the threshold yet take-up is incomplete, or the assignment rule is imperfectly enforced. The fuzzy design accommodates this case, in which the treatment probability jumps discontinuously at the cutoff without attaining the extremes of zero and one,
\[ \lim_{x\downarrow c}\Pr(D_i=1\mid X_i=x)\neq\lim_{x\uparrow c}\Pr(D_i=1\mid X_i=x). \]
The treatment effect is then identified as the ratio of the discontinuity in the outcome to the discontinuity in the treatment probability,
\[ \tau_{FRD}=\frac{\displaystyle\lim_{x\downarrow c}\mathbb{E}[Y_i\mid X_i=x]-\lim_{x\uparrow c}\mathbb{E}[Y_i\mid X_i=x]}{\displaystyle\lim_{x\downarrow c}\mathbb{E}[D_i\mid X_i=x]-\lim_{x\uparrow c}\mathbb{E}[D_i\mid X_i=x]}, \]

chunks.heading: The fuzzy design
chunks.title: Chapter 13, Regression Discontinuity — 13.2 The fuzzy design
chunks.body: a structure identical to the Wald instrumental-variables estimator of Chapter 9, with the cutoff indicator serving as an instrument for treatment. Under the continuity assumptions together with a monotonicity condition — no unit is deterred from treatment by crossing into eligibility — \(\tau_{FRD}\) is the local average treatment effect for the compliers at the cutoff, namely those units whose treatment status is changed by crossing the threshold. The sharp design is the special case in which the treatment probability jumps from zero to one.

chunks.heading: Estimation: local polynomial regression and the bandwidth
chunks.title: Chapter 13, Regression Discontinuity — 13.3 Estimation: local polynomial regression and the bandwidth
chunks.body: The conditional-mean limits are estimated by local polynomial regression: within a window of half-width \(h\) (the bandwidth) on each side of the cutoff, a low-order polynomial — in practice linear or quadratic — is fitted to the outcome against the centred running variable, and the two fitted intercepts at the cutoff are differenced to estimate \(\tau\). Observations are commonly weighted by a kernel that declines with distance from the cutoff (the triangular kernel is mean-squared-error optimal for a boundary point), conferring greatest influence on the most comparable units. In the fuzzy design the same local regression is applied to the treatment indicator, and the ratio of the two estimated discontinuities is formed.

chunks.heading: Key idea (Estimation: local polynomial regression and the bandwidth)
chunks.title: Chapter 13, Regression Discontinuity — 13.3 Key idea (Estimation: local polynomial regression and the bandwidth)
chunks.body:
Key Idea — the bandwidth trade-off
The bandwidth governs a bias–variance trade-off. A wide bandwidth admits more observations and lowers variance, but observations far from the cutoff may follow a curved relationship that a low-order polynomial approximates poorly, introducing bias. A narrow bandwidth restricts attention to the most comparable units, lowering bias, but uses fewer observations and raises variance. The estimate should be reported across a range of bandwidths, with stability as the bandwidth narrows taken as support for the design.

chunks.heading: Derivation (Estimation: local polynomial regression and the bandwidth)
chunks.title: Chapter 13, Regression Discontinuity — 13.3 Derivation (Estimation: local polynomial regression and the bandwidth)
chunks.body:
For the mathematically curious: optimal bandwidth and bias correction
Within a bandwidth \(h\), the variance of the discontinuity estimate falls roughly like \(1/(nh)\), while the bias from approximating a curved conditional mean by a polynomial of degree \(p\) grows like \(h^{p+1}\). Minimising the asymptotic mean squared error yields an optimal bandwidth that shrinks with the sample at the rate \(h^{*}\propto n^{-1/(2p+3)}\) — \(n^{-1/5}\) for local linear estimation. Data-driven selectors (Imbens and Kalyanaraman, 2012; Calonico, Cattaneo, and Titiunik, 2014) automate this choice. Because the MSE-optimal bandwidth balances squared bias against variance, the resulting point estimate retains a bias of the same order as its standard error, so conventional confidence intervals are mis-centred; the robust bias-correction procedure of Calonico, Cattaneo, and Titiunik (2014) removes the leading bias and adjusts the variance accordingly, and is the current standard for RD inference.

chunks.heading: Estimation: local polynomial regression and the bandwidth
chunks.title: Chapter 13, Regression Discontinuity — 13.3 Estimation: local polynomial regression and the bandwidth
chunks.body: High-order global polynomials — a single high-degree fit over the entire support of the running variable — should be avoided: they assign erratic weights to observations far from the cutoff, are sensitive to the chosen degree, and can manufacture spurious discontinuities, as documented by Gelman and Imbens (2019). Local linear or local quadratic estimation within a data-driven bandwidth is the preferred practice.

chunks.heading: Validity and falsification tests
chunks.title: Chapter 13, Regression Discontinuity — 13.4 Validity and falsification tests
chunks.body:
The credibility of an RD design rests on the continuity assumption, which, though not directly testable, carries observable implications that support a battery of falsification tests.
Manipulation of the running variable. Identification requires that units be unable to precisely control their position relative to the cutoff. Where they can — an applicant reclassified just above an eligibility threshold, a score nudged just past a passing mark — units just above come to differ systematically from those just below in the characteristic that enabled the sorting, and continuity fails. The leading diagnostic examines the density of the running variable at the cutoff: under no manipulation the density is continuous, whereas manipulation produces a discontinuity, with an accumulation of units on the favoured side and a deficit on the other. The McCrary (2008) density test, and the local-polynomial density test of Cattaneo, Jansson, and Ma (2020), formalize this check.

chunks.heading: Validity and falsification tests
chunks.title: Chapter 13, Regression Discontinuity — 13.4 Validity and falsification tests
chunks.body:
Continuity of covariates. Predetermined covariates — characteristics fixed before treatment — should display no discontinuity at the cutoff, since treatment cannot affect them. A jump in such a covariate signals a violation of continuity and casts doubt on the design. Standard practice applies the RD estimator to each covariate as a placebo outcome and confirms that the estimated discontinuities are null.
Placebo cutoffs and bandwidth sensitivity. Estimating a discontinuity at artificial cutoffs away from the true threshold should yield null effects; a significant jump at a placebo cutoff indicates that the conditional mean is not smooth and undermines the design. The estimate should further be shown to be stable across a range of bandwidths and polynomial orders.

chunks.heading: Implementation
chunks.title: Chapter 13, Regression Discontinuity — 13.5 Implementation
chunks.body:
The running variable is centred at the cutoff and an above-cutoff indicator is constructed; a local linear regression with separate slopes on each side is fitted within a bandwidth, and the coefficient on the indicator is the estimated discontinuity. The estimate is then examined across several bandwidths and the density of the running variable inspected at the cutoff.
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
c = 90.0 # cutoff of the running variable (score)
df["above"] = (df["score"] >= c).astype(int)
df["score_c"] = df["score"] - c # centre the running variable at the cutoff
# local linear regression within bandwidth h, separate slopes on each side
h = 10.0
window = df[df["score_c"].abs() <= h]
rd = smf.ols("y ~ above + score_c + above:score_c", data=window).fit(cov_type="HC1")
print(rd.params["above"]) # the discontinuity = the treatment effect
The demonstration below constructs data with a known discontinuity, estimates it by local linear regression, examines the sensitivity to the bandwidth, and inspects the density of the running variable at the cutoff as a manipulation check.

chunks.heading: Reading the output (13.5.1 Demonstration: the drinking age)
chunks.title: Chapter 13, Regression Discontinuity — 13.5 Reading the output (13.5.1 Demonstration: the drinking age)
chunks.body: Reading the output. The reported RD estimate is the difference between fitted mortality just above and just below age 21, close to the data-generating value of +9 per 100,000. It is to be interpreted strictly as the effect of legal drinking access for individuals at age 21 — the marginal cases — and not for the population at large; this local character is intrinsic to the design and should accompany every RD result. The bandwidth schedule exhibits the bias–variance trade-off: the narrowest window (±0.5 year) employs only the most comparable individuals but few of them, so the estimate is the noisiest, while the widest (±2 years) admits more observations at the risk of letting the underlying age–mortality slope, rather than the discontinuity, influence the estimate; the stability of the estimate near 9 across windows is reassuring. The upper panel displays the two local-linear fits meeting in a discrete step at 21, the magnitude of which is the effect. The lower panel is the manipulation (McCrary) check: the density of ages passes smoothly through 21 with no accumulation on either side — here guaranteed, since the date of birth cannot be chosen.

chunks.title: Chapter 13, Regression Discontinuity — 13.5 Reading the output (13.5.1 Demonstration: the drinking age)
chunks.body: Where the running variable is manipulable — a self-reported income, a gradable test score — a spike on the treated side of the cutoff would indicate sorting and invalidate the comparison.

chunks.heading: Instructor's take (13.5.1 Demonstration: the drinking age)
chunks.title: Chapter 13, Regression Discontinuity — 13.5 Instructor's take (13.5.1 Demonstration: the drinking age)
chunks.body:
★ Sharma's Take
The regression-discontinuity design yields an unusually credible estimate of an unusually specific quantity, and the specificity is essential to its interpretation. The estimate is the effect of treatment for units at the cutoff — the marginal cases — and is not informative about the effect for units far from it. This is not a defect: a precise estimate for the marginal units is exactly what is required by a decision concerning where to set the cutoff. But the estimate does not generalize as a randomized experiment on the whole population would, and the qualification “for units near the threshold” should accompany every statement of the result. The credibility of the design derives entirely from confining attention to the vicinity of the cutoff, and the reach of its conclusion is confined to the same vicinity.

chunks.heading: Chapter summary (13.5.1 Demonstration: the drinking age)
chunks.title: Chapter 13, Regression Discontinuity — 13.5 Chapter summary (13.5.1 Demonstration: the drinking age)
chunks.body:
Chapter Summary
In the sharp design, treatment is a deterministic function of the running variable crossing a cutoff; under continuity of the potential-outcome conditional means, the discontinuity in the outcome at the cutoff identifies the treatment effect for units at the threshold (Section 13.1).
In the fuzzy design, the treatment probability jumps at the cutoff; the effect is identified as the ratio of the outcome discontinuity to the treatment-probability discontinuity — a Wald/IV estimand giving the local effect for compliers (Section 13.2).
Estimation uses local polynomial (linear or quadratic) regression within a bandwidth, with kernel weighting; the bandwidth trades bias against variance, data-driven selection with robust bias correction is standard, and global high-order polynomials are to be avoided (Section 13.3).
The design's credibility rests on falsification tests: continuity of the running-variable density (manipulation), continuity of predetermined covariates, placebo cutoffs, and bandwidth sensitivity (Section 13.4).
