chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.title: Chapter 14,  — 14.0 Overview
chunks.body: Chapter 14 · Binary Outcomes

chunks.heading: The question
chunks.title: Chapter 14, Models for a Binary Dependent Variable — 14.0 The question
chunks.body:
The Question
When the outcome is a binary event — employed or not, default or not — how is the probability of the event modelled, and how are the coefficients interpreted?

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.title: Chapter 14, Models for a Binary Dependent Variable — 14.0 Overview
chunks.body: When the dependent variable is binary, recording the occurrence of an event, its conditional mean is the conditional probability of the event. Linear regression remains applicable but sits uneasily with a bounded probability, motivating the nonlinear index models that are the subject of this chapter. We develop the linear probability model, then the logit and probit models through a common latent-variable formulation, estimate all three by their appropriate methods, and treat at length the interpretation of their coefficients — the central difficulty of the subject — including marginal effects, the odds-ratio reading specific to logit, the latent-index reading specific to probit, and the systematic scaling relationship between the two. Goodness-of-fit measures and a full Python implementation conclude the chapter.

chunks.heading: Key idea
chunks.title: Chapter 14, Models for a Binary Dependent Variable — 14.0 Key idea
chunks.body:
Running example
Consider a lender deciding whether to approve a loan. For each applicant the outcome of interest is binary — the borrower either defaults or does not — and the lender wishes to model the probability of default as a function of observable characteristics, principally the applicant's debt-to-income ratio and credit score. The quantity to be modelled is therefore a conditional probability, bounded within \([0,1]\), and the questions the lender must answer are precisely those this chapter addresses: how a one-unit change in the debt-to-income ratio alters the probability of default, whether a higher credit score lowers it, and by how much. The method is developed on this example and estimated for a simulated loan portfolio in Section 14.7.

chunks.heading: Binary outcomes and the conditional probability
chunks.title: Chapter 14, Models for a Binary Dependent Variable — 14.1 Binary outcomes and the conditional probability
chunks.body: Let \(y\in\{0,1\}\) record the occurrence of an event. Its expectation conditional on regressors \(x\) is \(\mathbb{E}[y\mid x]=\Pr(y=1\mid x)\), since \(\mathbb{E}[y\mid x]=1\cdot\Pr(y=1\mid x)+0\cdot\Pr(y=0\mid x)\). Modelling the conditional mean of a binary outcome is therefore identical to modelling the conditional probability of the event, and every model in this chapter is a specification of \(\Pr(y=1\mid x)\). A binary outcome is a Bernoulli random variable, so its conditional variance is \(\Pr(y=1\mid x)\,[1-\Pr(y=1\mid x)]\), which depends on \(x\) — a fact with consequences for estimation developed below.

chunks.heading: Definition (The linear probability model)
chunks.title: Chapter 14, Models for a Binary Dependent Variable — 14.2 Definition (The linear probability model)
chunks.body:
Definition 14.1 — Linear probability model
The linear probability model (LPM) specifies the conditional probability as linear in the parameters and estimates it by ordinary least squares applied to the binary outcome:
\[ \Pr(y=1\mid x)=\beta_0+\beta_1 x_1+\cdots+\beta_k x_k. \]

chunks.heading: The linear probability model
chunks.title: Chapter 14, Models for a Binary Dependent Variable — 14.2 The linear probability model
chunks.body:
Each coefficient \(\beta_j\) is the change in the probability of the event for a one-unit change in \(x_j\), holding the others fixed — a constant partial effect, interpretable without further transformation. This directness, together with the familiarity of OLS and its convenience in specifications with fixed effects or instrumental variables, accounts for the model's continued use.
Two limitations follow from the linear form. First, the fitted probability is unbounded and may fall below zero or above one for sufficiently extreme regressor values, which is incoherent as a probability and distorts the implied partial effects in those regions. Second, because the outcome is Bernoulli, its conditional variance \(\Pr(y=1\mid x)[1-\Pr(y=1\mid x)]\) depends on \(x\); the errors are intrinsically heteroskedastic, and heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors are mandatory. The model is most defensible when the fitted probabilities lie predominantly in the interior of \([0,1]\), a condition examined in Sharma's Take.

chunks.heading: The latent-variable framework: logit and probit
chunks.title: Chapter 14, Models for a Binary Dependent Variable — 14.3 The latent-variable framework: logit and probit
chunks.body:
To constrain the fitted probability to \([0,1]\), the index models pass a linear index through a cumulative distribution function. A unifying derivation posits a continuous but unobserved latent variable \(y^{*}\) — a propensity, net utility, or creditworthiness — linear in the regressors,
\[ y^{*}=x'\beta+\varepsilon,\qquad y=\mathbf{1}\{y^{*}>0\}, \]
so that the event occurs when the latent propensity crosses a threshold normalized to zero. The probability of the event is then
\[ \Pr(y=1\mid x)=\Pr(\varepsilon>-x'\beta)=G(x'\beta), \]
where \(G\) is the cumulative distribution function of \(-\varepsilon\), assumed symmetric about zero. The two leading models differ only in the distribution assumed for \(\varepsilon\).

chunks.heading: Definition (The latent-variable framework: logit and probit)
chunks.title: Chapter 14, Models for a Binary Dependent Variable — 14.3 Definition (The latent-variable framework: logit and probit)
chunks.body:
Definition 14.2 — Logit and probit
The logit model takes \(G\) to be the logistic CDF, \(\Lambda(z)=\dfrac{e^{z}}{1+e^{z}}=\dfrac{1}{1+e^{-z}}\). The probit model takes \(G\) to be the standard-normal CDF, \(\Phi(z)=\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{z}\phi(u)\,du\). Both are S-shaped, increasing monotonically from 0 to 1, and both therefore deliver fitted probabilities strictly within \([0,1]\).

chunks.heading: The latent-variable framework: logit and probit
chunks.title: Chapter 14, Models for a Binary Dependent Variable — 14.3 The latent-variable framework: logit and probit
chunks.body: Because the latent variable is unobserved, its scale is not identified: only the sign of \(y^{*}\) is observed, so multiplying \(y^{*}\), \(\beta\), and \(\varepsilon\) by a positive constant leaves \(y\) unchanged. The scale is fixed by normalizing the variance of \(\varepsilon\) — to \(\pi^{2}/3\) in the logit, to \(1\) in the probit. The coefficients \(\beta\) are thus defined only up to this normalization, which is the origin of the systematic difference in their magnitudes across the two models (Section 14.5.5).

chunks.heading: Estimation by maximum likelihood
chunks.title: Chapter 14, Models for a Binary Dependent Variable — 14.4 Estimation by maximum likelihood
chunks.body:
The index models are nonlinear in the parameters and are estimated by maximum likelihood rather than least squares. With independent observations, observation \(i\) contributes probability \(G(x_i'\beta)\) when \(y_i=1\) and \(1-G(x_i'\beta)\) when \(y_i=0\), so the log-likelihood is
\[ \ell(\beta)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big[\,y_i\log G(x_i'\beta)+(1-y_i)\log\big(1-G(x_i'\beta)\big)\Big]. \]
The estimator \(\hat\beta\) maximizes \(\ell\). It has no closed form and is obtained by iterative numerical optimization, but under standard conditions it is consistent, asymptotically normal, and asymptotically efficient. Inference uses the maximum-likelihood apparatus: standard errors from the inverse information matrix, and Wald, likelihood-ratio, or score tests for hypotheses.

chunks.heading: Interpreting the coefficients
chunks.title: Chapter 14, Models for a Binary Dependent Variable — 14.5 Interpreting the coefficients
chunks.body: The interpretation of logit and probit coefficients is the principal source of difficulty, because in neither model is a coefficient a change in probability. We treat first the readings common to both models, then those specific to each, and finally the relationship between the two.

chunks.heading: 14.5.1 Sign, significance, and the latent index
chunks.title: Chapter 14, Models for a Binary Dependent Variable — 14.5 14.5.1 Sign, significance, and the latent index
chunks.body: In both models \(\beta_j\) is the effect of \(x_j\) on the latent index \(x'\beta\), expressed in the normalized units of that model's error distribution. Its sign gives the direction of the effect on the probability — a positive coefficient raises the probability of the event, a negative coefficient lowers it — and its \(z\)-statistic and \(p\)-value test significance exactly as in linear regression. What the raw coefficient does not convey, in either model, is the magnitude of the effect on the probability itself.

chunks.heading: 14.5.2 Marginal effects (both models)
chunks.title: Chapter 14, Models for a Binary Dependent Variable — 14.5 14.5.2 Marginal effects (both models)
chunks.body:
The effect of a regressor on the probability is the marginal (partial) effect, obtained by differentiating \(G(x'\beta)\):
\[ \frac{\partial \Pr(y=1\mid x)}{\partial x_j}=g(x'\beta)\,\beta_j, \]
where \(g=G'\) is the density — \(\lambda(z)=\Lambda(z)[1-\Lambda(z)]\) for the logit, \(\phi(z)\) for the probit. The marginal effect is the coefficient scaled by the height of the density at the index, so it is largest where the curve is steepest (near probability one-half) and smallest in the tails (near 0 or 1); it therefore varies across observations. Two scalar summaries are reported: the average marginal effect (AME), the partial effect averaged over the sample, \(n^{-1}\sum_i g(x_i'\beta)\,\beta_j\); and the marginal effect at the mean (MEM), \(g(\bar x'\beta)\,\beta_j\). The AME is generally preferred, as it does not rely on a possibly unrepresentative “average” unit. These probability-scale summaries are directly comparable across logit, probit, and the linear probability model, and in practice they agree closely.

chunks.heading: 14.5.3 The logit reading: log-odds and odds ratios
chunks.title: Chapter 14, Models for a Binary Dependent Variable — 14.5 14.5.3 The logit reading: log-odds and odds ratios
chunks.body:
The logit affords an interpretation unavailable to the probit. Inverting the logistic form renders the log-odds linear in the regressors,
\[ \log\frac{\Pr(y=1\mid x)}{1-\Pr(y=1\mid x)}=x'\beta, \]
so \(\beta_j\) is the change in the log-odds of the event per unit change in \(x_j\). Exponentiating, \(e^{\beta_j}\) is the odds ratio: a one-unit increase in \(x_j\) multiplies the odds of the event by \(e^{\beta_j}\), holding the other regressors fixed. An odds ratio above one signifies a positive effect and below one a negative effect, and — unlike the probability-scale marginal effect — the reading is constant across observations. Thus \(\beta_j=0.30\) gives an odds ratio \(e^{0.30}\approx1.35\), a 35% increase in the odds. The odds ratio is a multiplicative effect on the odds, not on the probability, and the two must not be conflated.

chunks.heading: 14.5.4 The probit reading: the latent z-score scale
chunks.title: Chapter 14, Models for a Binary Dependent Variable — 14.5 14.5.4 The probit reading: the latent z-score scale
chunks.body: The probit coefficient has no odds interpretation. Because the probit normalizes the latent error to unit variance, \(\beta_j\) is the change in the latent index — a standard-normal \(z\)-score — per unit change in \(x_j\). A probit coefficient of \(0.20\) means that a one-unit increase in \(x_j\) shifts the latent propensity by 0.20 standard deviations, moving the argument of \(\Phi\) by that amount and changing the probability by \(\phi(x'\beta)\times0.20\) at a given \(x\). This is coherent but less immediate than the odds ratio, which is one reason the logit is often preferred when a verbal effect size is wanted; the probit's appeal lies in its consistency with a normally distributed latent error and its tractability within models that already assume normal structure.

chunks.heading: 14.5.5 Why logit and probit coefficients differ — and why it does not matter
chunks.title: Chapter 14, Models for a Binary Dependent Variable — 14.5 14.5.5 Why logit and probit coefficients differ — and why it does not matter
chunks.body: Logit coefficients are systematically larger than probit coefficients, by a factor of roughly \(1.6\) (the ratio of error standard deviations is \(\pi/\sqrt{3}\approx1.81\), tempered in practice to about 1.6–1.7). This is a pure consequence of the differing scale normalizations — the logistic error has standard deviation \(\pi/\sqrt{3}\), the normal error has standard deviation one — and carries no substantive content. Translated to the probability scale, the two models deliver nearly identical marginal effects and nearly identical fitted probabilities, and the choice between them seldom affects any conclusion. The raw coefficients of the two models must therefore never be compared directly; only their marginal effects (or, for the logit, its odds ratios) should be interpreted.

chunks.heading: Key idea (14.5.5 Why logit and probit coefficients differ — and why it does not matter)
chunks.title: Chapter 14, Models for a Binary Dependent Variable — 14.5 Key idea (14.5.5 Why logit and probit coefficients differ — and why it does not matter)
chunks.body:
Key Idea
In a logit or probit, the raw coefficient gives only the sign and significance of an effect. To quantify the effect on the probability, report a marginal effect (the average marginal effect is standard), which is comparable across logit, probit, and the linear probability model. The logit additionally permits an odds-ratio reading, \(e^{\beta_j}\); the probit coefficient is a latent \(z\)-score effect with no odds interpretation. Logit coefficients exceed probit coefficients by a scale factor of about 1.6, with no difference in substance.

chunks.heading: Goodness of fit
chunks.title: Chapter 14, Models for a Binary Dependent Variable — 14.6 Goodness of fit
chunks.body: There is no \(R^{2}\) for an index model in the least-squares sense. Fit is assessed through the maximized log-likelihood and statistics derived from it. McFadden's pseudo-\(R^{2}\), \(1-\ell(\hat\beta)/\ell_0\), compares the fitted log-likelihood to that of an intercept-only model \(\ell_0\); it lies in \([0,1)\) but is not a proportion of variance explained and takes much smaller values than a familiar \(R^{2}\). A likelihood-ratio test assesses the joint significance of the regressors. The percentage correctly predicted classifies each observation by whether its fitted probability exceeds a threshold (commonly one-half) and compares this to the realized outcome; it is intuitive but can mislead when the event is rare, since predicting “no event” for every observation may attain a high hit rate while conveying nothing.

chunks.heading: Implementation
chunks.title: Chapter 14, Models for a Binary Dependent Variable — 14.7 Implementation
chunks.body:
The linear probability model is OLS on the binary outcome with robust standard errors; the logit and probit are maximum-likelihood fits whose coefficients are converted to average marginal effects, with the logit's coefficients additionally exponentiated to odds ratios.
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
import numpy as np
# linear probability model: OLS on 0/1, robust SE (the outcome is heteroskedastic)
lpm = smf.ols("default ~ dti + fico", data=df).fit(cov_type="HC1")
# logit and probit by maximum likelihood
logit = smf.logit("default ~ dti + fico", data=df).fit()
probit = smf.probit("default ~ dti + fico", data=df).fit()
# raw coefficients are on each model's latent scale - convert to probability effects
print(logit.get_margeff(at="overall").summary()) # average marginal effects
print(probit.get_margeff(at="overall").summary())
# logit only: odds ratios
print(np.exp(logit.params)) # exp(beta) = odds ratio
The demonstration below fits all three models to the same binary outcome; it reports the logit and probit coefficients with their ratio, the logit odds ratios, and the average marginal effects of all three models side by side, and plots the fitted-probability curves.

chunks.heading: Reading the output (14.7.1 Demonstration: loan default)
chunks.title: Chapter 14, Models for a Binary Dependent Variable — 14.7 Reading the output (14.7.1 Demonstration: loan default)
chunks.body: Reading the output. The linear probability model reports the effect of debt-to-income directly on the probability scale (about 0.06, or six percentage points of default risk per unit). The logit and probit raw coefficients are not comparable to this or to each other: they lie on different latent scales, which is why their ratio is approximately 1.6 for every coefficient — the logistic error is wider than the normal error by that factor, with no difference in substance. Three readings render the models interpretable. The average marginal effects translate both nonlinear models back to the probability scale, where they coincide with one another and with the linear model (dti near 0.06, fico near −0.11); these are the numbers to report. The odds ratios, available only for the logit, give a constant multiplicative reading: each additional unit of debt-to-income multiplies the odds of default by about 1.3, while each standard deviation of credit score multiplies them by about 0.62, a reduction. The probit coefficients are latent \(z\)-score effects: a unit of debt-to-income raises the default propensity by roughly 0.16 standard deviations.

chunks.heading: Reading the output (14.7.1 Demonstration: loan default)
chunks.title: Chapter 14, Models for a Binary Dependent Variable — 14.7 Reading the output (14.7.1 Demonstration: loan default)
chunks.body: The plotted logit and probit curves are visually almost indistinguishable and both remain within \([0,1]\), whereas the extrapolated linear fit crosses the boundaries — the practical content of the distinction between the models.

chunks.heading: Instructor's take (14.7.1 Demonstration: loan default)
chunks.title: Chapter 14, Models for a Binary Dependent Variable — 14.7 Instructor's take (14.7.1 Demonstration: loan default)
chunks.body:
★ Sharma's Take
The choice between the linear probability model and the logit or probit is commonly debated in terms of whether fitted probabilities can fall outside the unit interval, but the more pertinent consideration is the base rate of the event. For events occurring between roughly twenty and eighty percent of the time, the central portion of the S-shaped curve is nearly linear, the two approaches agree closely, and the linear model is preferable for its interpretability. The approaches diverge materially only for rare events, where the curve bends sharply and a linear model would predict probabilities outside the admissible range. The base rate should therefore be examined first: where the event is common, the linear model suffices; where it is rare, the nonlinear models are warranted, and the analysis of rare events also demands particular care with the quality of the data.

chunks.heading: Chapter summary (14.7.1 Demonstration: loan default)
chunks.title: Chapter 14, Models for a Binary Dependent Variable — 14.7 Chapter summary (14.7.1 Demonstration: loan default)
chunks.body:
Chapter Summary
For a binary outcome coded 0/1 the conditional mean is the conditional probability of the event, and the outcome is Bernoulli with conditional variance \(p(1-p)\) (Section 14.1).
The linear probability model is OLS on the binary outcome; coefficients are constant probability changes, but fitted probabilities may fall outside \([0,1]\) and robust standard errors are required (Section 14.2).
Logit and probit arise from a latent-variable model \(y^{*}=x'\beta+\varepsilon\), \(y=\mathbf{1}\{y^{*}>0\}\), taking the logistic and standard-normal CDFs respectively; both keep probabilities in \([0,1]\) and are estimated by maximum likelihood (Sections 14.3–14.4).
A raw logit or probit coefficient gives only the sign and significance; the effect on the probability is the marginal effect \(g(x'\beta)\beta_j\), summarized by the average marginal effect, which is comparable across logit, probit, and the linear model (Section 14.5.2).

chunks.heading: Chapter summary (14.7.1 Demonstration: loan default)
chunks.title: Chapter 14, Models for a Binary Dependent Variable — 14.7 Chapter summary (14.7.1 Demonstration: loan default)
chunks.body:
The logit coefficient is a log-odds effect, with \(e^{\beta_j}\) the odds ratio; the probit coefficient is a latent \(z\)-score effect. Logit coefficients exceed probit coefficients by a scale factor of about 1.6 with no change in substance (Sections 14.5.3–14.5.5).
Fit is assessed by the log-likelihood, McFadden's pseudo-\(R^{2}\), likelihood-ratio tests, and percentage correctly predicted (Section 14.6).
In Python the LPM uses smf.ols with robust SE; logit and probit use smf.logit/smf.probit, with get_margeff for marginal effects and np.exp(params) for the logit's odds ratios (Section 14.7).

chunks.body: Chapter 15 · Time Series I

chunks.heading: The question
chunks.title: Chapter 15, Stationarity and Spurious Regression — 15.0 The question
chunks.body:
The Question
Two unrelated series both trend over time, and a regression of one on the other reports a strong, significant relationship. Is the relationship real?

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.title: Chapter 15, Stationarity and Spurious Regression — 15.0 Overview
chunks.body: Time-series data violate the assumption of independent observations: successive values of an economic series are related, and many series wander without returning to a fixed level. This wandering produces a hazard absent from cross-sectional analysis — the spurious regression, in which unrelated series appear strongly related. This chapter develops the concepts of autocorrelation and stationarity, demonstrates the spurious-regression problem, and establishes the testing and differencing procedures that guard against it, with their Python implementation.

chunks.heading: Key idea
chunks.title: Chapter 15, Stationarity and Spurious Regression — 15.0 Key idea
chunks.body:
Running example
Consider an analyst who suspects that one macroeconomic series drives another — that a country's price level tracks its money stock, say, or that two national-income aggregates move together. Plotted over several decades both series climb steadily, and a regression of one on the other returns a large coefficient, a \(t\)-statistic in the dozens, and an \(R^2\) near unity. The fit is spectacular. Yet exactly this spectacular fit arises when the two series are entirely unrelated, provided only that each wanders over time. This chapter explains why — developing autocorrelation, stationarity, and the unit root — and supplies the tests and transformations that separate a genuine co-movement from a coincidence of two trending series. The running example is two independent random-walk series, estimated in Section 15.7.

chunks.heading: Time-series data and the autocorrelation function
chunks.title: Chapter 15, Stationarity and Spurious Regression — 15.1 Time-series data and the autocorrelation function
chunks.body: A time series is a realization of a stochastic process \(\{y_t\}\) indexed by time, in which the ordering of observations is informative because each value is statistically related to its predecessors. This dependence is the defining feature of time-series data and the source of both its structure and its hazards. It is summarized by the autocovariance and autocorrelation functions.

chunks.heading: Definition (Time-series data and the autocorrelation function)
chunks.title: Chapter 15, Stationarity and Spurious Regression — 15.1 Definition (Time-series data and the autocorrelation function)
chunks.body:
Definition 15.1 — Autocovariance and autocorrelation
For a series with constant mean, the autocovariance at lag \(h\) is \(\gamma(h)=\operatorname{Cov}(y_t,\,y_{t-h})\), and the autocorrelation function (ACF) is its standardized form
\[ \rho(h)=\frac{\gamma(h)}{\gamma(0)},\qquad \gamma(0)=\operatorname{Var}(y_t). \]

chunks.heading: Time-series data and the autocorrelation function
chunks.title: Chapter 15, Stationarity and Spurious Regression — 15.1 Time-series data and the autocorrelation function
chunks.body: The ACF, plotted against the lag \(h\), is the correlogram; it is the primary descriptive instrument of time-series analysis. A series of independent, identically distributed shocks with zero mean and constant variance — white noise — has \(\rho(h)=0\) for all \(h\neq0\) and serves as the benchmark of no temporal structure. Persistent, slowly decaying autocorrelation indicates that successive observations carry overlapping information, so the effective number of independent observations is below the nominal count; inference that ignores this dependence overstates precision, exactly as unmodelled clustering does in Chapter 11.

chunks.heading: Stationarity
chunks.title: Chapter 15, Stationarity and Spurious Regression — 15.2 Stationarity
chunks.body: Estimation and inference in time series require that the probabilistic structure of the process be stable over time; otherwise a single realization carries no repeatable information about the process generating it. This stability is stationarity.

chunks.heading: Definition (Stationarity)
chunks.title: Chapter 15, Stationarity and Spurious Regression — 15.2 Definition (Stationarity)
chunks.body:
Definition 15.2 — Weak (covariance) stationarity
A series \(\{y_t\}\) is weakly stationary if its first two moments are time-invariant: \(\mathbb{E}[y_t]=\mu\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(y_t)=\gamma(0)\) are finite constants, and the autocovariance \(\gamma(h)=\operatorname{Cov}(y_t,y_{t-h})\) depends only on the lag \(h\), not on the date \(t\). Strict stationarity, the stronger requirement that the entire joint distribution be invariant to time shifts, implies weak stationarity when second moments exist.

chunks.heading: Stationarity
chunks.title: Chapter 15, Stationarity and Spurious Regression — 15.2 Stationarity
chunks.body: Stationarity is what permits the past to inform the future: because the relationship between observations depends only on their separation, the dependence estimated from history continues to hold. A non-stationary series violates one or more of these conditions — its mean drifts, its variance grows, or its autocovariances change with the date — and the standard regression apparatus, derived for stationary (and in cross-sections, independent) data, no longer delivers valid inference. The central practical task of this chapter is to determine whether a series is stationary and, if not, to render it so.

chunks.heading: The autoregressive process and the unit root
chunks.title: Chapter 15, Stationarity and Spurious Regression — 15.3 The autoregressive process and the unit root
chunks.body:
The simplest dynamic model expresses the current value as a fraction of its predecessor plus a shock — the first-order autoregressive process,
\[ y_t=\phi\,y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t,\qquad \varepsilon_t\ \text{white noise}. \]
The behaviour of the process is governed entirely by the coefficient \(\phi\). When \(|\phi|<1\) the series is stationary: shocks decay geometrically, the process reverts to its mean, the variance is the finite constant \(\sigma^2/(1-\phi^2)\), and the autocorrelation function declines geometrically, \(\rho(h)=\phi^{h}\). When \(\phi=1\) the process becomes the random walk \(y_t=y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t\), the leading non-stationary case: shocks are permanent rather than transitory, the series has no tendency to return to any fixed level, and its variance \(t\sigma^2\) grows without bound. The value \(\phi=1\) is the unit root, the boundary separating stationary from non-stationary autoregressive behaviour.

chunks.heading: Derivation (The autoregressive process and the unit root)
chunks.title: Chapter 15, Stationarity and Spurious Regression — 15.3 Derivation (The autoregressive process and the unit root)
chunks.body:
Deterministic versus stochastic trends, and the order of integration
A series may trend for two distinct reasons. A deterministic trend, \(y_t=\alpha+\beta t+u_t\) with \(u_t\) stationary, departs from a fixed line only temporarily; it is rendered stationary by detrending (regressing on \(t\)). A stochastic trend, as in the random walk (optionally with drift, \(y_t=\mu+y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t\)), accumulates permanent shocks and is rendered stationary by differencing. Confusing the two — detrending a unit-root series or differencing a trend-stationary one — misspecifies the dynamics.
A series is integrated of order \(d\), written \(I(d)\), if it must be differenced \(d\) times to become stationary. A stationary series is \(I(0)\); a random walk is \(I(1)\), since its first difference \(\Delta y_t=\varepsilon_t\) is white noise; a series whose changes themselves wander is \(I(2)\). Most economic levels (prices, GDP, money) are well described as \(I(1)\); their growth rates are \(I(0)\).

chunks.heading: Proposition (Spurious regression)
chunks.title: Chapter 15, Stationarity and Spurious Regression — 15.4 Proposition (Spurious regression)
chunks.body:
Proposition 15.1 — Spurious regression
The regression of one independent \(I(1)\) series on another typically yields a large coefficient, a \(t\)-statistic that grows without bound with the sample size, and a high \(R^2\), falsely indicating a relationship where none exists. This is not an exceptional outcome but the usual result of regressing one non-stationary series on another.

chunks.heading: Spurious regression
chunks.title: Chapter 15, Stationarity and Spurious Regression — 15.4 Spurious regression
chunks.body:
The phenomenon was documented by Granger and Newbold (1974). Its mechanism is that two wandering series, over any finite sample, exhibit apparent co-movement that ordinary least squares registers as a relationship. The difficulty is not merely understated standard errors: under non-stationarity the usual asymptotics fail entirely — the \(t\)-statistic does not converge to a fixed distribution but diverges as the sample grows, so a larger sample makes the spurious relationship appear more significant rather than averaging it away. The high \(R^2\) is genuine arithmetic; the relationship it appears to certify is not.
A practical warning sign accompanies the spurious result: the residuals of a spurious regression are themselves highly persistent (close to a unit root), so the Durbin–Watson statistic is near zero. A regression whose \(R^2\) exceeds its Durbin–Watson statistic is a classic signature of spuriousness and should not be interpreted before the series are tested for stationarity.

chunks.heading: Key idea (Spurious regression)
chunks.title: Chapter 15, Stationarity and Spurious Regression — 15.4 Key idea (Spurious regression)
chunks.body:
Key Idea
For time-series data, a high \(R^2\) and a large \(t\)-statistic are not evidence of a genuine relationship; they are the expected symptoms of regressing one non-stationary series on another. The stationarity of every series must be assessed before any time-series regression is interpreted.

chunks.heading: Testing for a unit root
chunks.title: Chapter 15, Stationarity and Spurious Regression — 15.5 Testing for a unit root
chunks.body: Because stationarity governs the validity of every subsequent step, it must be tested rather than assumed. The standard procedure is the Dickey–Fuller test. Subtracting \(y_{t-1}\) from the AR(1) equation gives \(\Delta y_t=(\phi-1)y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t=\delta\,y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t\); the unit-root hypothesis \(\phi=1\) is thus the hypothesis \(\delta=0\). The test regresses the change on the lagged level and examines the coefficient on \(y_{t-1}\).

chunks.heading: Definition (Testing for a unit root)
chunks.title: Chapter 15, Stationarity and Spurious Regression — 15.5 Definition (Testing for a unit root)
chunks.body:
The Dickey–Fuller test
Null hypothesis \(H_0:\ \delta=0\) (a unit root, non-stationary) against \(H_1:\ \delta<0\) (stationary, mean-reverting). The statistic is the \(t\)-ratio on \(\hat\delta\), but under the null it does not follow the Student distribution; it has a non-standard (Dickey–Fuller) distribution whose critical values lie further from zero, so ordinary \(t\)-tables must not be used.

chunks.heading: Testing for a unit root
chunks.title: Chapter 15, Stationarity and Spurious Regression — 15.5 Testing for a unit root
chunks.body: The augmented Dickey–Fuller (ADF) test adds lagged differences \(\Delta y_{t-1},\dots,\Delta y_{t-p}\) to the regression to absorb residual autocorrelation, so the test concerns the unit root alone; the lag length is chosen by an information criterion. The regression is specified with no constant, with a constant (drift), or with a constant and trend, according to the series' appearance — an incorrect specification distorts the test. Because the null is non-stationarity, failure to reject indicates that the series should be treated as non-stationary. The test has low power against persistent but stationary alternatives, so it is prudent to corroborate it with a complementary test such as KPSS, whose null is stationarity.

chunks.heading: Differencing and the order of integration
chunks.title: Chapter 15, Stationarity and Spurious Regression — 15.6 Differencing and the order of integration
chunks.body: A series found to contain a unit root is rendered stationary by differencing — replacing it by its period-to-period change \(\Delta y_t=y_t-y_{t-1}\). The first difference of a random walk is its white-noise increment, which is stationary; an \(I(1)\) series is thereby reduced to \(I(0)\) by one difference, and an \(I(d)\) series by \(d\) differences. A spurious relationship in levels disappears under differencing, confirming its spurious nature, whereas a genuine relationship survives. The procedure is therefore to test each series, difference until stationary, and conduct the regression in the transformed variables — with the important exception, developed in Chapter 16, of cointegrated series, whose long-run relationship differencing would discard. One caution: over-differencing a series that is already stationary introduces a non-invertible moving-average structure and inflates the variance, so one differences only as far as the unit-root tests require.

chunks.heading: Implementation
chunks.title: Chapter 15, Stationarity and Spurious Regression — 15.7 Implementation
chunks.body:
The augmented Dickey–Fuller test is provided by statsmodels.tsa.stattools.adfuller, whose second return value is the p-value; differencing uses the diff method (or numpy.diff). A regression in differences typically pairs with autocorrelation-robust (HAC) standard errors (Chapter 16).
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
# ADF test: H0 is a unit root (non-stationary). Large p -> treat the series as non-stationary.
stat, pvalue = adfuller(df["gdp"], autolag="AIC")[:2]
print(pvalue)
# difference to stationarity, then regress in differences with HAC standard errors
df["d_gdp"] = df["gdp"].diff()
df["d_x"] = df["x"].diff()
reg = smf.ols("d_gdp ~ d_x", data=df.dropna()).fit(cov_type="HAC", cov_kwds={"maxlags": 4})
print(reg.params["d_x"])
The demonstration below contrasts a stationary AR(1) with a random walk through the ADF test and the autocorrelation function, then generates two independent random walks, exhibits the spurious relationship in levels, and shows its disappearance under differencing.

chunks.heading: Reading the output (15.7.1 Demonstration: stationarity, unit roots, and spurious regression)
chunks.title: Chapter 15, Stationarity and Spurious Regression — 15.7 Reading the output (15.7.1 Demonstration: stationarity, unit roots, and spurious regression)
chunks.body: Reading the output. The stationary AR(1) is rejected for a unit root by the ADF test (small p-value), and its autocorrelation function decays geometrically, the lag-\(h\) value tracking \(\phi^{h}\); the random walk is not rejected (p near one), confirming the unit root. In the spurious experiment, the regression in levels of two independent random walks produces a large, highly significant coefficient and a high \(R^2\) — the spurious relationship of Proposition 15.1, and exactly the spectacular fit promised in the running example, here arising between series with no connection whatever. After differencing, the relationship vanishes: the coefficient becomes insignificant and the \(R^2\) collapses to nearly zero, confirming that nothing genuine was present. The ADF test recovers the truth directly — the levels carry a unit root, the differences do not — which is why each series must be tested, and differenced where necessary, before any time-series regression is believed.

chunks.heading: Instructor's take (15.7.1 Demonstration: stationarity, unit roots, and spurious regression)
chunks.title: Chapter 15, Stationarity and Spurious Regression — 15.7 Instructor's take (15.7.1 Demonstration: stationarity, unit roots, and spurious regression)
chunks.body:
★ Sharma's Take
A discipline applicable to any relationship measured over time is to determine whether it persists in differences. A genuine relationship, in which movements of one series drive movements of another, manifests in the period-to-period changes as well as in the levels: when one series moves, the other responds. A spurious relationship resides only in the shared wandering of the levels and disappears under differencing. The most informative single question to pose of a striking time-series correlation is therefore whether it survives in the differenced data. A relationship dramatic in levels but absent in differences reflects two series wandering in coincidental company rather than a mechanism connecting them; this consideration alone would invalidate a substantial portion of confident time-series claims.

chunks.heading: Chapter summary (15.7.1 Demonstration: stationarity, unit roots, and spurious regression)
chunks.title: Chapter 15, Stationarity and Spurious Regression — 15.7 Chapter summary (15.7.1 Demonstration: stationarity, unit roots, and spurious regression)
chunks.body:
Chapter Summary
A time series is a stochastic process whose dependence is summarized by the autocovariance and autocorrelation functions; the correlogram is the basic descriptive tool and white noise is the benchmark of no temporal structure (Section 15.1).
Weak stationarity — constant mean and variance and lag-only autocovariances — is what makes the past informative about the future and the standard regression apparatus valid (Section 15.2).
An AR(1) is stationary when \(|\phi|<1\) (geometric ACF, mean reversion) and a random walk when \(\phi=1\); \(\phi=1\) is the unit root. Trends may be deterministic (detrend) or stochastic (difference), and a series is \(I(d)\) if \(d\) differences make it stationary (Section 15.3).
Regressing one \(I(1)\) series on another produces a spurious relationship: a divergent \(t\)-statistic and a high \(R^2\) even when the series are independent, with a near-zero Durbin–Watson statistic as the signature (Proposition 15.1; Granger–Newbold).
The (augmented) Dickey–Fuller test takes a unit root as its null and has a non-standard distribution; failure to reject means the series is treated as non-stationary, corroborated by KPSS (Section 15.5).

chunks.heading: Chapter summary (15.7.1 Demonstration: stationarity, unit roots, and spurious regression)
chunks.title: Chapter 15, Stationarity and Spurious Regression — 15.7 Chapter summary (15.7.1 Demonstration: stationarity, unit roots, and spurious regression)
chunks.body:
Differencing reduces an \(I(1)\) series to stationarity and dispels spurious relationships, but over-differencing a stationary series is harmful; cointegrated series are the exception (Section 15.6; Chapter 16).
In Python, adfuller performs the test and diff differences; regressions in differences pair with HAC standard errors (Section 15.7).
