chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.title: Chapter 16,  — 16.0 Overview
chunks.body: Chapter 16 · Time Series II

chunks.heading: The question
chunks.title: Chapter 16, Cointegration and Forecasting — 16.0 The question
chunks.body:
The Question
Chapter 15 prescribed differencing for non-stationary series. But if two series are bound together in the long run, does differencing discard the relationship? And how is a model's predictive performance properly assessed?

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.title: Chapter 16, Cointegration and Forecasting — 16.0 Overview
chunks.body: Chapter 15 established that non-stationary series should be differenced before regression. This prescription has an important exception: when two non-stationary series are tied together in the long run, a relationship that differencing would destroy. This chapter develops cointegration, the formal expression of such a long-run relationship, together with the assessment of forecasting models by out-of-sample evaluation and the correction of standard errors for autocorrelation, with their Python implementation.

chunks.heading: Key idea
chunks.title: Chapter 16, Cointegration and Forecasting — 16.0 Key idea
chunks.body:
Running example
Consider an analyst tracking two non-stationary price series — a commodity quoted in two markets, say, or an asset and its futures contract. Each price wanders like a random walk, so neither is stationary; yet they never drift far apart, because whenever the gap widens, arbitrage pulls them back together. Differencing each series, as Chapter 15 would prescribe, throws away precisely this long-run tie. The two prices are cointegrated: a particular combination of them is stationary even though each is not, and an error-correction model measures how fast the gap closes when it opens. The running example is a cointegrated pair \(y_t=\beta x_t+u_t\) with stationary \(u_t\), estimated in Section 16.7, where the Engle–Granger test confirms the relationship and the error-correction model recovers the speed of adjustment.

chunks.heading: Cointegration
chunks.title: Chapter 16, Cointegration and Forecasting — 16.1 Cointegration
chunks.body: Chapter 15 prescribed differencing for any non-stationary series. There is one important exception. Two \(I(1)\) series may wander individually yet never drift far apart: whenever the gap between them widens, economic forces pull it back. A particular linear combination of the two is then stationary even though each series is not, and that combination expresses a stable long-run relationship the series obey. Such series are cointegrated.

chunks.heading: Definition (Cointegration)
chunks.title: Chapter 16, Cointegration and Forecasting — 16.1 Definition (Cointegration)
chunks.body:
Definition 16.1 — Cointegration
Two \(I(1)\) series \(y_t\) and \(x_t\) are cointegrated if there is a constant \(\beta\) (the cointegrating coefficient) such that the combination \(u_t=y_t-\beta x_t\) is \(I(0)\) (stationary). The vector \((1,-\beta)\) is the cointegrating vector, and \(u_t\) is the equilibrium error — the deviation from the long-run relationship \(y_t=\beta x_t\), which is mean-reverting rather than accumulating.

chunks.heading: Cointegration
chunks.title: Chapter 16, Cointegration and Forecasting — 16.1 Cointegration
chunks.body: For cointegrated series the levels regression of \(y_t\) on \(x_t\) is not spurious but informative: because the residual is stationary, ordinary least squares estimates the cointegrating coefficient consistently — indeed super-consistently, converging at rate \(T\) rather than \(\sqrt{T}\). Differencing, by contrast, would discard exactly the long-run relationship that distinguishes cointegration from the spurious case of Chapter 15. The two situations — two series wandering in coincidental company versus two tied together — are separated by whether a stationary linear combination exists.

chunks.heading: The error-correction model
chunks.title: Chapter 16, Cointegration and Forecasting — 16.2 The error-correction model
chunks.body:
Cointegration has an equivalent dynamic representation that unites the long-run relationship with short-run movement. If \(y_t\) and \(x_t\) are cointegrated, their changes obey an error-correction model (ECM):
\[ \Delta y_t=\alpha\,(y_{t-1}-\beta x_{t-1})+\gamma\,\Delta x_t+\varepsilon_t,\qquad \alpha<0. \]
The term \(u_{t-1}=y_{t-1}-\beta x_{t-1}\) is the previous period's equilibrium error. Its coefficient \(\alpha\) is the speed of adjustment: when \(y\) lies above its long-run relation with \(x\) (so \(u_{t-1}>0\)), the negative \(\alpha\) pulls \(\Delta y_t\) downward, closing a fraction \(|\alpha|\) of the gap each period; the term \(\gamma\,\Delta x_t\) captures the immediate short-run response. The model thus separates the long run — the equilibrium the series return to — from the short run, how they move between corrections.

chunks.heading: Proposition (The error-correction model)
chunks.title: Chapter 16, Cointegration and Forecasting — 16.2 Proposition (The error-correction model)
chunks.body:
Proposition 16.1 — Granger representation theorem
Two \(I(1)\) series are cointegrated if and only if an error-correction model relates them. Cointegration (a stationary linear combination) and error correction (a mean-reverting adjustment toward that combination) are two expressions of the same fact: a stable long-run relationship whose deviations are corrected rather than accumulated.

chunks.heading: Testing for cointegration
chunks.title: Chapter 16, Cointegration and Forecasting — 16.3 Testing for cointegration
chunks.body:
The Engle–Granger procedure tests cointegration in two steps. First, regress \(y_t\) on \(x_t\) in levels and form the residual \(\hat u_t\), the estimated equilibrium error. Second, test \(\hat u_t\) for a unit root: a stationary residual means deviations from the relationship mean-revert, so the series are cointegrated; a residual with a unit root means the apparent relationship is spurious. Because \(\hat u_t\) is itself estimated — the regression chooses \(\hat\beta\) to make the residual as small as possible — the ordinary Dickey–Fuller critical values are too lenient, and the test uses larger cointegration-specific critical values (Engle–Granger / MacKinnon).
The Engle–Granger test handles a single cointegrating relationship between two series. With more than two series there may be several cointegrating vectors, and the Johansen procedure — a system maximum-likelihood method — tests for and estimates their number. In either case the substantive prerequisite is a restoring mechanism: a reason the gap should close.

chunks.heading: Key idea (Testing for cointegration)
chunks.title: Chapter 16, Cointegration and Forecasting — 16.3 Key idea (Testing for cointegration)
chunks.body:
Key Idea
Differencing is correct for series that merely wander concurrently but destroys the relationship between cointegrated series, which must be analyzed in levels through the cointegrating regression and its error-correction model. The two cases are separated by whether the (individually non-stationary) series possess a stationary linear combination.

chunks.heading: Forecasting
chunks.title: Chapter 16, Cointegration and Forecasting — 16.4 Forecasting
chunks.body: A time-series model produces a forecast by projecting its estimated dynamics forward. For an AR(1), \(\hat y_{t+1}=\hat c+\hat\phi\,y_t\) is the one-step forecast; multi-step forecasts are obtained by iterating, \(\hat y_{t+h}=\hat c+\hat\phi\,\hat y_{t+h-1}\), each step feeding the previous forecast back in. Two features deserve emphasis. First, forecast uncertainty grows with the horizon: each additional step compounds the innovation variance, so forecast intervals widen as \(h\) increases — for a stationary series they widen toward the (finite) unconditional variance, while for a random walk they widen without bound. Second, every forecast must be judged against a benchmark. For many economic series the hardest benchmark to beat is the naive random-walk forecast — “tomorrow equals today” — and a model earns its complexity only by beating that benchmark out of sample.

chunks.heading: Evaluating forecasts
chunks.title: Chapter 16, Cointegration and Forecasting — 16.5 Evaluating forecasts
chunks.body: A model's fit to the data on which it was estimated — its \(R^2\) — is an unreliable measure of predictive performance, because the model was fitted to those very observations. The appropriate measure is performance on data not used in estimation.

chunks.heading: Definition (Evaluating forecasts)
chunks.title: Chapter 16, Cointegration and Forecasting — 16.5 Definition (Evaluating forecasts)
chunks.body:
Definition 16.2 — Out-of-sample evaluation
The data are partitioned into an earlier training period and a later test (holdout) period. The model is estimated on the training period and its forecasts compared with the realized outcomes in the test period. A model that fits the training period well but forecasts the test period poorly has fitted noise rather than structure.

chunks.heading: Evaluating forecasts
chunks.title: Chapter 16, Cointegration and Forecasting — 16.5 Evaluating forecasts
chunks.body: Forecast accuracy is summarized by the root-mean-square error, \(\mathrm{RMSE}=\sqrt{\tfrac1n\sum_t (y_t-\hat y_t)^2}\), which penalizes large errors heavily, or the mean absolute error, \(\mathrm{MAE}=\tfrac1n\sum_t|y_t-\hat y_t|\), which is more robust to outliers; each is read relative to the benchmark. Whether one model's out-of-sample accuracy is significantly better than another's is assessed by the Diebold–Mariano test for equal predictive accuracy, which examines whether the mean difference of the two models' loss series is zero. Out-of-sample evaluation is the principal safeguard against overfitting and the foundation of the predictive methods of Chapter 17.

chunks.heading: Autocorrelation-robust standard errors
chunks.title: Chapter 16, Cointegration and Forecasting — 16.6 Autocorrelation-robust standard errors
chunks.body: Even when a time-series regression is correctly specified in stationary variables, its disturbances are typically serially correlated, so the conventional standard errors of Chapter 4 — derived under independence — are understated, exactly as unmodelled clustering understates them in Chapter 11. The Newey–West (HAC: heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent) standard errors correct for both serial correlation and heteroskedasticity, leaving the coefficient estimates unchanged and adjusting only their reported precision. The correction sums residual autocovariances up to a chosen lag (the bandwidth, set with maxlags): too few lags leaves dependence uncorrected, too many adds noise. HAC standard errors are appropriate for essentially any regression on time-ordered data.

chunks.heading: Implementation
chunks.title: Chapter 16, Cointegration and Forecasting — 16.7 Implementation
chunks.body:
The Engle–Granger cointegration test is provided by statsmodels.tsa.stattools.coint.
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import coint
# Engle-Granger test: H0 is NO cointegration (no stable long-run relationship)
stat, pvalue, _ = coint(df["y"], df["x"])
print(pvalue) # small p-value: reject -> the two non-stationary series are cointegrated
Out-of-sample evaluation partitions the sample by time, estimates on the training period, and measures error on the test period; autocorrelation-robust (Newey–West) standard errors are requested with cov_type="HAC".
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
import numpy as np
# evaluate a model out of sample: fit on the early period, predict the later period
train = df.iloc[:split]
test = df.iloc[split:]
model = smf.ols("y ~ x1 + x2", data=train).fit(cov_type="HAC", cov_kwds={"maxlags": 4})
pred = model.predict(test)
rmse = np.sqrt(np.mean((test["y"] - pred)**2)) # out-of-sample error, the honest test
print(rmse)

chunks.heading: Implementation
chunks.title: Chapter 16, Cointegration and Forecasting — 16.7 Implementation
chunks.body: The demonstration below first builds a cointegrated pair, confirms cointegration by the Engle–Granger test, and recovers the cointegrating coefficient and the error-correction speed of adjustment; it then turns to forecasting, evaluating one-step-ahead forecasts on a held-out period against the random-walk benchmark.

chunks.heading: Reading the output (16.7.1 Demonstration: cointegration, error correction, and forecasting)
chunks.title: Chapter 16, Cointegration and Forecasting — 16.7 Reading the output (16.7.1 Demonstration: cointegration, error correction, and forecasting)
chunks.body: Reading the output. The Engle–Granger test rejects the null of no cointegration (small p-value), and the cointegrating regression recovers the true coefficient \(\beta\approx1.5\) with a stationary residual — the equilibrium error mean-reverts, exactly the arbitrage-restored gap of the running example. The error-correction model estimates a negative speed of adjustment \(\alpha\), the fraction of any deviation closed each period; a larger \(|\alpha|\) means faster return to equilibrium. In the forecasting block, the AR(1)'s one-step error on the held-out period is the honest measure of accuracy, and it is read against the random-walk benchmark: the model earns its keep only by beating “tomorrow equals today” out of sample, which here it does.

chunks.heading: Instructor's take (16.7.1 Demonstration: cointegration, error correction, and forecasting)
chunks.title: Chapter 16, Cointegration and Forecasting — 16.7 Instructor's take (16.7.1 Demonstration: cointegration, error correction, and forecasting)
chunks.body:
★ Sharma's Take
The question whether two series are cointegrated or merely spuriously related is presented as statistical, but its substantive form is whether a mechanism exists that restores the relationship when it is disturbed. A genuine long-run relationship has an economic basis — arbitrage that eliminates a price differential, a budget constraint linking expenditure to income, a policy rule connecting two rates. Before a cointegration test is conducted, the analyst should be able to name the restoring mechanism. Where the mechanism can be specified, a stable relationship is plausible and the test confirms an existing hypothesis; where no restoring force can be identified, a relationship that the test appears to detect should be regarded with suspicion, since a borderline test result may arise by chance as readily for unrelated series as a spurious one does. The mechanism is logically prior to the test, and the test should not be permitted to supply it.

chunks.heading: Chapter summary (16.7.1 Demonstration: cointegration, error correction, and forecasting)
chunks.title: Chapter 16, Cointegration and Forecasting — 16.7 Chapter summary (16.7.1 Demonstration: cointegration, error correction, and forecasting)
chunks.body:
Chapter Summary
Two \(I(1)\) series are cointegrated if a linear combination \(y_t-\beta x_t\) is stationary; \((1,-\beta)\) is the cointegrating vector and that combination is the mean-reverting equilibrium error (Definition 16.1).
Cointegrated series are analyzed in levels, where OLS estimates \(\beta\) super-consistently; differencing would destroy the long-run relationship (Section 16.1).
The error-correction model \(\Delta y_t=\alpha(y_{t-1}-\beta x_{t-1})+\gamma\Delta x_t+\varepsilon_t\) links short-run change to the lagged disequilibrium; \(\alpha<0\) is the speed of adjustment, and by the Granger representation theorem cointegration and error correction are equivalent (Section 16.2; Proposition 16.1).
The Engle–Granger two-step test regresses the levels and tests the residual for a unit root using cointegration-specific critical values; the Johansen procedure handles several series and multiple cointegrating vectors (Section 16.3).
Forecasts are iterated forward; their uncertainty grows with the horizon, and a model must beat a benchmark — typically the random walk, “tomorrow equals today” (Section 16.4).

chunks.heading: Chapter summary (16.7.1 Demonstration: cointegration, error correction, and forecasting)
chunks.title: Chapter 16, Cointegration and Forecasting — 16.7 Chapter summary (16.7.1 Demonstration: cointegration, error correction, and forecasting)
chunks.body:
Predictive performance is judged out of sample on a holdout by RMSE or MAE, with the Diebold–Mariano test for significantly better accuracy; in-sample \(R^2\) is not a measure of forecast accuracy (Section 16.5; Definition 16.2).
Newey–West (HAC) standard errors correct time-series inference for serial correlation and heteroskedasticity, leaving the coefficients unchanged. In Python, coint tests cointegration and cov_type="HAC" supplies the robust errors (Sections 16.6–16.7).

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.title: Chapter 17,  — 17.0 Overview
chunks.body: Chapter 17 · Prediction and Causal Inference

chunks.heading: The question
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.0 The question
chunks.body:
The Question
Algorithms that predict outcomes from many inputs have become extraordinarily accurate. Two questions follow. First, how are such methods constructed, and what do they optimize? Second — and this is the deeper question for an econometrician — can the predictive power of these methods be harnessed to estimate a causal effect, or does prediction belong to a different enterprise altogether?

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.0 Overview
chunks.body: This chapter develops two bodies of method that have reshaped applied econometrics. The first is penalized regression — the ridge and lasso estimators — which control the variance of an estimator by deliberately introducing bias, and which form the predictive core of modern statistical learning. The second is double (or debiased) machine learning, a framework that uses flexible predictive methods to estimate causal effects in the presence of many control variables. The treatment is self-contained: each estimator is defined formally through the optimization problem it solves, its statistical properties are derived or stated precisely, and its implementation in Python is presented in full. The chapter is longer and more demanding than those preceding it, as befits material that sits at the current research frontier yet rests entirely on the foundations the earlier chapters established.

chunks.heading: Key idea
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.0 Key idea
chunks.body:
Running example
Two tasks recur through this chapter, and they pull in opposite directions. In the first, a lender must predict which applicants will default from hundreds of candidate features; only out-of-sample accuracy matters, and the lasso of Section 17.5 keeps the few features that carry signal while discarding the rest. In the second, an analyst must estimate a causal effect — the effect of a training program on subsequent earnings, say — when many observed characteristics confound the comparison through unknown, nonlinear channels; here predictive accuracy is beside the point, and a coefficient lifted from an accurate predictive model is biased (Section 17.6). The double-machine-learning estimator of Sections 17.7–17.10 reconciles the two, letting a flexible learner absorb the confounders while protecting the causal parameter; the running causal example — a treatment whose effect is obscured by many nonlinear confounders — is estimated in Section 17.10, and extended to panel data, where unobserved unit effects confound as well, in Section 17.11.

chunks.heading: Two estimation problems
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.1 Two estimation problems
chunks.body:
It is essential at the outset to distinguish two objectives that are frequently conflated.
The first is prediction. Given a vector of predictors \(x\), the goal is to construct a function \(\hat f(x)\) whose value is close, on average, to the realized outcome \(y\) for observations not used in estimation. Predictive quality is judged solely by out-of-sample accuracy; the interpretation of the individual coefficients of \(\hat f\) is immaterial.
The second is causal inference. Here a particular covariate, the treatment \(d\), is singled out, and the goal is to estimate the effect on \(y\) of an exogenous change in \(d\), holding fixed the remaining covariates. As established in Chapters 1, 3, and 9, this requires an identifying assumption about the relationship between \(d\) and the unobserved determinants of \(y\); predictive accuracy is neither necessary nor sufficient for it.

chunks.heading: Key idea (Two estimation problems)
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.1 Key idea (Two estimation problems)
chunks.body:
Key Idea
Predictive accuracy and causal validity are distinct properties of an estimator. A model may predict \(y\) with high accuracy while yielding a severely biased estimate of the effect of any particular covariate, and conversely. The methods of statistical learning are, in the first instance, prediction methods. Their use in causal inference requires that they be embedded within an identification strategy, a point developed formally in Sections 17.6–17.9.

chunks.heading: The bias–variance decomposition
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.2 The bias–variance decomposition
chunks.body:
Consider estimating a regression function \(f(x)=\mathrm{E}[y\mid x]\) from a sample, obtaining an estimate \(\hat f\). Fix a target point \(x_0\) and let the data at that point be generated by \(y_0 = f(x_0) + \varepsilon\), where \(\varepsilon\) has mean zero and variance \(\sigma^2\) and is independent of the training sample. The expected squared prediction error at \(x_0\), taken over both the training sample and the new disturbance \(\varepsilon\), admits the decomposition
\[ \mathrm{E}\big[(y_0 - \hat f(x_0))^2\big] \;=\; \underbrace{\sigma^2}_{\text{irreducible}} \;+\; \underbrace{\big(f(x_0) - \mathrm{E}[\hat f(x_0)]\big)^2}_{\text{bias}^2} \;+\; \underbrace{\mathrm{Var}\big(\hat f(x_0)\big)}_{\text{variance}}. \]
The three terms are distinct in origin. The irreducible error \(\sigma^2\) reflects noise in the outcome itself and cannot be reduced by any estimator. The squared bias measures how far the estimator is centred from the truth; it is large when the model is too rigid to represent \(f\). The variance measures the sensitivity of the estimate to the particular training sample; it is large when the model is so flexible that it adapts to sample-specific noise.

chunks.heading: The bias–variance decomposition
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.2 The bias–variance decomposition
chunks.body: The decomposition makes precise a tension that governs every modelling choice. Increasing model flexibility — adding regressors, raising polynomial degree, deepening a tree — reduces bias but raises variance. Restricting flexibility does the reverse. Because the two terms enter the prediction error additively and with opposite responses to flexibility, there exists an intermediate degree of flexibility that minimizes their sum. The estimators of this chapter are devices for locating that minimum in a disciplined way.

chunks.heading: Definition (The bias–variance decomposition)
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.2 Definition (The bias–variance decomposition)
chunks.body:
Definition 17.1 — Overfitting
An estimator overfits when its flexibility is great enough that variance dominates the prediction error: the in-sample fit is excellent because the estimator has adapted to the noise of the training sample, but out-of-sample accuracy is poor because that noise does not recur. Overfitting is diagnosed by a large gap between in-sample and out-of-sample error.

chunks.heading: Cross-validation
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.3 Cross-validation
chunks.body: Because bias and variance cannot be observed directly, the degree of flexibility must be selected by estimating out-of-sample prediction error. The standard procedure is \(K\)-fold cross-validation.

chunks.heading: Definition (Cross-validation)
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.3 Definition (Cross-validation)
chunks.body:
Definition 17.2 — \(K\)-fold cross-validation
Partition the \(n\) observations into \(K\) disjoint subsets (folds) of approximately equal size, \(I_1,\dots,I_K\). For each \(k\), estimate the model on the observations not in fold \(k\) and compute its mean squared prediction error on the observations in fold \(k\). The cross-validation estimate of prediction error is the average of these \(K\) fold-specific errors,
\[ \mathrm{CV} \;=\; \frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K} \frac{1}{|I_k|}\sum_{i\in I_k}\big(y_i - \hat f^{(-k)}(x_i)\big)^2, \]
where \(\hat f^{(-k)}\) denotes the estimator fitted with fold \(k\) removed. To select a tuning parameter, \(\mathrm{CV}\) is computed over a grid of candidate values and the value minimizing it is chosen.

chunks.heading: Cross-validation
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.3 Cross-validation
chunks.body: The validity of the procedure rests on a single principle: each prediction is evaluated on data that played no part in producing it, so the cross-validation error is an approximately unbiased estimate of genuine out-of-sample error. The choice \(K=5\) or \(K=10\) is conventional, trading computational cost against the variance of the estimate.

chunks.heading: Penalized regression: ridge and lasso
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.4 Penalized regression: ridge and lasso
chunks.body:
Ordinary least squares chooses coefficients to minimize the residual sum of squares alone. When the number of predictors \(p\) is large relative to the sample size \(n\), this objective is minimized by coefficients that fit the training noise, producing high variance; and when \(p\) exceeds \(n\) the minimizer is not even unique. Penalized regression addresses both problems by adding to the least-squares objective a penalty that increases with the magnitude of the coefficients, thereby constraining their size.
Throughout this section the predictors are assumed standardized — each rescaled to have mean zero and unit variance — so that a single penalty applies comparably across predictors measured in different units. The intercept is not penalized.

chunks.heading: Definition (17.4.1 The ridge estimator)
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.4 Definition (17.4.1 The ridge estimator)
chunks.body:
Definition 17.3 — Ridge regression
For a penalty parameter \(\lambda \ge 0\), the ridge estimator solves
\[ \hat\beta^{\,\text{ridge}}(\lambda) \;=\; \arg\min_{\beta}\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big(y_i - \beta_0 - \sum_{j=1}^{p}x_{ij}\beta_j\Big)^{2} \;+\; \lambda\sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j^{2}. \]
The first term is the familiar residual sum of squares; the second, the \(\ell_2\) penalty, is \(\lambda\) times the sum of squared coefficients.

chunks.heading: 17.4.1 The ridge estimator
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.4 17.4.1 The ridge estimator
chunks.body:
The parameter \(\lambda\) governs the strength of the penalty. At \(\lambda=0\) the estimator reduces to ordinary least squares. As \(\lambda\to\infty\) every coefficient is driven toward zero. Intermediate values shrink the coefficients toward zero by an amount that the data, through the residual-sum-of-squares term, can resist in proportion to the evidence for each coefficient.
Remark 17.1 — closed form and the \(p>n\) case
Collecting the standardized predictors into the \(n\times p\) matrix \(X\) and the outcomes into the vector \(y\), the ridge objective is \(\lVert y - X\beta\rVert^2 + \lambda\lVert\beta\rVert^2\), whose unique minimizer is
\[ \hat\beta^{\,\text{ridge}}(\lambda) \;=\; \big(X^{\top}X + \lambda I\big)^{-1}X^{\top}y. \]
(Matrix notation here merely abbreviates the sums above.) The term \(\lambda I\) adds \(\lambda\) to each diagonal entry of \(X^{\top}X\), which guarantees the matrix is invertible for any \(\lambda>0\) — even when \(p>n\), where \(X^{\top}X\) alone is singular and ordinary least squares is undefined. This is the precise sense in which the penalty stabilizes estimation in high dimensions.

chunks.heading: Definition (17.4.2 The lasso estimator)
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.4 Definition (17.4.2 The lasso estimator)
chunks.body:
Definition 17.4 — Lasso regression
For a penalty parameter \(\lambda \ge 0\), the lasso estimator solves
\[ \hat\beta^{\,\text{lasso}}(\lambda) \;=\; \arg\min_{\beta}\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big(y_i - \beta_0 - \sum_{j=1}^{p}x_{ij}\beta_j\Big)^{2} \;+\; \lambda\sum_{j=1}^{p}\lvert\beta_j\rvert. \]
The penalty — the \(\ell_1\) penalty — is \(\lambda\) times the sum of the absolute values of the coefficients.

chunks.heading: 17.4.2 The lasso estimator
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.4 17.4.2 The lasso estimator
chunks.body:
The ridge and lasso objectives differ only in whether the coefficients are penalized through their squares or their absolute values. This apparently minor difference has a decisive consequence: the lasso sets some coefficients exactly to zero, and thereby performs variable selection, whereas ridge shrinks all coefficients toward zero but sets none of them exactly to zero.
The reason is made exact in the special case of orthonormal standardized predictors, where each penalized estimator has a closed form in terms of the ordinary least squares coefficient \(\hat\beta_j^{\,\text{ols}}\):
\[ \hat\beta_j^{\,\text{ridge}} = \frac{\hat\beta_j^{\,\text{ols}}}{1+\lambda}, \qquad \hat\beta_j^{\,\text{lasso}} = \operatorname{sign}\!\big(\hat\beta_j^{\,\text{ols}}\big)\,\max\!\Big(\big|\hat\beta_j^{\,\text{ols}}\big| - \tfrac{\lambda}{2},\,0\Big). \]

chunks.heading: 17.4.2 The lasso estimator
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.4 17.4.2 The lasso estimator
chunks.body:
The ridge solution multiplies every coefficient by the common factor \(1/(1+\lambda)\): a proportional shrinkage that never reaches zero for a finite \(\lambda\). The lasso solution subtracts the constant \(\lambda/2\) from the magnitude of each coefficient and truncates at zero — the operation known as soft-thresholding. Any coefficient whose least-squares magnitude is at most \(\lambda/2\) is set exactly to zero; the remainder are pulled toward zero by the fixed amount \(\lambda/2\). Variable selection is thus a direct consequence of the constant, non-vanishing derivative of the absolute-value penalty, in contrast to the derivative \(2\beta_j\) of the squared penalty, which vanishes as \(\beta_j\to 0\) and so cannot force a coefficient to the boundary.
Remark 17.2 — the geometric view

chunks.heading: 17.4.2 The lasso estimator
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.4 17.4.2 The lasso estimator
chunks.body: Penalized estimation may equivalently be written as minimizing the residual sum of squares subject to a constraint on the penalty: \(\sum_j\beta_j^2 \le t\) for ridge, \(\sum_j|\beta_j| \le t\) for lasso. The ridge constraint region is a sphere; the lasso constraint region is a diamond (a cross-polytope) whose vertices lie on the coordinate axes. The least-squares contours generically first touch the diamond at a vertex — a point at which some coordinates are exactly zero — whereas they touch the smooth sphere at a generic point with all coordinates nonzero. This is the geometric counterpart of the soft-thresholding formula.

chunks.heading: 17.4.3 Selecting the penalty
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.4 17.4.3 Selecting the penalty
chunks.body: The penalty parameter \(\lambda\) controls the position of each estimator on the bias–variance spectrum: small \(\lambda\) yields low bias and high variance (approaching ordinary least squares), large \(\lambda\) yields high bias and low variance. It is therefore selected to minimize estimated out-of-sample error by cross-validation (Definition 17.2), evaluated over a grid of candidate values. Because every penalized coefficient is shrunk toward zero, both estimators are biased toward zero by construction; this bias is the price paid for the reduction in variance, and it is acceptable when the objective is prediction. Section 17.6 shows why it is not acceptable when the objective is the estimation of a causal effect.

chunks.heading: Estimating ridge and lasso in Python
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.5 Estimating ridge and lasso in Python
chunks.body:
Ordinary least squares is estimated with statsmodels, which reports the full inferential table familiar from Chapter 4.
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
# fit an ordinary least squares regression of wage on schooling
model = smf.ols("wage ~ educ", data=df)
result = model.fit()
print(result.summary()) # full table: coefficients, se, t, p, R-squared
beta_educ = result.params["educ"] # the estimated slope
se_educ = result.bse["educ"] # its standard error
Penalized estimators are provided by scikit-learn. Two preliminary points are important. First, the predictors must be standardized before penalization, because the penalty depends on the scale of the coefficients; StandardScaler performs this transformation.
import numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
# X is an (n by p) array of predictors; standardize each column to mean 0, variance 1
scaler = StandardScaler()
Xs = scaler.fit_transform(X) # penalty now treats every predictor on equal footing
Second, scikit-learn denotes the penalty parameter \(\lambda\) by alpha. The estimators Ridge and Lasso take a fixed penalty, while RidgeCV and LassoCV select it by cross-validation over a supplied grid.

chunks.heading: Estimating ridge and lasso in Python
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.5 Estimating ridge and lasso in Python
chunks.body:
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge, Lasso, RidgeCV, LassoCV
# fixed penalty strength (alpha is scikit-learn's name for lambda)
ridge = Ridge(alpha=1.0).fit(Xs, y)
lasso = Lasso(alpha=0.1).fit(Xs, y)
# choose the penalty automatically by k-fold cross-validation
ridge_cv = RidgeCV(alphas=np.logspace(-3, 3, 25)).fit(Xs, y)
lasso_cv = LassoCV(cv=5, random_state=0).fit(Xs, y)
print("chosen lambda (ridge):", ridge_cv.alpha_)
print("chosen lambda (lasso):", lasso_cv.alpha_)
print("predictors kept by lasso:", int(np.sum(lasso_cv.coef_ != 0)))
The fitted coefficients are returned in the coef_ attribute and the selected penalty in alpha_. For the lasso, the number of nonzero entries of coef_ is the number of predictors retained. The cell below applies these estimators to a designed problem in which only five of one hundred and twenty candidate predictors genuinely enter the outcome, and scores each estimator on a held-out test set.

chunks.heading: Reading the output (17.5.1 Demonstration)
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.5 Reading the output (17.5.1 Demonstration)
chunks.body: Reading the output. Ordinary least squares, fitting all one hundred and twenty predictors, attains the worst held-out error because it fits the noise of the eighty redundant predictors. Ridge improves on it by shrinkage. The lasso attains the best held-out error and, in addition, recovers the five genuine predictors while setting the great majority of the redundant coefficients exactly to zero. The cross-validated penalty is reported as alpha.

chunks.heading: Why penalized regression does not estimate causal effects
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.6 Why penalized regression does not estimate causal effects
chunks.body:
Consider the apparently natural strategy of estimating the effect of a treatment \(d\) by applying the lasso to a regression of \(y\) on \(d\) together with a large collection of controls \(X\), and reading off the coefficient on \(d\). This strategy is invalid, for two distinct reasons.
First, the lasso shrinks every penalized coefficient toward zero, including the coefficient on \(d\). The resulting estimate of the treatment effect is attenuated by an amount that depends on \(\lambda\) and is generally unknown. A penalized coefficient is not a consistent estimator of a structural parameter.

chunks.heading: Why penalized regression does not estimate causal effects
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.6 Why penalized regression does not estimate causal effects
chunks.body: Second, and more seriously, the lasso selects controls according to their value in predicting the outcome. A variable may be a weak predictor of \(y\) yet a strong predictor of the treatment \(d\); such a variable is, by the omitted-variable analysis of Chapter 3, an important confounder, since its omission biases the treatment coefficient in proportion to its association with \(d\). The lasso, judging relevance by outcome prediction alone, may set its coefficient to zero, reintroducing precisely the omitted-variable bias the controls were meant to remove. Selection of controls by outcome prediction is therefore systematically misaligned with the requirements of causal inference.

chunks.heading: Key idea (Why penalized regression does not estimate causal effects)
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.6 Key idea (Why penalized regression does not estimate causal effects)
chunks.body:
Key Idea
A coefficient produced by a regularized estimator is not a valid estimate of a causal effect: it is attenuated by the penalty, and the variable-selection step discards confounders that predict the treatment but not the outcome. The flexibility of statistical learning is nonetheless valuable for causal inference, provided it is directed at the prediction subproblems and kept away from the target parameter itself. The construction that achieves this is developed next.

chunks.heading: The partially linear model and orthogonalization
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.7 The partially linear model and orthogonalization
chunks.body:
The framework that reconciles flexible prediction with causal estimation is the partially linear model:
\[ y \;=\; \theta\, d \;+\; g(X) \;+\; u, \qquad \mathrm{E}[u\mid d,X]=0, \]
\[ d \;=\; m(X) \;+\; v, \qquad \mathrm{E}[v\mid X]=0. \]
Here \(\theta\) is the scalar causal parameter of interest — the effect of the treatment, assumed constant across units — while \(g(X)=\mathrm{E}[y\mid X, d=0]\) and \(m(X)=\mathrm{E}[d\mid X]\) are unknown functions of the controls, permitted to be nonlinear and high-dimensional. These two functions are termed nuisance functions: they are not of direct interest, but must be estimated en route to \(\theta\).
The route is the partialling-out identity of Chapter 3 (the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem), now applied with general nuisance functions. Define the two residuals
\[ \tilde y \;=\; y - \mathrm{E}[y\mid X], \qquad \tilde d \;=\; d - m(X) \;=\; v. \]

chunks.heading: The partially linear model and orthogonalization
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.7 The partially linear model and orthogonalization
chunks.body:
Substituting the model for \(y\) and using \(\mathrm{E}[y\mid X] = \theta\, m(X) + g(X)\) gives \(\tilde y = \theta\,\tilde d + u\). Because \(\tilde d = v\) is, by construction, orthogonal to the controls and to \(u\), the parameter \(\theta\) is identified as the coefficient of a simple regression of \(\tilde y\) on \(\tilde d\):
\[ \theta \;=\; \frac{\mathrm{E}[\tilde y\,\tilde d]}{\mathrm{E}[\tilde d^{\,2}]}. \]
This is the population analogue of regressing the outcome residual on the treatment residual. The construction residualizes both variables with respect to the controls; the role of the second residualization — of the treatment — is established in the following section.

chunks.heading: Double machine learning
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.8 Double machine learning
chunks.body: The identification result of Section 17.7 requires the nuisance functions \(\mathrm{E}[y\mid X]\) and \(m(X)\), which are unknown. Double machine learning estimates them with flexible predictive methods — penalized regression, random forests, gradient boosting, or others — and forms the residuals from the fitted values.

chunks.heading: Definition (Double machine learning)
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.8 Definition (Double machine learning)
chunks.body:
Definition 17.5 — The double machine learning estimator
Let \(\hat\ell(X)\) and \(\hat m(X)\) be estimates of \(\mathrm{E}[y\mid X]\) and \(\mathrm{E}[d\mid X]\). Form residuals \(\hat{\tilde y}_i = y_i - \hat\ell(X_i)\) and \(\hat{\tilde d}_i = d_i - \hat m(X_i)\). The estimator of \(\theta\) is
\[ \hat\theta \;=\; \frac{\sum_i \hat{\tilde d}_i\,\hat{\tilde y}_i}{\sum_i \hat{\tilde d}_i^{\,2}}, \]
the slope of the regression of the outcome residual on the treatment residual.

chunks.heading: Double machine learning
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.8 Double machine learning
chunks.body: The decisive property of this estimator is its insensitivity to errors in the estimated nuisance functions. Suppose \(\hat\ell\) and \(\hat m\) deviate from the true \(\ell\) and \(m\) by small amounts. One may show that the resulting error in \(\hat\theta\) depends, to first order, only on the product of the two nuisance errors, not on either separately. Because each error is small, their product is of second order and hence negligible. An estimating equation with this property — that the first-order effect of nuisance error vanishes — is said to satisfy a Neyman orthogonality condition.

chunks.heading: Double machine learning
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.8 Double machine learning
chunks.body: The orthogonality is precisely what the double residualization secures, and it is why the naive single-residualization strategy fails. Had only the outcome been residualized, the error in \(\hat\theta\) would depend on the nuisance error to first order, so that the slow convergence of a flexible, regularized nuisance estimator would transmit directly into a first-order bias in \(\theta\) — the regularization bias of Section 17.6. Residualizing the treatment as well removes that first-order channel, leaving only the harmless second-order product. Under the orthogonality condition, and with the cross-fitting of Section 17.9, \(\hat\theta\) is consistent and asymptotically normal at the parametric rate \(\sqrt{n}\), so that conventional standard errors and confidence intervals are valid even though the nuisance functions are estimated by methods that converge more slowly.

chunks.heading: Cross-fitting
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.9 Cross-fitting
chunks.body: One further safeguard is required. If a nuisance function is estimated on the same observations to which it is then applied, a flexible estimator will have partially fitted the noise of those observations, so the residuals are correlated with that noise. This correlation induces a bias in \(\hat\theta\) that does not vanish even asymptotically. The remedy is cross-fitting, an application of sample splitting.

chunks.heading: Definition (Cross-fitting)
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.9 Definition (Cross-fitting)
chunks.body:
Definition 17.6 — Cross-fitting
Partition the sample into \(K\) folds. For each fold \(k\), estimate the nuisance functions on the observations outside fold \(k\), and use those fitted functions to compute the residuals \(\hat{\tilde y}_i,\hat{\tilde d}_i\) for the observations inside fold \(k\). Every observation thus receives residuals computed from nuisance estimates that did not use it. The estimator \(\hat\theta\) is then formed from the assembled residuals as in Definition 17.5.

chunks.heading: Cross-fitting
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.9 Cross-fitting
chunks.body: Cross-fitting is the same out-of-sample principle as cross-validation (Definition 17.2), applied here not to select a tuning parameter but to ensure that each residual is statistically independent of the nuisance estimate that produced it. Together, Neyman orthogonality and cross-fitting permit the use of arbitrary high-quality predictive methods for the nuisance functions while retaining valid inference on \(\theta\).

chunks.heading: Estimating a causal effect by double machine learning in Python
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.10 Estimating a causal effect by double machine learning in Python
chunks.body:
The estimator is assembled from components already encountered: a flexible learner for the two nuisance predictions, a manual cross-fitting loop, and a final residual-on-residual regression with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors. The learner below is an ensemble of randomized trees (ExtraTreesRegressor); any flexible regressor may be substituted.
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import ExtraTreesRegressor
import statsmodels.api as sm
def fit_learner(seed):
return ExtraTreesRegressor(n_estimators=80, min_samples_leaf=3, random_state=seed)
K = 5
folds = np.array_split(np.random.default_rng(0).permutation(len(y)), K)
y_res = np.zeros(len(y))
d_res = np.zeros(len(y))
for k in range(K):
test = folds[k]
train = np.concatenate([folds[j] for j in range(K) if j != k])
# predict each test fold from a learner trained on the OTHER folds (cross-fitting)
y_res[test] = y[test] - fit_learner(0).fit(X[train], y[train]).predict(X[test])
d_res[test] = d[test] - fit_learner(1).fit(X[train], d[train]).predict(X[test])
# the causal effect is the slope of the residual-on-residual regression
final = sm.OLS(y_res, d_res).fit(cov_type="HC1")
theta = final.params[0]
se = final.bse[0]

chunks.heading: Estimating a causal effect by double machine learning in Python
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.10 Estimating a causal effect by double machine learning in Python
chunks.body: The loop iterates over folds, fits each nuisance function on the complementary folds, and predicts the held-out fold, so that every residual is computed out of sample. The final regression of y_res on d_res returns the estimate theta and its standard error se. The cell below applies the procedure to data in which twenty controls influence both the treatment and the outcome through nonlinear functions, so that the true effect is obscured by confounding.

chunks.heading: Reading the output (17.10.1 Demonstration)
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.10 Reading the output (17.10.1 Demonstration)
chunks.body: Reading the output. The naive regression of the outcome on the treatment alone is severely biased by confounding. Including the controls linearly reduces the bias only partially, because the confounding operates through nonlinear functions that a linear specification cannot represent. Double machine learning, which estimates those functions flexibly and residualizes both variables with cross-fitting, recovers the true effect and reports a confidence interval that contains it.

chunks.heading: Double machine learning with panel data
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.11 Double machine learning with panel data
chunks.body:
The estimator of Sections 17.8–17.10 controls flexibly for observed confounders. Panel data (Chapter 11) offer a complementary protection against a class of unobserved confounders: those that are constant within a unit over time. The two devices combine, so that a single estimator handles observed time-varying confounders flexibly and unobserved time-invariant confounders by the within transformation.
Augment the partially linear model with a unit-specific effect:
\[ y_{it}=\theta\,d_{it}+g(X_{it})+\alpha_i+u_{it},\qquad d_{it}=m(X_{it})+\alpha_i^{d}+v_{it}. \]
The term \(\alpha_i\) collects the time-invariant characteristics of unit \(i\), observed or not; because it enters both the treatment and the outcome it is a confounder of exactly the kind the controls \(X\) may fail to capture. As in Chapter 11, the within transformation — subtracting each unit's time average — eliminates \(\alpha_i\) without its ever being observed:
\[ \ddot y_{it}=\theta\,\ddot d_{it}+\big[g(X_{it})-\bar g_i\big]+\ddot u_{it}. \]

chunks.heading: Double machine learning with panel data
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.11 Double machine learning with panel data
chunks.body:
Double machine learning is then applied to the within-transformed data: a flexible learner estimates the conditional expectations of \(\ddot y\) and \(\ddot d\) given the controls, the residuals are formed, and \(\theta\) is the slope of their regression. Two adjustments are essential.
First, cross-fitting must split on units, not observations. Because observations from the same unit are dependent, placing some of a unit's periods in the training fold and others in the test fold would let the nuisance estimate borrow within-unit information about the held-out periods, reintroducing the bias cross-fitting exists to remove. Every observation of a unit must therefore fall in the same fold.
Second, inference must be clustered by unit. The within-transformed disturbances \(\ddot u_{it}\) remain correlated within a unit, so the final residual-on-residual regression is fitted with cluster-robust standard errors (Chapter 11), clustering on the unit.

chunks.heading: Key idea (Double machine learning with panel data)
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.11 Key idea (Double machine learning with panel data)
chunks.body:
Key Idea
Combining the within transformation with double machine learning yields an estimator robust on two fronts at once: flexible control for observed time-varying confounders, through the machine-learning nuisance estimates, and exact control for unobserved time-invariant confounders, through the fixed effects. The price is that cross-fitting must respect the panel structure — folds are formed from whole units, and standard errors are clustered by unit.

chunks.heading: Double machine learning with panel data
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.11 Double machine learning with panel data
chunks.body: One caution carries over from Chapter 11: the within transformation removes only the time-invariant component of unobserved confounding. A confounder that varies over time and is unobserved is not addressed by fixed effects and, if also outside \(X\), leaves the estimator biased — the limitation taken up in general in Section 17.12.

chunks.heading: Reading the output (17.11.1 Demonstration)
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.11 Reading the output (17.11.1 Demonstration)
chunks.body: Reading the output. The unit effect \(\alpha_i\) confounds the treatment but is never observed. Pooled regression is badly biased, and even double machine learning that flexibly controls for the observed \(X\) remains biased, because the learner cannot see \(\alpha_i\). Adding the within transformation removes \(\alpha_i\) exactly; double machine learning on the within-transformed data — cross-fitted by unit and with standard errors clustered by unit — recovers the true effect and reports a confidence interval that contains it. Observed confounders are handled by the learner; the unobserved time-invariant confounder is handled by the fixed effects.

chunks.heading: Scope and limitations
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.12 Scope and limitations
chunks.body: The validity of the double machine learning estimator rests on the assumption embedded in the partially linear model of Section 17.7: that conditional on the controls \(X\), the treatment residual \(v\) is uncorrelated with the outcome disturbance \(u\). This is the unconfoundedness (or selection-on-observables) assumption, and it requires that \(X\) contain all common causes of \(d\) and \(y\). No estimation method can establish this assumption from data; it is an identifying restriction justified by subject-matter knowledge.

chunks.heading: Scope and limitations
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.12 Scope and limitations
chunks.body: The contribution of double machine learning is therefore precisely delimited. It relaxes the functional-form requirement of conventional control-variable regression, permitting the confounders to enter through unknown, possibly nonlinear, high-dimensional functions while preserving valid inference on the treatment effect. It does not relax the identifying requirement that the confounders be observed. When an important confounder is unobserved, the estimator is biased, and identification must instead be sought through the instrumental-variables strategy of Chapter 9 or the quasi-experimental designs of Chapters 12 and 13 — within which, it should be noted, machine learning may still be employed for the associated prediction subproblems.

chunks.heading: Key idea (Scope and limitations)
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.12 Key idea (Scope and limitations)
chunks.body:
Key Idea
Double machine learning addresses the problem of flexible control for observed confounders; it does not address the problem of identification in the presence of unobserved confounders. The distinction between these two problems is the organizing theme of the entire book, and it is not dissolved by the introduction of more powerful predictive methods.

chunks.heading: Heterogeneous effects
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.13 Heterogeneous effects
chunks.body: The partially linear model restricts the treatment effect \(\theta\) to be constant across units. When the effect is believed to vary with observed characteristics — that is, when one seeks the conditional effect \(\theta(x)\) — the same orthogonalization-and-cross-fitting template extends to estimate it: the final residual-on-residual regression is replaced by a flexible model relating the outcome residual to the treatment residual as a function of covariates. The causal forest is the leading instance of this extension. The methods lie beyond the scope of this chapter, but the underlying principle — orthogonalize to protect the causal parameter, cross-fit to keep predictions honest — is the one developed above, and it is the durable lesson of this material.

chunks.heading: Instructor's take (Heterogeneous effects)
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.13 Instructor's take (Heterogeneous effects)
chunks.body: ★ Sharma's Take

chunks.heading: Instructor's take (Heterogeneous effects)
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.13 Instructor's take (Heterogeneous effects)
chunks.body: The intended use of an estimate should determine the method chosen to produce it, and the two purposes treated in this chapter call for opposite priorities. When the object is to rank or flag units — to identify which applicants are likely to default or which patients require monitoring — the relevant criterion is out-of-sample predictive accuracy, and the interpretability of individual coefficients is irrelevant; the flexible, regularized methods of Sections 17.2–17.5 are appropriate, and they should be evaluated by cross-validation alone. When the object is to intervene — to determine the consequence of altering a policy, a price, or a rule — predictive accuracy is no longer the operative criterion, and a coefficient extracted from an accurate predictive model is, as Section 17.6 demonstrates, generally a biased estimate of the causal quantity required. The recurring and costly error in applied work is the use of a predictive model's coefficients to guide intervention.

chunks.heading: Instructor's take (Heterogeneous effects)
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.13 Instructor's take (Heterogeneous effects)
chunks.body: Double machine learning is significant precisely because it supplies a principled means of retaining the flexibility of predictive methods while restoring the discipline of causal estimation; it should be understood not as a prediction method but as an estimator of a causal parameter that happens to use prediction methods as components.

chunks.heading: Chapter summary (Heterogeneous effects)
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.13 Chapter summary (Heterogeneous effects)
chunks.body:
Chapter Summary
The expected prediction error of an estimator decomposes into irreducible noise, squared bias, and variance; flexibility lowers bias and raises variance, and the optimal flexibility minimizes their sum (Section 17.2).
Cross-validation estimates out-of-sample error by evaluating predictions on held-out folds, and is used to select tuning parameters (Section 17.3).
Ridge regression adds an \(\ell_2\) penalty and shrinks coefficients proportionally toward zero without setting any to zero; the lasso adds an \(\ell_1\) penalty and, through soft-thresholding, sets some coefficients exactly to zero, performing variable selection (Section 17.4).
Penalized coefficients are biased toward zero and are not valid estimates of causal effects; moreover, lasso selection by outcome prediction may discard confounders, reintroducing omitted-variable bias (Section 17.6).
In the partially linear model, the causal parameter is identified as the coefficient of a regression of the outcome residual on the treatment residual, with both residualized against the controls (Section 17.7).

chunks.heading: Chapter summary (Heterogeneous effects)
chunks.title: Chapter 17, Penalized Regression and Double Machine Learning — 17.13 Chapter summary (Heterogeneous effects)
chunks.body:
Double machine learning estimates the nuisance functions by flexible methods and exploits Neyman orthogonality, which renders the estimator insensitive to first-order nuisance error; cross-fitting removes the bias from in-sample nuisance estimation. Valid \(\sqrt{n}\) inference on the causal parameter follows (Sections 17.8–17.9).
With panel data, the within transformation removes unobserved time-invariant unit effects while the machine-learning nuisances handle observed time-varying confounders; cross-fitting is then performed over whole units and standard errors are clustered by unit (Section 17.11).
The method relaxes the functional-form requirement of control-variable regression but retains the unconfoundedness requirement; identification with unobserved confounders still requires the designs of Chapters 9, 12, and 13 (Section 17.12).
